A Mob Thwarted.
WILLIE TENN
ANGEL
A Mob Thwarted.
NASHVILLE, TENN., August 17.—A mob composed of co'ored men was organized at Tullahoma last night to lynch Albert Smartt, the negro who killed Samuel Strabler, his brother-in-law, and proceeded to the building in which the preiminary examination of the prisoner was being conducted.
Justice Thomas ordered Smartt to be remanded to jail without bond, and an officer, learning of the presence of the mob, induced the angry negroes to believe that Sm rit would be kept in town and guarded only by two men.
Watching his opportunity, the officer quietly slipped the prisoner out and leaping into a buggy drove hastily to Manchester, where Smartt was lodged in jail. The members of the mob were indignant over the removal of Smartt, and it is possible that an attendant may be mad to lynch him at Manchester, as the feeling against him is very strong.

INDIANA AND ILLINOIS NEWS A Falling Derrick Instantly Kills Two Men at Work in a Stone Quarry. Two Men Lodged in Jail, Charged with Being the Xenia Murderers—Mrs. Doran Attempts to Burn the Columbus Jail. INDIANA.
Two Men Instantly Killed by a Falling Derrick in a Stone Quarry. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

BLOOMINGTON, Oct. 23.—A terrible accident is reported from Ellettsville, eight miles north of Bloomington, in which George Aiken and George Johnston were instantly killed. Both men were working in the large stone quarry of Matthews Bros. About 8 o'clock the derrick was being operated by the engineer, when, without notice, the boom was taken up so high that the cap came off, allowing an arm, sixty feet in length, to fall to the ground. Both men were directly under the falling timber, and it killed them instantly. Johnston was thirty years of age, and Aiken twenty-two. The remains of Aiken were taken to Stinesville, where his parents live.

Three Men Arrested for the Xenia Murder. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MARION, Oct. 22.—The murderers of Andrew J. Morgan, of Xenia, who was shot and killed on Sunday morning, are believed to be in the hands of the officers. Yesterday three men, two of them answering the description of Morgan's slayers, attracted the attention of the officers of Red key, thirty miles east of this city, on the Chicago, St. Louis & Pittsburg railway. These men were pursued, and after a nearly all-night chase were captured this morning in Delaware county, and taken to Muncie, from which place they were taken to Peru this evening to await trial. On them was found several articles taken from a store at Bunker Hill, fifteen miles from Xenia the night before the murder. The most plausible theory connects three men with the Xenia tragedy, and the men in custody are believed to be the perpetrators of that crime. The names of the men in custody are John Carroll, Frank Rowe and John Ryan. The two first named were formerly residents of Muncie.

Mrs. Doran's Attempt at Self-Destruction. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

COLUMBUS, Oct. 23.—Mrs. Mary Doran, the Indianapolis woman confined in the county jail here, awaiting trial for the murder of her husband, made a desperate attempt at self-cremation last night. She fired a large pile of rubbish in one of the ventilators, which opened into her cell. The highly inflammable material made a great blaze, but the prompt arrival of the fire department saved the structure. Mrs. Doran appears to greatly regret the failure of her plan and threatens suicide by some other method.

Minor Notes.

Jack Coombs has been bound over to the Montgomery Circuit Court on the charge of assault and battery with intent to kill a man named Gray, last Saturday. Gray was severely cut on the shoulder and arm.

Mrs. Stryker, wife of Charles W. Stryker, expostmaster of Rockville and chairman of the Republican central committee, died very suddenly, yesterday. She was attacked with a fit of coughing and before a physician could be summoned was dead.

The statement in a Democratic paper that Mr. Remmel, of Winchester, had declined to make good an offer to wager $500 on the success of Harrison is untrue. The Journal's Winchester correspondent reports that Mr. R. has deposited a $25 forfeit, and is prepared to put up the $500 whenever it is covered by some Democrat's corresponding sum.

ILLINOIS.

A Colored Man Sent to the Penitentiary for Three Years for Assault with Intent.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

BLOOMINGTON, Oct. 23.—Frank Shelby, a colored man who has been on trial for several days for a deadly assault on Charles Poulton, was sentenced, to-night, by the jury, to three years in the penitentiary. Poulton is a street-car driver, and one dark night last May, about 10 o'clock, at a lonely spot at the end of the line, was assaulted by two colored men, who attempted to take his cash box. He resisted heroically and was beaten almost to death with a shoe-hammer, but clung to his box and took it to headquarters with its contents. For several months he lingered at the point of death.

Leg Crushed by the Cars.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MATTOON, Oct. 23.—Conductor Grant Courtney, whose home is in Indianapolis, was knocked from the side of the car to which he was clinging as his train was moving through Charleston, this morning, by the target gates at the crossing, and falling with his left leg on the track it was crushed. He was brought to this city and the leg amputated above the knee.

On Trial for Killing a Tramp.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

DANVILLE, Oct. 23.—The trial of Elisha Allen, the deputized constable who shot and killed a tramp in this city on the 7th of last August, is now in progress. The court-house is crowded and a great deal of interest is manifested.

Brief Mention.

Mr. R. M. Brown, father of T. Eddy Brown, of Chicago, secretary for Illinois of the Y. M. C. A., died at Normal Monday, aged sixty-five years.

The board of commissioners of Peoria, has sued for material use in the construction of the bridge over the Illinois river. The amount involved is $5,000.

Henry, Ben and John Wilkin are under arrest at Breeze, for assaulting and stabbing John Swartz in a saloon row on Sunday. The Wilkins narrowly escaped being lynched.

The public schools of Ramsay have been closed on account of a throat trouble resembling diphtheria which prevails among the children. One little boy, Georgie Baker, died on Monday, and others are sick with the disease.

The boiler of the Fairfield woolen-mills exploded on Monday, doing damage to the building to the amount of $1,000. The boiler, which is a large one, was thrown 100 feet, tearing down the east wall in its flight. A number of employes standing near miraculously escaped serious injury.

An interesting relic has just been brought out at Duquoin in the shape of a warranty deed, bearing the date of June 27, 1821. The deed was executed for a piece of land, the stipulated price being $200, $100 of which is paid in hand—one-half in whisky and the other in merchandise. The remaining $100 was secured by note, to be paid twelve months from date, half in land-office money and the balance in whisky. The mortgagee was fully determined to have his share of whisky, and even rated it higher than "land-office money."

THE VALLEJO EXPLOSION. Progress of the Investigation By the Coroner's Jury. VALLEJO, Cal., Feb. 28.—Many witnesses were examined by the coroner's jury to-day regarding the ferry boat explosion. The general testimony showed that while the Julia was not a new boat, she was regarded as a safe one. It was stated that the boiler guage showed 105 pounds. The boat was allowed to carry 110 pounds. The explosion could not have occurred from the petroleum tank or pipes, as they were all found in good condition by divers to-day. The number of passengers on the boat is estimated all the way from thirty to sixty. Fifteen bodies have been recovered. The hull of the boat will be raised to-morrow if possible, when the full extent of the fatalities will be definitely learned. Conkling Declines.
Conkling Declines.

PITTSBURG, Feb. 28.—The secretary of the Conkling club of this city, has received a letter from Roscoe Conkling in reply to one addressed to him recently, proposing his name for the presidential nomination. Mr. Conkling says in substance he is not an aspirant for political preferment, but the honor done him is gratifying. Without reference to any candidates, it will be a great satisfaction if the club's bearing his name can "contribute in any way to reinstate the organization whose wisdom and earnestness proved so useful during the most tragic and trying period of our history. To see that party again triumphant and united is inspiration enough for all republicans."

The Gould-Sage Case.

New York, Feb. 28.—The foreman of the

The Gould-Sage Case.

New York, Feb. 28.—The foreman of the grand jury considering the Gould-Sage case, to-day asked Judge Cowing in regard to the statute of limitations as applying to section 541 of the penal code: "Does the statute begin to run in relation to withholding from the date the crime was committed or from the discovery of the fact!"

The judge replied in substance: "So far as section 541 is concerned, the crime against that section is committed when fraudulent misappropriation occurs. In my judgment the statute of limitations commences to run from that date. You have to determine whether the fraudulent misappropriation actually took place within five years. There is one exception to this rule. If at the time of its occurrence the trustee who is charged with it was residing out of the jurisdiction of the court, then the statute does not begin to run till he comes within jurisdiction."

The jury will report definitely on the case to-morrow, but it is generally considered a foregone conclusion that no indictment will be handed in.

Two Murderers Lynched.

Cairo, Ill., Feb. 28.—Last night at Clinton, Ky., Sam Price, a white man, who killed the sheriff, and Bill Reams, a colored chicken thief, who shot a farmer named Jackson, were taken out of the jail by masked men and hanged.
bill-reams-clinton-1888-02-27.A10:
HANGED HIM TWICE.
Sam Price Was Not Dead When Cut Down and the Mob Swung him Up Again.
the mob had completed their mission of hanging the two murderers to a tree and had quietly dispersed, the citizens began gathering about. Finally the County Judge approached the body of Samuel Price, and with his his knife cut the rope, the body falling in a heap to the ground. A few moments later the astonished crowd saw the breast of the supposed dead man heave, and heard a faint sigh escape from his lips. His eyes suddenly opened with a broad broad stare, and he raised himself to a sitting position, and talked faintly to those about him. While thus conscious, he was asked to pray that his life might be spared, but he quickly replied:

"I never prayed in my life, and don't know how. It's no matter. They'll hang me any how, some day."

At this point the mob, that had obtained word of the strange resuscitation, returned and finished the job by hoisting Price again to the limb of the tree, two men resting their weight on his legs until his neck was broken. The men had ropes enough to hang the several persons confined in the jail implicated in the Winter tragedy, and did go so far implicated as to break into the cell of the mother of Sam Price, and had had slipped a rope about her neck. Then a cry was raised that she was innocent, and she was released. The others were overlooked in the excitement, and were saved.

Jackson, in Clinton, and when ordered out of the yard by Jackson he drew a revolver and fired two shots, both taking effect in the breast, causing Jackson's death a few hours later.
bill-reams-clinton-1888-02-27.A15:
LYNCH LAW AT CLINTON. TWO MURDERERS HUNG BY THE CITIZENS.
Clinton has again been the scene of the uprising of outraged citizens, sometimes justly called mobs, but in this instance the provocation was so great, and the patience, sense of justice and self-protection so taxed, that there appears, from the information before us, ample justification before right-minded public sentiment, for the citizens taking the law into their own hands and punishing the murderers.

On Saturday night, Bill Reams, said to be a notoriously bad and dangerous negro, was caught in the act of stealing chickens from the coop of Mr. Jackson, who kept a restaurant, and being halted and recognized by Jackson, Reams commenced shooting, and wounded Jackson to the extent that he died the next day. The next day Reams was arrested, taken before Jackson, who clearly and emphatically identified him as the murderer, and the identification, we are told, was corroborated by several other positive circumstances, leaving no possible doubt as to his guilt.

This murder, following so closely upon the recent murder of sheriff Winters, who was one of the truest and noblest of men, and who was murdered because he was the representative of law and order, aroused the public feeling as to the insecurity of life and the necessity of teaching outlaws and murderers a summary and terrible lesson. As a result, a body of citizens, said to be 40 or 50 in number, Monday night, visited the county jail, demanded the keys, but were refused, but finally pernaded the jailer to surrender to overwhelming force, the two prisoners, Sam Price, the murderer of Sheriff Winters, and Bill Reams, the murderer of Jackson, taken
omers, Sam Price, the murderer of Sheriff Winters, and Bill Reams, the murderer of Jackson, taken from the jail, and hung, until they were dead, dead, dead.

It is not proper to justify mob law and it is a pity that it is ever to be even tolerated in a correct minded public sentiment; but so long as good men are so frequently murdered and hangings and punishments so infrequent, so long will lynch law be accepted and tolerated as a part of the unwritten law of the land. The COURIER does not assume to criticise the law's delay, the sentimentality of juries, the indifference of citizens in helping and supporting arresting officers, the tardiness of such officers, or the technical and special pleadings of lawyers, because in their spheres, each have reasonable and justifying arguments, but it looks only at the fact that murders and killings are of frequent occurrence in all these counties, and that arrests and punishments are not frequent. The COURIER's honest opinion is that, the great cause for this increase of crime and the few arrests and punishments rests mainly upon the indifferent public sentiment in regard to such crimes, that is to say, that the bulk and body of our people are so thoroughly absorbed and engaged in their own private interests and affairs that they are neglectful of a proper active sense of the duty that they owe as citizens to the enforcement of the laws, and hence the arrest of criminals is left to a few officers, unsupported. In the old time, when a citizen was killed, whole neighborhoods quit their private business and rallied to the officers, until the violator of law was arrested and held for trial. The same public sentiment upheld and
cere, until the violator of law was arrested and held for trial. The same public sentiment upheld and supported courts and juries at the trial and demanded punishment of the guilty. This law-enforcing sentiment has fallen into remarkable disuse, and hence mob law when a good people realize the consciousness of their own long neglected duty through the murder of some specially honored and good citizen like Sheriff Winters was.

The Atlanta Constitution in speaking of the tide of emigration being turned Southward says: "Why not come South? Both man and nature in this section are kind to new-comers. The lands are productive and cheap. The settlers who come among us will not have to dwell in a wilderness. They will find themselves surrounded by all the comforts of civilization and they will soon learn to forget the very name of blizzard. Why remain to freeze, and starve, and struggle on the bleak prairies of the Northwest when the garden spot of the world is waiting for the people to take possession of it and enjoy it!

The Nesbitt pistol law, which has passed the Lower House of the State Legislature, imposes a fine of $100 for carrying concealed a deadly weapon, and $100 for selling pistols, &c. This is a foolish law, in as much as it will only force the sale of pistols into other States. If the law could be made universal it might do, but with other States making no similar penalties, it will not lessen pistol purchases, but only drive the trade elsewhere. The Senate ought to kill the bill.

The usual spring kick about the wheat crop is beginning to be heard among the farmers. Was there ever a season when the honest husbandman did not proclaim that there was certain to be a famine before the year was done? Last pear the same complaint was heard about the wheat and yet the Purchase never harvested a bigger crop.—[Paducah News.

There is not so much noise made just now, says the Covington Commonwealth, about the wonderful Wichita boom, nor the bouncing Birmingham boom, nor the commanding boom of Chattanooga. Meanwhile Kentucky is progressing on the safe and solid plan. She has all things needful within her own borders, and is steadily developing her resources.

DOUBLE LYNCHING.
Two Assassins Swing Off Quietly at Clinton, Ky.
CARROT, Feb. 28 - At two o'clock this
morning a morning of fifty men broke into the jail at Clinton, Ky., and took therefrom Sam Price, white, and Wm. Remus, black, and swung them over the limb of a convenient sycamore tree. The bodies were permitted to hang until after daylight, when they were cut down by the authorities and buried. The mob is said to have been composed of men residing in Hickman County, many of them not even wearing masks of any kind. Most of the avengers, however, wore handkerchiefs over their faces, but as is usual with organizations of that character were silent and acted under a leader who appeared to know his business. About three months ago Sam Price was arrested near his home in Clinton by Sheriff Henry Winter for some violation of the law. Acting for permission to enter his mother's house for a change of clothing, he suddenly reappeared at the door with a rifle and shot the Sheriff dead in his tracks. This deed was applauded by the mother, who was on the spot, and who undoubtedly was largely instrumental in causing the murder. After a long chase and a reward of $1,200 had been offered the fugitive was captured at Dresden, Teen., and brought to Kentucky a few weeks ago, being kept in the Dresden jail some time on account of lynching if he were confined at Clinton. Two brothers-in-law of Price and his mother, all more or less implicated in the murder, were in the jail, but were unmolested. Remus on Saturday night was detected in stealing chickens from the yard of J. P. Jackson, residing in the city limits of Clinton, and when ordered off the yard he drew a revolver and fired two shots, both taking effect in the breast of Jackson, causing his death a few hours later. The excitement was intense when the passenger train passed Clinton this morning. It is claimed that some of the mob was recognized, but it is not probable any effort will be made to arrest the offenders. It was a clanish party which organized for an expedition of that character, and it is unlikely they will ever expose one another.

WEIGHTED DOWN.
Two Men Swing On To the Legs of a Hanging Negro, To Help Break His Neck.

Cario, Ill., March 1.—Captain John Cox, of Ballard county, Ky., reports a remarkable incident in connection with the double lynching at Clinton, on Tuesday night. Price, one of the men, was not dead when the mob left the scene, but, after being cut down by the county judge became conscious and talked to those around him. Word was sent to the leaders of the mob, who returned about daylight, and completed the job by again hanging the victim—two men at the same time hanging upon each of his feet and finally breaking his neck. The negro died almost immediately after being hauled up to the limb. The cell of the mother of Price was also broken open, and, for a time, she, also, was threatened with the rope, but better counsel prevailed, and the attempt was abandoned.

THE CRIME AND THE LYNCHING.

CLINTON, Ky., March 1.—On Saturday night Mr. J. M. Jackson, a worthy citizen of this village, was shot and fatally wounded by a negro who was prowling about his house for the purpose of robbery. Jackson lived until 6 o'clock Sunday morning, when he died in great agony, but not before he was able to positively identify his murderer as one Remus, a worthless negro. Naturally the atrocious deed created the most intense excitement in the usually quiet little place, and threats of lynching were rife Sunday as soon as Jackson's death was announced. A strong guard was placed about the jail that night, but no demonstration seems to have been made. Monday night the guard at the jail was increased. Between 12 and 1 o'clock, however, the building was surrounded by a mob of 70 or 80 men, who demanded the keys. These were refused by the jailer and the County Judge, County Attorney and Sheriff expostulated with the crowd and endeavored to persuade them to let the law takes its course. Their efforts were in vain. The mob was composed of men determined to execute their revenge at all hazards, and the officers were sternly told that if they did not give up the keys the jail would be blown up. The guards inside refused to fire on the mob, evidently being more or less in sympathy with it, and
that if they did not give up the keys the jail would be blown up. The guards inside refused to fire on the mob, evidently being more or less in sympathy with it, and there seems to have been nothing left for the officers to do but surrender, which they did. In the jail with the negro was Sam Price, who murdered Sheriff Winters, of Hickman county, a few weeks ago. Probably desiring to make a clean job of it, the mob took him along as well as Remus. Carrying them to a brickyard in the eastern

part of the town the two murderers were strung up to a tree and left hanging there until the next morning, when they were cut down by the authorities, and Price's body was turned over to his relatives. The remains of the negro were buried.

HE JUMPED DOWN.

A Texas Criminal Assists a Band of Lynchers in His Own Execution.

CARTHAGE, TEXAS., March 1.—At an early hour yesterday morning four hundred men forced open the jail, took out Tom Forsythe, who yesterday confessed that he had murdered County Treasurer Hill by cutting off his head, and that he had robbed him of $6,000. He was taken to a tree in the jail yard, his hands were tied behind him, and a rope was placed around his neck. A ladder was put up and Forsythe ascended, requesting as he did so, that he be allowed to execute himself. A word of command was given by the leader of the lynchers and Forsythe jumped, from the limb on which he stood. His neck was broken and death occurred instantaneously. The lynchers took the body into the court house, and laid it on the blood spots of the murdered man in the Treasurer's office.

A BLOODY TRAGEDY.
A PARTY OF GENTLEMEN ON THE WAY TO CHURCH ASSAULTED BY NEGROES. THREE SHOT—A LYNCHING.
Jackson, Miss., Aug. 13—Utica, a town on the Little J road, thirty miles from here, in this county, was the scene of a terrible tragedy followed by a lynching. From parties who arrived here your correspondent learns the particulars as follows:

Mr. E. B. Robertson, accompanied by a young lady; were walking to church, when they encountered on the sidewalk a crowd of six negroes, who instead of yielding the sidewalk to the lady, pushed her in a very rude manner. Robertson remonstrated, and was cursed by the negroes, who said they would 'get him' on his return after church.

Robertson was joined by three or four of his friends and was telling them of the conduct of the negroes when his party was rushed upon by the six negroes who began firing on the whites who, being unarmed were unable to return the fire. Three of the whites were shot. Dr. L. W. Holliday was shot through the head; his brains oozing out he is bound to die.

Armand, White, received a serious wound through the thigh, and Frank Wallice was slightly shot in the arm. All the negroes escaped for the time, except Bob Broom. the ring leader, who it is known fired the shot through Holliday's brain. He was caught around the body by Mr. Robertson until assistance came. He was taken out of the calaboose by a hundred or more men and hung to a tree near the cemetery on the edge of the town. A rope was thrown over a limb and he was hauled up until choaked to death.

In the meantime two other negroes, Ike Broom, brother of the negro hung, and Sam Harris were captured and carried to the Raymond jail. It is not certain if either of them did any of the shooting, though they were of the party who made the murderous attack. The three other negroes, at least two of whom, Vice Rainy and Curtis Shortney, brothers, engaged in the shooting, are still at large, but are being hotly pursued by the friends of the murdered Holliday and if caught there may be more lynching.

There is great excitement in the whole southern end of the county. The whites were not armed and did not fire a shot. The cooler heads of the community tried to prevent the lynching of Broom, but the indignation at the foul and unprovoked murder of Holliday, and the shooting of White Wallace, was so great that it was impossible to restrain the mob.

Holliday at Utica about three weeks ago, was this morning taken from an east-bound freight train at a point six miles west of Utica and, it is supposed, lynched. Lawyer Townsend Forfeits $1,000. Lawyer John D. Townsend, who offered on Tuesday night to bet $10,000 to $8,000 with Editor Phillips of Texas Siftings that Cleveland would be elected, sent $1,000 forfeit to Mr. Phillips last night. DISCUSSING THE LETTERS. NOBODY MUCH BRIGHTENED BY GEN. HARRISON'S ACCEPTANCE.
Recognized, but Not So with any Strong Features—Campaign Meetings.

The discussion of the Harrison letter occupied most of the attention at the different political headquarters yesterday. At the Democratic bureau in West Twenty-ninth street it was viewed with satisfaction, as not dangerous. Comptroller Theodore W. Myers said: "Mr. Harrison's position is that the surplus shall be expended, not for the benefit of those from whose pockets it has been taken, but for their problematical posterity; for he would meet the request of a long-suffering, heavily over-taxed people for a return of their money by a denial, and an offer instead of the privilege of paying a heavy premium to be allowed to forestall a debt, in no wise pressing, which should properly be discharged by future generations. I fail to see either merit or justice in such methods."

The Hon. Howard Ellis of New Jersey said: "Harrison's letter undertakes most improperly to show what the Democratic policy is and misrepresents the Mills bill, and takes the position of a scold who puts an opponent in a false position, and then lectures him about it."

Col. M. V. Gannon of Omaha made similar criticisms and then talked about the Maine election, saying that Mr. Lewellyn Howard, one of the largest owners of stumpage lands in the State, had told him that in his locality there were about 500 more Democrats than Republicans, but that the voting would show about the same figures the other way, owing to the use of soap by the Republicans.

Thomas C. F. Crain said: "The most noticeable thing about it is the brief and incomplete way in which he disposes of the tariff question, suggesting Democratic argument without in any manner refuting it. It seems to me that this part of the letter is weak, even from a protection standpoint, consisting as it really does in the mere assertion, repeated in many forms, that protection is advantageous. The position taken that the Mills bill is unwise because of its tendency rather than because of what it accomplishes, while no better scheme for a revision of the tariff is indicated, seems to me to show a lack of definite knowledge as to what tariff revision should be. The proposition that the surplus now in the Treasury should be used in the purchase of bonds is probably the most distinctively unwise suggestion of the letter. The fact that these bonds are now held at a large premium precludes their purchase on any basis equitable to the people. The other parts of the letter are mainly noticeable by their studied effort to please everybody about everything. As a whole, I think it lacks the comprehensive grasp, individuality, and statesmanship of Cleveland's letter."

At the Republican headquarters the tone of comment is indicated by what Secretary J. Sloat Fassett said: "The letter has the ring of true Americanism. It meets with clearness and dignity the important subject of international relations, as well as boldly declares the attitude of Gen. Harrison on civil service and all other questions. But there is no bluster, no turgid rhetoric, no attempts to becloud the issues. In these respects it is in refreshing contrast to the manifesto of the present incumbent, who calls himself 'We.'"

Danglinfi From a Limb.

RALEIGH, N. C., September 14.—[Special.]—News was received here tonight of another lynching, which is the thirtieth this year. It occurred at Whiteville, Columbus county. Night before last a body of masked men, a hundred or more, entered the jail and demanded the keys from the jail. With a score of revolvers pointed at him, he surrendered the keys and the lynchers went to the cell where Sherman Farrior, colored, was confined for an outrage committed on an aged white woman, took him and departed. Yesterday, suspended to the limb of a large oak, about one mile from the jail, the body of Sherman Farrior was found with a placard pinned on his breast bearing the words:

We protect the virtue of our women. Beware!

Farrior was a man of bad character, and had repeatedly been engaged in robbery. The crime that cost him his life was outraging Mrs. E. A. Sosser on the 29th of August. He was given a preliminary hearing before two magistrates last Monday, and was committed to jail to await trial. The evidence against him was conclusive.

A Life For a Life.

SAN FRANCISCO, September 14.—Alex Goldensen, who shot and killed a fourteen-year-old girl named Mamie Kelly, on November 10, 1886, was hanged in the county jail a few minutes after noon to-day.

No hanging since the days of the vigilance committee has excited greater interest on the Pacific coast. His crime came near causing riot, and two ineffectual attempts were made to lynch him by assaulting the city jail, but in each instance, serious action was prevented by the police. Notwithstanding popular feeling against the young murderer, the legal fight in his behalf was prolonged for nearly two years.

The murderer's last night was passed in drinking, card playing and blasphemy. The only known cause for the shooting of his victim was her refusal to accept his attentions. Goldensen was eighteen years old when he committed the murder, and was a person of vicious habits.

A Negro Hung.

COLUMBIA, S. C., September 14.—Dock Dorgan, a negro boy nineteen years old, was hanged in jail at Bennettsville today, for the murder, in April last, of William E. Coxe, Jr., a white boy of about the same age. He met his death calmly, and declared that he was going to heaven. He died without a struggle, his neck being broken.

He Will Surely Hang.

SAN FRANCISCO, Cal., September 11.—[Special.]—Young Alex. Jack Goldenson, the hoodlum murderer of little Mamie Kelly, will hang without fail on Friday next. Goldenson's lawyers obtained an order from Probate Judge Coffey for a jury to decide on Wednesday whether the condemned youth is insane or not. Yesterday the lawyers interviewed Governor Waterman at Santa Cruz and begged for one month's respite. Waterman became indignant, as he has been much annoyed by Goldenson's mother, and said:

“fI would hang him tomorrow if I could, to end the matter. He is nothing but a licentious murderer and killed the poor girl because her voluptious appearance awakened a libertine's desires in him, and because she would not submit to his unholy wishes.”

In conversation with a reporter, Governor Watermon said: “I have investigated this case thoroughly. I went to the school Mamie Kelly attended and found her the pet of teachers and scholars. I have learned that $25,000 has been offered to any lawyer who would get me to change Goldenson's sentence to imprisonment for life. Attorneys have threatened me by saying the Jewish vote would go against me. I don't care if all the Jewish vote or any other vote goes against me. I intend to do just what is right and legal, but I know the threats to be a lie, as many leading Hebrews have come to me and asked to have Goldenson hanged as soon as possible. Even if the people of California should come two by two up to Sacramento and kneel down and beg me, I would not do anything as it is an unpardonable offense, and he shall be hanged.'

The condemned youth still preserves his bravado and ridicules the attempt of his mother and lawyers to secure a reprieve on the insanity plea. The sheriff, backed by the governor's refusal to interfere, will not permit Goldenson to be taken to court on Wednesday. When the prisoner leaves the condemned cell it will be to go to the gallows. The jailers believe Goldenson will weaken, in spite of his boast that he wants the privilege of placing the noose around his own neck.

Mormons In Roanoke County.
Rumors of the progress made on Back Creek, in this county, by the Missionaries of the Mormon church, reach us every few days, causing considerable uneasiness and indignation. It is said that about forty people have professed conversion to the Mormon faith, and announce their intention to emigrate to Utah in the early spring. event-1888-03.A3:
ROANOKE MORMONS
THE LATTER-DAY SAINTS IN THE COUNTY.
Work of the Elders in Back-Creek Community—Many Converts—Threats of Expulsion.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]

ROANOKE, VA., March 9, 1888.

An account of the hold the pernicious so-called religious sect known as the Latter-Day Saints has obtained on quite a number of the people of Roanoke county will be interesting to your thousands of readers. Some of your readers who understand the moral putridity of Mormonism will be at a loss to understand how a so-called religion, universally condemned, could fasten itself upon the intelligence, faith, and charity of a community. But it has obtained lodgment in the community known as Back Creek, in this county, and numbers among its supporters some very intelligent people. The majority of the membership are of that class of people who depend upon the superior intelligence of others for guidance in nearly all matters, especially those affecting their spiritual wellbeing, hence it is that two Mormon elders, assisted by the most intelligent, influential, and the wealthiest citizen of the community, who early espoused the Mormon faith, have been able to induce some twenty-five or thirty men and women to embrace their teachings and over half that number to receive their ordinance of baptism. These emissaries have been operating in that section for several months, quietly but persistently, as the result of their efforts will show. They followed a Mormon bishop who suddenly appeared there several months ago and preached one or more sermons. He is said to have been very intellectual, thoroughly posted on the scriptures, and very eloquent. The people being unused to pulpit oratory of a high order were easily captivated by him, and he left them in a reflective mood very auspicious for the early appearance and labors of the elders. A number of the converts contemplate emigrating to Utah in the spring, while one will settle on the Mormon reservation in Colorado.

The engrafting of this cancerous growth on the civilization of our county has aroused deep indignation of their elders when interrogated on this article of the Mormon faith intensifies the bitterness of the masses of the people and strengthens their determination to effect the expulsion of the emissaries at the earliest practical moment. The feeling of indignation is, perhaps, partly due to the fact that among the converts are several young, beautiful, and intelligent ladies, whom the elders, perhaps, design to marry when they get them safely within the Territory.

Up to this writing only one minister of the Gospel has invaded the Mormon stronghold and contended with them for the supremacy of the truth over error. It was reported that he routed them in a debate, but the fact that he did not return again indicates that he either failed to do so or regarded the people there as being so firmly joined to their idols that little could be accomplished in the way of their divorcement.

MOREHEAD, KY., March 12.—The report that Hiram Pigman, who is reputed to have been the slayer of Craig Tolliver, had died of alcoholism here last Friday, proves to be incorrect. Although apparently dead, and pronounced so by his physician, Pigman rallied and is still alive.

An old negro of Atlanta applied to the police the other day for protection against an old woman who was trying to conjure him. He said he found nailed over his door a red flannel bag, tied with white strings, and that he knew it was a "conjure bag," and that his life was in danger. The officer opened the little red bag, and it contained a bit of horse-shoe, a few grains of gunpowder and some snake root. "I knowed it, I knowed it," the old colored man exclaimed as he looked at the bag, his eyes stretching until they almost popped out of their sockets, moving backward from the bag as he said: "Dat ole woman has conjured me, and I'll die shoor." St. Joseph, Mo., March 21.—[Special Telegram to the Bee.]—William M. Stigall, postmaster at Stewartsville, Mo., was arrested to-day and brought before the United States commissioner at this place on a charge of taking and opening letters addressed to others, and was bound over in the sum of $1,000 to the April court. Stigall has an inordinate curiosity for prying into other people's business and for the past six weeks more than half the letters addressed to the different business men in the town have been opened. LONDON, March 21.—In the commons today Parnell moved a second reading of his arrears-of-rent bill. The Irish Party Downed.

[Copyright 1888 by James Gordon Bennett.]

LONDON, March 21.—[New York Herald Cable—Special to the BEE]—Parnell, on whose pale face a strong light was thrown through the opposite windows, spoke this afternoon on his arrears bill in his usual deliberate and collected manner. His bill proposed that Irish courts have power to reduce certain arrears upon all holdings of less than £100 a year and to enable the tenant to pay the balance by installment. He protested against the scheme suggested last year by the government, compelling tenants seeking relief from arrears to place their debts in the hands of the court so that creditors should stand on the same footing. He argued strongly that rent was not like a debt due to a shopkeeper, because the latter's claim was not exorbitant and because he had not used his claim as a means of turning the poor man out of his house. Upon this issue the whole of the controversy subsequently turned. Parnell was brief but impressive. He stated frankly that even if the government should accept his bill it would not in any degree lessen the demand of the Irish people for a parliament of their own.

"How is it," he asked, "that you cannot settle the Irish land question? It is because you know nothing about it. You go to Birmingham for your information about Ireland instead of to Cork or to South Tyrone."

This hit at Chamberlain was received with cheers, while T. W. Russell swallowed with delight this sugared morsel thrown to him. Russell has been sent all over the country by the tories and unionists as advocates of their cause. He now displays many signs of a tendency to flop over. Parnell's allusion to him seemed almost like the announcement of Russell's approaching reception into the nationalist fold. Moreover, when Parnell made the allusion to the impossibility of continuing to govern Ireland from Westminister, Russell joined in the hearty cheers of the regular Parnellites.

Presently Chamberlain stood up and began his remarks by quoting the Americanism "catch on," but the phrase is not so much of a novelty as Joe seems to fancy. I hope he has brought back some fresher sayings and some livelier jokes than this. He made, as he always does, a shrewd, telling speech, contending that it was a gross injustice to wipe off the arrears rent and leave all the other arrears outstanding. He had a lively passage-at arms with Dillon, and it cannot be said that Dillon got the best of it. Chamberlain is an exceedingly prickly, awkward customer to lay hold of. Nothing seems to shake his possession or disturb the clear exercise of his faculties. He succeeded this afternoon in impressing even his enemies with his acuteness and ability.

Dillon delivered one of his fiery harangues and stirring enough to move the most sluggish heart. Irish eloquence has no more brilliant a representative in the house.

The vote was first taken on Parnell's main bill, which was rejected by 828 to 243, a majority of 85, only 99 votes short of a full house. The amendment offering to treat all creditors alike was then adopted, but thus the whole question is left where it was last year. A tenant must pay all his debts or none. We shall, however, hear much more of the arrears difficulty.

A MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT.

SUCICHED IN CHURCH. Eugene Zenzius Drinks Carbolic Acid During a Prayer Meeting. INDIANAPOLIS, July 7.—Eugene Zenzius, a
During a Prayer Meeting.
INDIANAPOLIS, July 27.—Eugene Zenzius, a a young married man of St. Paul, Minn., who has been here for some weeks with his wife, attended prayer meeting services at Meridan street church last night, and upon entering was handed a hymn book by one of the ushers and took part in the services. Suddenly leaving the room he entered a class room adjoining, and a moment later the congregation was startled by his groans. Going into the room Zenzius was found dying from the effects of carbolic acid, which he had drank from a bottle which lay by his side. He was in terrible agony, and died in a few moments. He was comparatively unknown here, and it is supposed he committed suicide on account of failure to get work.

Beatrice for Safety.
BEATRICE, Neb., July 27.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Fremont Emmons, the man charged with the murder of Bertha Schultz last night at the Exchange hotel, Pawnee City, was brought to the Gage county jail at 4 o'clock this morning for safe keeping. He was brought by Sullivan and Levendorff, deputy sheriffs, and R. A. Huntley, of Pawnee. He had deliberately stabbed the girl on account of having been rejected in marriage. She lived but twenty minutes. The citizens grew so furious over the matter that Emmons was hurried out of town to avoid being lynched. Since arriving here he seems to have forgotten all about the traced. His examination will be held to-morrow at Pawnee. He claims that he was engaged to the girl and says he bore no ill will against her.

CHICAGO, July 27.—The people of Lake View, Chicago's nearest northern suburb, were startled early this morning by a loud report in the neighborhood of No. 675 Lincoln avenue. HE LAYS IT ALL TO WHISKY.
With the Rope About His Neck He Delivers an Address on the Evils of Intemperance-Other State News.
Made Him Walk the Trestle.
PAWNEE CITY, Neb., July 31.—[Spc]
PAWNEE CITY, Neb., July 31.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.]—Fremont Emmons, the murderer of Bertha Schultz, is no more. Last night just before midnight a mob came into town from near Dubois, the home of the murdered girl, composed of a hundred men well organized and armed to the teeth. They at once surrounded the court house square, shutting off every avenue of escape should such an attempt be made, and one of them commenced the hunt for the murderer. Search revealed the fact that the jail was open. The vigilantes at once conjectured that the officers of the law were trying to spirit him away and this proved to be true. After continuing the search until about 1 o'clock, however, Emmons was found in the third story of the court house under guard of the officers. With a shout of "Here he is," the crowd started for their man. He tried to defend himself with a chair, but both Emmons and the guards were soon overpowered and the prisoner taken away from them. The mob was organized before reaching town, and every move was like clockwork. The prisoner was taken to the Chicago, Kansas & Nebraska railroad bridge in the west part of the city; a minister was called to pray for him. He was then permitted to pray for himself and to make a short speech. In his prayer he asked God to forgive him for the murder of Miss Schultz and to pardon the men who were about to take his life, if they were guilty of any crime. In his address he reviewed his life for the past two years. He said he had once been a christian but had fallen into evil ways through drink. He admonished young men to avoid it as a deadly enemy to their happiness in life. He said he had killed Miss Schultz because she had refused his love and had told things about him which were untrue. When he had finished speaking a handkerchief was placed about his face and he was told to move out on the trestle or he would be pushed. He said he preferred to jump and when he got to the edge of the track stopped at the command given and jumped. The jump was eighteen feet below and left him hanging about four feet above ground. His neck was broken instantly and he died without a struggle. The sheriff cut him down this morning and a coroner's inquest was held.

He left his watch in the hands of the minister for his relatives who live in Kansas.

The crime for which Emmons was hung was commited here last Thursday. Emmons was second cook at the Exchange hotel and Bertha Schultz was the laundry girl. He proposed to her and she rejected him. He told her he would kill her unless she married him, and sharpened his pocket knife with the avowed purpose of carrying out his threat.

In the evening about 7, as she was returning from a visit, Emmons met her in the yard adjoining the hotel. A few words passed between them, when, with a quick movement, he drew the knife and plunged it into her breast. She fell to the ground crying: "He's killed me! He's killed me! Where is my dear mother?" and died in about twenty minutes.

Emmons was at once placed under arrest by the sheriff and taken to jail. On the way there he admitted to the officer that he had sharpened his knife for the purpose of killing the girl. Miss Schultz was poor but of good reputation, while Emmons was known as a hard character. Her home was near Dubois, where she had a mother living.

Another Lynching in Nebraska.
Another Lynching in Nebraska.

Fremont Emmons, who deliberately stabbed to death Miss Elizabeth Schultz at Pawnee City, Nebraska, a few days ago, because she had refused his proposal of marriage, was taken from the authorities at Pawnee City and lynched by a mob. Emmons was second cook at the Exchange hotel and Miss Schultz was laudress at the same house. One evening Emmons met her in a neighboring yard, and stabbed her with a shoemaker's knife near the heart, killing her instantly. He was arrested and lodged in jail. Intense excitement and fear of lynching prevailed. The officers accordingly spirited him out of town and took him to the penitentiary at Lincoln. Later he was returned to Pawnee City to be given preliminary hearing. He waived examination and was recommitted. Emmons pretended to know nothing of the murder. He no doubt had determined to feign insanity. Next morning at 2 o'clock a mob from the vicinity of Dubois, the home of the murdered girl, entered Pawnee City and surrounded the court house, in which is located the jail. They found the jail open and Emmons gone. A thorough search of the court house was then made, resulting in the discovery of Emmons under guard of the officials in the third story. The guards were overpowered and the prisoner taken from them. He made no resistance. The mob took Emmons to the railroad bridge in the western part of the city, and a minister was called on to pray for him. Emmons then made a few remarks. He warned young men against the use of whisky, declaring it the cause of his ruin. He refused to say anything of the crime for which he was soon to swing. He neither admitted nor denied it. At the conclusion of his speech he prayed briefly for himself. The rope being tied around his neck and fastened to the bridge, he was commanded to jump. At the second command Emmons made the fatal leap. He fell nearly ten feet. His neck was broken. He scarcely made a struggle. The mob then quietly dispersed, leaving the body hanging to the bridge, to be claimed by his relatives. The citizens of Pawnee had no hand in the affair, although many of them were silent witnesses at a distance.

A NEBRASKA LYNCHING.
Fremont Emmons Lynched for the Murder of Bertha Schultz—His Last Words a Temperance Lecture.

PAWNEE CITY, Neb., Aug. 1.—Fremont Emmons, the murderer of Bertha Schultz, was brought here from Beatrice Monday for preliminary examination and bound over to the district court. His presence caused great excitement and about midnight a crowd began to gather, determined to lynch him. He was concealed in the third story of the court house, but the crowd soon discovered his hiding place and took him away from the officials by force. A rope was placed around his neck and he was led through the public streets to the high Chicago, Kansas & Nebraska trestle over the Burlington & Missouri track. Arriving there the citizens asked that Emmons should be identified as the party wanted. The identification was complete and he was given an opportunity to make a statement. He gave the history of his life for the past two years, in which he claimed to have been a Christian, but had lately fallen from grace. He admonished the young men to reform from the habit of using strong drink. He also stated that he had been disappointed in love and that Miss Schultz had circulated false reports in regard to him. He maintained that he knew nothing about committing the murder and asked if a minister was present and that if he would pray for him, after which he asked to pray for himself. In his prayer he asked God to forgive him for committing the murder and that God would forgive all those who were implicated in punishing him if they were guilty of any sin.

The doomed man then took several steps further out on the trestle and his arms being tied behind him and his legs free he was told to jump. The rope was fastened to a cross tie on the wagon roadway and Emmons jumped about thirteen feet and died without a struggle.

About seven o'clock last Thursday evening Emmons who was second cook at the Exchange Hotel deliberately went into the back yard where Bertha Schultz, a chambermaid, was hanging out clothes, grasped her by the right arm, pulled her half around and thrust a knife into her left breast with such force that the blow was heard by passers by quite a distance away. When he withdrew the knife, the girl screamed, took a few steps and fell dead. The murderer was arrested and later taken to Beatrice to prevent the enraged citizens lynching him. The weapon used was a shoe knife, which he had sharpened for the purpose. He had asked the girl to marry him, but she had refused. Emmons was a good looking, intelligent man, aged about twenty-five years. He was at one time a Methodist evangelist.
fremont-emmons-pawnee-city-1888-07-31.A28:
BY THE ROPE ROUTE.
Eremont Emmons, the Pawnee City Murderer. Commits Suicide.
Beatrice dispatch: Fremont Emmons, the murderer of Bertha Schultz, was lynched at Pawnee City, the scene of the crime, at an early hour this morning. The particulars are as follows: Sheriff Strunk, of Pawnee county, left Beatrice yesterday with Emmons, arriving at Pawnee City in the afternoon. The prisoner was promptly arraigned before Judge Belding and given a hearing. He plead not guilty and waived examination. The people were all the more infuriated at Emmons' effrontery in pleading not guilty to a charge so heinous and so clearly proven, and before dark groups of men could be seen gathered at different places in town. That Emmons' fate was sealed went without question. Slowly the groups of men drifted towards the court house, in the basement of which building is also the jail. The county attorney and a deputy sheriff, noticing the danger, sought to elude the hungry mob by taking the prisoner to the third floor of the building. About 1 o'clock forty masked men entered the building, and proceeding to the basement found the doors of the jail unlocked, and their bird flown. After making a careful search here they proceeded to the court room, which was in turn ransacked. Not finding him here some one cried, "Look up on the third floor." The mob broke down the door leading up stairs, and a mad rush was made for the landing, where they espied standing before them Deputy Sheriff Liebienderfor, who commanded a halt. The command was obeyed for a second only. A rush for Emmons was made, and in a few moments he was dragged down stairs, a rope was put about his neck, and he was marched off in the direction of the Rock Island depot. Near this depot is a wagon bridge over the railroad, to which they were first going to hang the victim, but owing to the protestations of citizens living near there they marched him to a railroad bridge spanning the B. & M. tracks. Here the rope was fastened to a tie and Emmons was given thirty minutes to say what he desired. He talked rationally and prayed frequently, acknowledging having committed the crime. Having finished, Emmons was told to jump from the bridge. He refused at first, but when told he would be pushed off he hesitated, then leaped into the space below. The drop was about twelve feet and his neck was apparently broken. He died without a struggle. A coroner's jury was empanelled this morning at sunrise, who cut the body down and returned a verdict of death at the hands of people unknown.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

Pawnee City dispatch: There was great excitement here yesterday among the citizens when Fremont Emmons, the villain who so brutally murdered Bertha Schultz on last Friday evening, was brought in on the Rock Island road from Beatrice, where it will be remembered he was taken by the sheriff to prevent his being lynched. On stepping from the train, with a deputy on each side, he rushed for the bus as if afraid of being foully dealt with. The news soon spread that he was in the city, and everyone was curious to see him. He was taken before Judge Belding for preliminary examination, which he waived and was placed in jail under the court house. Great excitement prevailed during the afternoon and evening, and it became almost certain that justice would be meted out in a much speedier manner than through the courts. Groups of men, engaged in earnest conversation, could be seen on every corner, but about midnight everything became quiet and all seemed well. Deputies Liebendorfer and Sullivan were arranging to take Emmons away, as an attack was feared at most any time, and had taken him out of his cell, but found they were being closely watched and were afraid to risk starting with him, so they determined to secret him in the court house, which they did. Between 2 and 3 o'clock a.m. a body of about 200 men marched steadily into the court yard, two men being detailed as guards at each corner of the building. The jail door had been left open and the mob soon found it was empty, but were determined not to be baffled in their purpose, and began a thorough search of the court house. They soon found their man, and a rope was immediately put around his neck, when the party marched to a high railroad bridge on the Rock Island road crossing the B. & M. Here Emmons was told he had but a short time to prepare to die. After saying all that he wished, a minister was called for by the crowd. One responded, when "hats off" was the order, and the minister led in prayer, being followed by the prisoner. Rising from his knees he said: "Boys, I will die like a man. I won't show the white feather. Now I am ready. Where is your leader?" With this the party started for the bridge, and the rope was finally tied to a beam, his hands pinioned, and he was told to step off. He said if it was to step off or be pushed off he chose the former. Feeling his way to the end of the bridge he sprang off with a drop of about sixteen feet, and was found dangling in the air by the coroner. The verdict of the coroner's jury is that Emmons came to his death at the hands of parties unknown. The prisoner confessed he had deliberately murdered the girl because she had refused to marry him. The sentiment of our people generally is that the law should have taken its course, but that full justice was done the wretch. At this time everything is as quiet as if nothing unusual had happened.

A MURDER MYSTERY
A MISSING MAN'S BODY FOUND.
Disclosures Concerning a Case County Crime-A Lake Gives Up Its Dead Killed by a Horse Other State News.
VANDALIA, May 4.—On the 23d of last December, John Aikens, a colored man living in Calvin township, Cass county—a township that is largely inhabited by colored people—mysteriously disappeared. He had attended a shooting match, and was very drunk when he started home. At the house of one Gus Harris he drank some more, and since then has not been seen.

Stories were told of an altercation that was heard near the shore of Shave Head Lake, in which Aikens' voice was identified and it has been generally believed that he was murdered and the body put into the lake. Color was given to this idea later, by the statements of a young colored man named Lewis Wilson, who said Harris did the killing, and that the deed was done at or near the Harris house, and that he and Harris put the body into the lake. Wilson was held by the officers to await further developments, but escaped Wednesday. He has been recaptured and is now in jail, as is also Gus Harris, who was arrested on strong suspicion some time ago.

Yesterday, however, Wilson's story was confirmed in part. When the body of Aikens was found in the lake near the house of Alexander Aikens by two fishermen. It was taken to Alexander's house and an inquest begun. There were marks of a heavy blow on the neck, one behind the ear, and the forehead was crushed.

Last Sunday when divers were at work on the lake in search of Aikens' body over 1,500 people were gathered there.

Aikens was 28 years of age and of good parentage, and was very popular in the Long Lake region and other parts of the township.

Wilson claims that Harris and himself took Aikens' body from the barn where Harris put it after the murder, and, conveying it to Shave Head Lake, they weighted it down with a bag of sand securely, as they supposed. Wilson says Harris insisted that his stepmother, who was an old flame of Aikens', had tried to kill Aikens by poison in his drink the day of the murder. This portion of Wilson's story dovetails in with other facts the officers know. Other arrests are expected, and it is believed that as many as many as five persons are directly interested and equally guilty.
gus-harris-vandalia-1888-05-04.A4:
Murdered Man's Body Found.
ELKHART, May 4.—The body of John Aikens, the young farmer whose supposed murder, a few miles south of here, in January, created a great deal of excitement, and concerning which young Wilson made a confession, has been found floating in Long lake, with neck broken and the head crushed. The body has on the overcoat in which he was clad the night he was killed. Wilson, in his confession, stated that he was compelled to assist Harris in disposing of the body after the latter had committed the crime, but his statement is supposed to have been made for the purpose of diverting the suspicion which attached to him. Wilson and Harris are held for the crime.

WOLVERINE WHISPERINGS.
A young man named Wilson has been held for trial at Cassopolis, charged with the murder of a man named Akin. Dr. Harris, Gus Harris and Charles Copley, whom Wilson charged with the crime, were discharged.

A Cadillac man has been sentenced to 30 days in jail for disturbing the salvation army.

Nine veterans in the state soldiers' home are so badly paralyzed that they can only move about by means of wheeled chairs.

The project of building a narrow gauge road from Allegan to South Haven is again being agitated.

At the annual convention of the W. C. T. U. of Michigan, held in Coldwater, the following officers were elected for the ensuing year: President, Mrs. Mary T. Lathrop, Jackson; corresponding secretary, Mrs. Emma A. Wheeler, Grand Rapids; recording secretary, Mrs. C. H. Johnson, Flint; treasurer, Mrs. Fannie E. Holden, Reed City. Mrs. David Preston of Detroit was elected delegate-at-large to the national convention, and Mrs. Andrews of Three Rivers alternate. The organization is in a flourishing condition, there being 450 unions at the present time. The amount of money expended for temperance work was $16,000.

Several weeks ago a Polish woman's house in Alpena, was set on fire by a passing locomotive and all the furniture and one child burned. She sued for damages and recovered $192 in the circuit court, but the railroad company carried it up to the supreme court. A few days ago a letter came addressed to Geo. L. Maltz, which contained a check for $200 for this woman, from Gen. R. A. Alger's private fund, to help her in this hour of need.

The democratic state convention for the nomination of state officers will be held in Detroit July 19.

The Cincinnati, Jackson & Mackinac rail road company has decided not to extend its line through to Saugatuck this summer.

Sam. W. Bennett, a well-known young man of Lansing, who has been an employee of the state house of representatives during the several sessions of the legislature, and who has many friends throughout the state, has been sent to the Detroit house of correction. Whisky did it.

Work on the new Masonic home at Grand Rapids will soon be commenced.

The national commissioner of agriculture, in his report on the wages for farm labor says the result of the investigation is almost identical with that of three years ago. Michigan is the 11th of the states in the amount paid laborers per month with board, being exceeded by California, Colorado, Nevada, Oregon, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, Minnesota, Iowa and Nebraska in the order named. The average wages without board in Michigan is $25.20, and with board $17. In 1879 it was $22.88 without and $12.76 with board, and in 1889 without board it was $31.01 and with board $20.03. The average day wages in harvest in Michigan are $1.80 without and $1.40 with board. There are 154,008 farms in Michigan, 138,597 of which are cultivated by their workers.

Lieut. Fred Shubel, Jr., of Lansing, has been appointed adjutant of the first regiment M. S. T.

Half fare on all roads to the military encampment of the Sons of Veterans at Owosso June 5, 6, 7, 8.

Thomas Wright, the Sunday-school missionary, says that two new missionaries have commenced to labor in northern Michigan, and one of them writes of organizing a Sunday-school where there has been no religious service of any kind for over a year, though the place is on a railroad. In two other settlements not on a railroad he found the same condition of things had existed for over three years. Sabbaaths are spent in fishing and hunting. A family was found in which were three girls above ten years of age who had never before heard a sermon or attended a Sunday-school. More missionaries are needed for the service.

C. H. Hackley has given Muskegon $100,-000 for a public library.

The collector at Port Huron has issued an order prohibiting Canadian musicians from supplying music on this side of the river for public and private entertainments.

The Methodist Protestant conference in session at Adrian adopted a resolution announcing its unaltered opposition to any form of liquor license, high or low, and condemning any clergyman signing a petition for a license to sell. A clause of the resolution condemning the use of tobacco provoked an animated discussion, a large proportion of the clergy using the weed. Westminster, Md., was selected as the place of holding the next conference.

Reed Richardson, a leading farmer of Alpena county, 16 miles from Alpena, was working in the field with a roller, when the pole broke and he fell under the roller and was killed. He was a pioneer of the county and highly respected.

All work at the Detroit mine near Ishpeming has been suspended. The Detroit is one of the big mines of the district.

A wooden-ware factory will soon be added to Lansing's industries.

George Corwin, the oldest resident of Genesee county, died at his home near Swartz Creek a few days ago.

The railroad mileage in the Upper Peninsula has nearly doubled in the past five years.

The annual reunion of the Seventh Michigan Infantry will be held at Jonesville June 26 and 27. Mrs. Gen. Baxter and Gen. Wilson will be present. The G. A. R. Post and W. R. C. are making preparations for the event and will heartily welcome all who come.

James K. Perriman, convicted of bigamy at Grand Rapids, has been sentenced to five years in Jackson.
The changes which have been made in the license laws has practically caused prohibition in many of the smaller towns.
Senator Palmer says he will not serve as chairman of the republican state central committee.

hickman-boston-1888-10-05.A5:
A CONVENIENT LIAB
Trinidad, Colo., Oct. 5. — Parties who were in the city to-day from Boston brought the news of a cold-blooded murder which was perpetrated near there on the 2nd inst. and the subsequent lynching of the murderer by indignant citizens. The particulars of the murder are as follows: For some time past a man named Hickman has had a woman living with him who was ostensibly proving up a claim, but who was generally known as Hickman's mistress. Of late a man named Booth has been paying his attentions to this woman, and rumor had it that they were to be married soon. On
hickman-boston-1888-10-05.A6:
the day of the killing Booth visited the woman and Hickman ran him off the place and also shot him with a shotgur, the shot, however, failing to take effect. Hickman then returned to the house and after re-loading his gun started after Booth again, overtaking him and firing a load of shot into his breast killing him instantly. The murderer then went home.

As soon as the affair was noised over the community and the cowardly and cold-blooded manner in which it was done became known the indignation of the citizens knew no bounds, and a few hours later a mob consisting of about seventy-five men went to Hickman's house, and taking him out, strung him up to a convenient limb.

The street car strike is on at Chicago.
A hopeless split is announced among the New York City Democracy.
The American Secular Union began its session in Pittsburgh yesterday.
Blaine was compelled to cancel two appointments in Michigan, on account of a cold contracted at Adrian.
J. H. Gaffney will umpire the games between New York and St. Louis clubs for the world's championship.
Giovana Dendero has surrendered himself to the Boston police, stating that he killed a relative near Genoa, Italy, on the 12th of last May.

A fast mail has been arranged between New York and Chicago and New York and St. Louis. It will be one hour faster than the mail heretofore between the points named.

A slight trouble growing out of the Philadelphiaans refusing to march with a Confederate flag in line was amicably arranged, and the day was passed pleasantly.

Gallus Boheninlan, proprietor of the New York Hotel at West Superior, Wis., shot himself through the right lung by an accidental discharge of a gun while hunting. Physicians say he cannot live.

Phillip Palledoni, the Italian who murdered his brother, June 22, 1887, suffered the death penalty at Bridgeport, Conn. Palledoni was twenty-four years of age. He could neither read nor write, and could speak but a few words in English.

A man named Hickman, living at Boston, Colorado, shot and instantly killed J. C. Booth, a man who was in the habit of paying visits to the woman Hickman was living with. The murderer was taken from his home an hour afterwards by a mob of seventy-five men and lynched.

While engaged in cards a dispute arose between Tim Keller and Dick Amey at Escauaba, Mich., when Keller whipped out a revolver and fired, the ball taking effect in the head, entering immediately above the bridge of the nose. The wounded man is dying and considerable excitement prevails.

While the police were arresting drunken Indians in Spokane Falls, W. T. they were fired at. A number of shots were exchanged. The citizens then rallied to the aid of the police, and one Indian was killed. His body is now floating down river. There were twenty-five or thirty Indians of the Nez Perce and Spokane tribes.

Last July a negro named Moore was lynched at Charleston. Ill., for an alleged criminal assault upon a woman. MRS. BEVERLIN DEAD. The Grafton Woman who was Abused, Deserted and Slandered by her Inhuman Husband Dies While the Inhuman Brute Walks the Streets Slandering Her. Grafton Eagle. The people of Grafton have often
other community, an occurrence that has called forth such universal condemnation and indignation as the treatment of Mrs. Israel Beverlin by the monster in human form who has figured before the public for some years past as the most notorious, unblushing villain that has ever tramped our streets. Barely escaping the penitentiary on a technicality of law, he has destroyed the lives of two women, whom he had deceived as to his true character; the father of four illegitimate children and an infant scarce two weeks old whose mother he slandered and villified while suffering the travail and pangs of child birth.

The columns of this paper have heretofore contained much of the doings of Israel A. Beverlin for the past four years and has shown him to be the most consummate hypocrite that has ever disgraced the town. Having driven his wife from her home last June and sold off his property that he might join the Ohio woman, who seems to have become infatuated with him, he left Grafton about the last days of July and turned up in Macomb, Ohio, where he visited his new inamorati. His wife, who had found a home with Mr. Chas. W. Good, brought suit for divorce and to recover the property which belonged to her, and also brought suit at Findlay, Ohio, against Mary Dean for $10,000 damages for alienating the affections of her fickle monster husband. Beverlin returned to Grafton about ten days ago to try to obtain proof for Mrs. Dean to establish that his wife had left him and refused to live with him, and the depositions were taken at John W. Mason's office on Tuesday of last week, his brother, Sam P. Beverlin, alone swearing that she had left him in the summer of 1887 and went to New York, yet he refused to state that she returned in the fall of that year and lived with Beverlin until June 9th, 1888. The facts are that her trip to New York was to visit her people. Her life with Beverlin from the date of her marriage 1885, seems to have been fairly pleasant until Beverlin formed his acquaintance with Mrs. Dean last fall and winter. In December last Mrs. Beverlin learned of Beverlin's relations with the woman and this brought about trouble. Mrs. Beverlin succeeded in getting from the mail box of Beverlin, to which she carried a key, several letters written by Mrs. Dean, two of which we publish that the public may know just how awfully gone the "old thing" is.

MACOMB, OHIO, Dec. 11th, 1887.

DEAR BABE: I now seat myself to write just a few lines to tell you I am well, hoping this will find you the same. We are having rain and cloudy weather here and plenty of mud. * * I do not owe you a letter, but May wrote to her cousin so I had nothing to do I thought I would write to "my cousin." I had company to-day. Friend Nuremburg and wife, he is splendid musician, can play on anything and we had a plenty of music; he is teaching the orchestra and is leader of the band. I am going to take lessons on the cornet. I will be happy if I can learn to play with the band would you not like to be present when I take my first lesson? Don't you think my lungs will be strong enough—163. I am going to mail all my letters on the train for I believe they hold them here in this office. I will mail this letter on the 12th, Monday, at 5 o'clock, write if you get it when due at your place. Dear friend, I hope this will find you well and enjoying yourself.

Yours with respect, yours with esteem, your forever.

M. D.

MACOMB, O., Jan. 29, 1888.

DEAR BABE: Yours of the 15th duly received. Glad to hear you are well and hope this will find you well in both mind and body for I do not know any remedy for fretting. I can perhaps prescribe for you when you come. Deer one I shall look for you the first of the month come and stay as long as you can leave home but you must quit fretting and get your face straitened up before you start. It has been cold here all the week but it is warm and raining too day. Everything is dull here now have not one sleigh ride this winter we are talk of going to Lipsic this week are going in a big sleigh about one dozen ladies are not going too have any gentlemen along. * * Deer Babe I can hardly wait until the time comes when I can see you be sure and come next month as early in the month as convenient but suit your self answer this letter as soon as convenient and give me time to answer this week will tell you everything when you come. Yours with love and respect, yours forever, and a kiss for Baby 6.

"M.D."

WANTED TO TAR AND FEATHER HIM.

The people of Grafton came within one of tarring and feathering Isreal A. Beverlin a few days ago. It is alleged by the press of that town that Beverlin's outrageous and inhuman treatment of his wife, caused her death. The Eagle-Sentinel says: "Mrs. Beverlin gave birth to a child on the 15th inst. and seemed to be improving rapidly. Beverlin had returned before and appearing on the streets denounced her as unchaste, using her name in the most wanton manner. This coming to her ears greatly excited her and she became delirious and wild and grew rapidly worse. This Beverlin well knew, yet he never went near her, not even when informed that she was dying, but he walked our streets, whistling and grinning, while his poor victim was writhing in the agonies of death. After her death he went to Mr. Good's, took charge of the body, and on Saturday morning shipped it to Seneca, Ohio, accompanying it on the same train. A crowd collected on the platform at the depot and threats of tar and feathers and lynching were freely made and it only awaited a leadership to have carried the threats into execution. The feeling among our best citizens is intense against this monster in human form, remembering his life as he has lived it here for the past 25 years."

HIS CONSCIENCE TROUBLED HIM.

On last Monday Aaron Tatterson, who lived on Seaman's Fork of Reedy, in Roane county, became tired of life and left the world by the strap line. It is reported that he and one Maclin Cain had concocted a blackmailing scheme by which they got into trouble with a young man named Schafer and another named Delaney. The plan as we learn was about as follows: Cain would get one of these young men to go somewhere with him, and on the road they would find a coat or vest and Cain would tell him to take it, and they would have some fun. About this time Tatterson would appear from behind some object and demand his money of the young man with a large bonus not to report the matter to the authorities. It was the forfeits of these young men in the way of property that disclosed their methods, and Mr. Tatterson's conscience troubled him so that he committed suicide by hanging himself until dead in a shed in the rear of his stable. Before he killed himself he tacked a note on the stable door telling where he might be found. He was a man about 35 years old, with a wife and five children.

LOOKOUT FOR SWINDLERS.

There were several strangers selling a patent wire fence in Monongalia last week. They, we understand, employed some agents, agreeing to pay them a certain per cent. for every thousand rods of the fence sold, on condition that they would execute their negotiable notes for a certain sum payable to the strangers. The persons who bit at this inscrious bait took it for granted that they would not be called upon to pay the notes until after they had sold enough of the fence for their per cent. on same to equal the amount of their notes. Well, they were slightly mistaken in this calculation. The notes, aggregating about eighteen hundred dollars, were discounted by one of our banks, and they will have to be paid when due, whether or not the agents ever sell an inch of the fence. The strangers have, of course, gone to pastures new.

FATAL ACCIDENT.

On Friday last, as Mr. George Eyler, of Mineral county, was coming into Keyser with two loads of bark, the driver of the foremost team looked around and saw Mr. Eyler pulling on his line. He turned his attention to his own team for a minute, and on looking around again saw that Eyler's team looked excited, and that their master could not be seen. Jumping from his horse and running back, he found Mr. Eyler lying senseless in the road, and borrowing the horse of Mr. L. S. Evy, who came up just at the moment, he started for a doctor. Returning, he found Mr. Eyler lying motionless upon his face in the road. He picked him up and turned his face upward, but found that life was extinct.

Senator Camden and a large party of capitalists and stockholders, accompanied President H. G. Davis on a tour of inspection over the West Virginia Central Railroad last week. This is becoming one of the most important railroads in the State.

A distressing mistake occurred on Saturday evening at Alton, Upshur county, by which Samuel W. Boyles lost his life, and three others narrowly escaped. Boyles owned a small store, and feeling indisposed took a small quantity of what he supposed was alcohol, that he had in stock, but which proved to be a poisonous preparation made for photographers; from the effects of it, Boyles died Sunday. Several others tasted the liquid and became very sick, but did not swallow enough to cause fatal effects.

The South-bound passenger train on the Ohio River Railroad, due here from Wheeling at 11:45, was an hour and forty-five minutes late to-day, and the cause was a collision of that train with the North-bound way train. Owing to some misunderstanding of orders the two trains collided at Harness' Switch, just above Waverly, resulting in the serious injury of at least one person, and the bruising up of several others. The man who was the worst hurt is named James Donehoo, and he is the proprietor of a hotel in Williamstown. He sustained a severe contusion of the shoulder, besides other injuries, and now lies in a critical condition. Dr. Ross, of Waverly, attended to the injuries of the wounded man, and he is doing as well as could be expected. Several other persons were more or less hurt, but their names could not be learned. —State Journal.
