And the Grafton Eagle adds: The intelligent citizens of Grafton know that Beverlin is such a character as the West Virginia paper makes him out to be and yet tolerate the loathsome creature here in the town where he committed his deeds while the people of a distant state and town are threatening tar and feathers if he takes up his residence there. A horrible outrage was perpetrated in Harrison Township on Wednesday evening last. McKinley, a near neighbor, who asked her to help him catch a rabbit which had gone into a log near by. She set down her milk pail and went to him, but as soon as she was close enough he put his

as she was close enough he put his arms around her and threw her to the ground, after which, notwithstanding her struggles he effected a rape. She says he then threatened to kill her unless she promised to keep secret what had been done. This she would not do, and McKinley then took a knife, cut her throat and ran away. The girl lay still for a moment or two, fearing if she moved he would return, but finally rose up and started for the house. She beame too weak to go far and sank down, but called as loud as she could for help. Her mother heard her and came running out. The girl told the story to her mother, and a few minutes later the man McKinley came up and said, "I didn't do it," after which he became very much excited, went to his house and began to pray. Murder at Fulton.
FULTON, Mo., Oct. 23.—Last night about 8 o'clock and during services in the Pilgrim's Rest (colored) Church there was a bloody scene enacted. While the choir were singing the opening hymn Jackson Emmerson drew a revolver from his pocket and, pointing it at his wife, Mina Emmerson, fired without effect. He then fired again, the ball entering the back of the head, and coming out above the eyes, killing her instantly. The fiend then fired two more shots into her body and left the church. Subsequently he gave himself up to the authorities, and is now in jail. The cause of the shooting is not known. The colored people are greatly excited, and talk of lynching is heard among them. The inquest is now in progress. The colored preacher jumped through a window and the entire congregation stampeded from the church.

The British Americans.

CHICAGO, Oct. 24.—The British-American national association, in session to-day, adopted a report making eligible to membership any male person of good moral character, who is already, or who intends to become an American citizen, being not less than eighteen years of age, of British birth or son or grandson of such person.

The national association held its final session this evening. Officers were elected as follows: President, George E. Gooch of Chicago; secretary, J. Henry Williams of Philadelphia; treasurer, George G. R. L. Jones of Chicago. The election of vice presidents was deferred until the states not represented in convention shall declare their intention of affiliating with the association. A resolution was adopted requiring the different branches throughout the country to put forth every honest endeavor possible to secure in their respective states the enactment of electoral reforms providing for the adoption of the Australian system of voting, "to the end that absolute secrecy may be vouchsafed each voter as he casts his ballot, and to the end that local primary machines and political bosses may be abolished." The convention adjourned to meet in Boston on the third Wednesday in June, 1889.

An Editor's Woes.

PHILADELPHIA, Oct. 24.—This week's Journal of United Labor, in its editorial columns, says that positive information has been received from a number of sources that the mail list of the paper for the last week in August is in the possession of the republican national committee, and that it was surreptitiously taken from the office of the Journal. The editor announces that an investigation is now in progress, and by the time the next issue of the paper goes to press he hopes to make a complete exposure of the means employed to secure the list.

The Universalists.

CHICAGO, Oct. 24.—The first regular day's session of the Universalist church general convention was held to-day in St. Paul's church. The session was opened at 9 o'clock with a meeting for prayer and praise, after which the convention was formally opened by the election of Hon. Hossew W. Parker of New Hampshire as presiding officer. A collection was taken up for the Gunn ministerial relief fund and Rev. Charles H. Eaton, D. D., of New York delivered the sermon, at the conclusion of which a recess was taken.

Capsized by the Wind.

NEW YORK, Oct. 24.—Shortly before 1 o'clock this afternoon the Spanish brig Almogayar, of Barcelona, was capsized by the wind in Buttermilk channel. The vessel overturned on a tug boat which was passing at the time, causing considerable damage. No lives were lost. The ship carried no ballast, which caused her to capsize so easily.

The Indian Scare.

Sr. PAUL, Oct. 24.—It is learned that the scare at Standing Rock agency over the reported uprising of the Crows against the Sioux proved groundless. Frosthead, an obscure medicine man, and a worthless Indian, claimed to have dreamed that the Crows were coming and got the young bucks to start out after them. A company of cavalry has returned them to the agency.

SHENANDOAH, Ia, Oct. 24—(Spectral Telegram to THE BEE.)—An enthusiastic and largely attended meeting in behalf of Major Anderson, independent candidate for congress in the Eighth district was held here to-day. Ex-Senator Van Wychk, of Nebraska, arrived this morning and was the orator of the day. At an early hour delegations from the surrounding country began to arrive and the crowd was soon swelled by the arrival of delegations from Hamburg, Sidney, Riverton and Farnagut. At 2 p. in. Mr. Van Wyck began his address, which lasted about two hours and a half, during which he paid a high tribute to the course pursued by Major Anderson during the two years he has served as representative, and eulogised in the highest terms the independent and fearless manner in which the major has dealt with the questions before the people and his fidelity in carrying out the policy intrusted to him. He reminded his hearers that to be true to themselves and the principles they uphold the voters of the district should relect the major to assist in carrying out the good work already begun. The ex-senator's speech was received with frequent applause. To-night Major Anderson addressed a large audience in the opera house, and as usual met with a hearty reception. Delegations arrived to-night from Red Oak and Essex by special train over the Burlington. A parade and torchlight procession took place and great enthusiasm was displayed. This has been a very successful meeting and augers well for the success of Mr. Anderson.

Two Murderers Break Jail.
Fulton. Mo., Nov. 8.—Three prisoners broke jail here Tuesday night between 8 and 11 o'clock. There were four others in jail at the time, but they declined to go and one, Wm. Reeves, who did escape, after eating breakfast in the country Wednesday morning, returned to be locked up. Robt. J. Clanton and Jack Emerson are the two escaped. Clanton stands indicted for the mur-of three men, having killed them all at one time, and as the evidence, goes, without cause or provocation. Emerson is the man who murdered his wife in a colored church in Fulton on the 22d of last month, by shooting her four times with a pistol.

The county court this morning offered a reward of $200 for the capture and conviction of these two men. Clanton is 48 years old, 5 feet, spare made, dark eyes, thin haired and bald, wears a mustache and chin whiskers.

Emerson, 23 years old, quite black, slender in build, 5 feet 6 inches high, has a full forehead, stammers and has the second finger off of the right hand at the third joint. He is very quick of movement and of a very nervous temperament. Both men are considered dangerous.

In a fit of jealousy on the 5th Allen Taylor (colored) killed his wife at Nashville, Tenn., and then took his own life.

SAMUEL RAY was on the 5th sentenced at New York to two years and four months' imprisonment for illegal registration.

NEAR Trinidad, Col., on the 5th two miners were killed by a natural gas explosion in the Starkville coal mine. The mine was badly wrecked.

It was said on the 5th that the Wheeling & Lake Erie, the Dayton, Fort Wayne & Chicago and the Cincinnati, Hamilton & Dayton railways would be consolidated.

BUCK & TREXLER, of Crawfordsville, Tenn., general merchants, failed on the 5th for $100,000.

COUNTERFEIT twenty-five-cent pieces of the issue of 1877 were in circulation at Tipton, Ind., on the 5th. A large number of people had been imposed upon, and several of the merchants had been heavily victimized.

The orders directing the United States steamship Kearsarge to proceed to Hayti to protect American interests were countermanded on the 5th.

At Long Island City, N. Y., on the 5th Joseph Kugler, aged fifty-five years, a milkman, was trampled to death by a party of seven horsemen, one or whom threatened to shoot persons who attempted to rescue Kugler.

THOMAS P. LITTLE, aged sixty-five years, of Altoona, Pa., died on the 5th of heart disease. He was a bachelor and lived a miser's life. Bonds and money to the amount of $60,000 were found concealed in his trunk.

The post office at Higginson, Conn., was robbed for the sixth time within a few years on the 5th. The thieves secured about $120 worth of booty.

The annual report on the 5th of the Auditor of State showed that the total municipal indebtedness of Kansas was $31,107,646.90. Leavenworth led, with $2,-069,389.39.

The National horse show was formally opened in Madison Square Garden in New York on the 5th.

The fishing schooner Goldsmith Maid, with thirty thousand pounds of fresh fish, was run into and sunk in Boston harbor on the 6th, and Peter Landry and Howard Monroe were drowned.

A large portion of the town of Wycliffe, Ky., was destroyed by fire on the morning of the 6th.

A fire which started in the city hall building at Haverhill, Mass., on the 6th destroyed several business houses, causing a loss of over $100,000.

In answer to an inquiry from the United States Consul at Havre respecting the right of certain Chinese sailors shipped from the United States on American vessels and paid off and discharged abroad to reship and return to the United States the Secretary of the Treasury said on the 6th that the Chinese could not return.

HENRY KAEHLER, of Chicago, drowned himself in Chicago river on the 6th while insane, and his wife was also drowned while endeavoring to save him.

CAPTAIN HEALY, of the revenue cutter Bear, on the 6th stated at New Bedford, Mass., that he gave no credence to the report that a number of whaling vessels had been caught in the ice in Arctic waters.

CATHERINE SOXS, aged eighty-eight years, Barbara Arnold, aged forty two years, and Lydia Fetrow, inmates of the county almshouse at York, Pa., were suffocated by gas in their room on the 6th.

A political riot occurred in Portsmouth, Va., on the 7th between whites and blacks, during which three white men and one colored man were fatally shot.

Three murderers, Robert Clanton, T. T. Whitington and Jackson Emerson, made their escape from the jail at Fulton, Mo., on the 7th.

A desperate duel occurred on the 7th in the town of Livingston, Ky., over politics, in which five men were killed and the sixth mortally wounded.

William Marshall, a prominent Cass County (Ind.) farmer, was instantly killed on the 7th while blasting stumps with dynamite.

Archibald Pelon, of Grayling, Mich., was lynched on the 7th by masked men for brutally assaulting an aged widow and a young married lady.

A train on the Savannah & Western road containing 125 passengers bound for the Macon fair was wrecked near Ella-ville, Ga., on the 7th, and six persons were killed.

During the twenty-four hours ended on the 7th there were 34 new cases of yellow fever at Jacksonville, Fla., and 3 deaths from the disease. Total cases to date, 4,376; total deaths, 370.

Mrs. George Hirsh of Navarro County, Tex., on the 7th gave birth to six children. The mother and children were doing well. There were four boys and two girls. Mrs. Hirsh is twenty-seven years old.

A Frenchman who was sent to the Baltimore (Md.) work house on the 7th claimed to have walked every step of the way from Texas to that city.

An order was issued at Washington on the 7th directing the resumption of the sunrise guns at the various army posts throughout the country, and the daily raising and lowering of the colors.

A BLAZE on the 7th in the warehouse attached to Moran & Healy's packing-house in the Chicago stock yards did damage to the extent of $50,000.

HENRY MENIX, who lives in the Jacksonville district. Telfair County, Ga., was ninety-nine years old on the 7th. He had never taken a dose of medicine, and had not missed eating a meal on account of sickness in sixty years.

JAMES G. HUTCHISON, of Crawfordsville, Ind., hanged himself on the 8th on account of financial trouble.

During the twenty-four hours ended on the 8th there were 25 new cases of yellow fever at Jacksonville, Fla., and 3 deaths from the disease. Total cases to date, 4,401; total deaths, 373.

In Cincinnati on the 8th an unknown man attempted to chloroform and abduct Mrs. J. P. Kelly, but fled when she succeeded in giving an alarm.

A General Smuggling Business.
ST. PAUL, December 16th—There is every reason to believe that the smuggling conspiracy which the Federal officials here discovered, is more far-reaching than at first supposed. It is certain that the operations of the smugglers were not confined to opium, but large quantities of silks and other costly fabrics from China have been landed in British Columbia and brought to various points on the Canadian Pacific Railroad, consigned to the smugglers.

The Humbled Anarchists.
CHICAGO, December 16th—Two or three small meetings of Anarchists and Socialists were held to-day, but developed nothing sensational. Mrs. Parsons, contrary to announcement, did not arrive home tonight from her trip to Europe. A committee of her friends who were to meet her at the depot, were notified last evening that she would not reach the city till tomorrow.

Robbed in an Opium Joint.
NEW YORK, December 16th—B. Edward Kennedy, a horse-trainer of Trenton, N. J., came to Newark last night with $2,700 in his pocket and had a high time, winding up in a Sixth-ward opium joint. He awoke after midnight and found his companions and money gone. His companions were Jack Hollis (or Hollis or Hawkins), a Boston thief, and Andy Barker. Hollis was arrested on Kennedy's complaint.

Wanderer Waldron.
DETROIT, December 16th—Banker Waldron is at Windson, across the river, under an assumed name. He is remaining out of the State to avoid service of papers in his wife's suit for divorce. She can secure a divorce, but she cannot get alimony without the service. She wants $100,000. She has $25,000 that he left with her when he went to Europe, and he offers to give her $50,000 more, which she refuses.

Death of a Former Californien.
NEW YORK, December 16th—Alexander B. Davis was found dead Friday night in his room at 445 Hicks street, Brooklyn. He was 64 years old and lived alone. He built the first hydraulic flume in California. At one time he was very wealthy. Twenty years ago he sold the Little Chief silver mine in Colorado, which he owned, for $1,000,000. He died of heart disease.

A Railroad Official's Sad End.
BALTIMORE, December 16th.—Byron H. Holmes, Purchasing Agent of the Pennsylvania Railroad, committed suicide this morning by shooting himself through the head. He was in the company of two notorious gamblers at the time, and had been with them all day. Holmes is alleged to be a defaulter to the company. He had been on a spree for a long time.

Four Rounds Settled Him.
NEW YORK, December 16th.—Mike Cushing, of Brooklyn, and Pete Walsh, of Pittsburg, weighing 130 pounds each, fought a game fight to a finish at Rutherford, N. J., this evening. The contest was short, sharp and decisive, Cushing having the best of the battle all through. Though Walsh was game, and took his mauling well, he was knocked out in the fourth round.

Railroad Combination Still Talked Of.
CHICAGO, December 16th.—Another conference of railroad capitalists is to be held in New York this week to consider a means of saving Western properties from the bankruptcy which threatens them. The purpose is to form a company in which is to be concentrated the control and management of all the roads west, southwest and northwest of Chicago.

Silver in a New York Town.
GLENS FALLS, December 16th.—Silver and gold have been discovered in a quartz ledge in this town. The ledges are inclosed between magnesium limestone, with well-defined walls of rock. Specimens of the croppings assayed were found to yield from $50 to $100 a ton. Many claims have been filed and citizens are beginning to catch the mining fever.

Mason Will Fight no More.
WHEELING, December 16th.—John Lamp and George Mason fought a duel with knives at Howard's Chapel, in Morgan county, last night. The trouble grew out of a watch trade. The combat ended by Lamp running his knife through Mason's neck, killing him instantly. Minor wounds were received previously on each side.

Clearing-House Reports.
BOSTON, December 16th.—A table compiled from special dispatches to the Post from the managers of leading clearing houses of the United States, shows the total gross exchanges for the week ended December 15, 1888, were $1,087,773,408, an increase of 6.6 per cent., as compared with the corresponding week in 1887.

Went Crazy Over Faith Cure.
SPRINGFIELD (Ill.), December 16th. — George Smith, who became insane from attending a meeting of believers in faith cure, yesterday attempted to murder his four-months-old baby, and was to day taken to an asylum. The meeting will probably be suppressed.

Wite Murder and Suicide.
PHILADELPHIA, December 16th. — John Ferguson, aged 42 years, engineer of Flanagan's woolen mills at Manayunk, shot his wife and himself to-day at Mill Creek. They leave a little son. Ferguson recently recovered from diphtheria, which is supposed to have left his mind affected.

Hearst Did Not Buy Him.
NEW YORK, December 16th. — Senator Heart is authority for the following statement: "I have not bought Ormonde, never thought of doing so, and have no idea how the report started." It is generally believed that a Buenos Ayres syndicate has secured Ormonde.

From Diamond to Stage.
NEW YORK, December 17th. — Mike Kelly, Boston's baseball beauty, has been engaged by Hoyt & Thomas for $1,000 to play the part of Tough in the "Tin Sold er" during Christmas and New Year's week at the Fourteenth street Theater.

Murdered by White Caps.
KANSAS CITY, December 16th. — James McDonald, who was brutally beaten by White Caps on Monday, died yesterday while under the influence of opiates given him to alleviate his sufferings. The murderers have left no trace of their identity.

Steamer and Cargo, Burned.
MEMPHIS, December 16th. — The steamer T. Barkssale, with 981 bales of cotton and 1,200 sacks of seed, together with the books and papers of the boat, was burned yesterday at Hendricks' Landing on the Yazoo river.

Dynamite, Explosion.
BRAFORD (Pa.), December 16th. — A dynamite magazine three miles from Bradford, containing 800 pounds of dynamite, blew up this morning, doing great damage to the surrounding property. No one was injured.

Carkeek and Connors to Wrestle.
MILWAUKEE, December 16th. — Jack Carkeek and Thomas Connors to-day signed an agreement to wrestle here for $250 a side the latter part of January.

Morton Back in New York,
New York, December 16th.—Vice-President-elect Morton returned to-night and announced that he was fagged out, and reused to be interviewed.

WHITE CAPS BUSY. The Order Extended to Kansas. Operations Begun Upon People Living About Agra.
AGRA, KAN., Dec. 12—About six months ago three families moved to this township from southern Indiana, and soon it was reported that a secret organization was being formed in a very quiet way and meetings being held at one of their homes.

About a month ago mysterious and threatening notices sent to several persons—all signed "K. D. W. C." No notice was taken of them and soon they were again left, this time with apparent finger prints of blood on the envelopes, while the notices bore a large red cross across the face. They gave several persons until a certain time to leave the county, and were signed in full: "Kansas Division of White Caps." But still nothing serious was thought of it.

Last Wednesday night about twenty horsemen, each wearing a long white cap, cone shape, coming down over their shoulders with holes for mouth, nose and eyes, and each body enveloped in a long robe of red with each horse covered with a blanket of black, rode up to the house of a farmer near here. Each carried a water pail, and, having filled them near by, they went to the house of the man who is too lazy to work and seemed never to have taken a bath. The door was opened by the man, who had on nothing but an undershirt. They siezed and overpowered him, and, taking him outside, tied his hands and feet and each man deliberately poured a pail of cold water over him, then left him and rode away, leaving a sign with the words printed in red thereon: "Leave the County. The man went the next day.

Monday night the Whitecaps appeared in a stronger force and visited James McDonald, a citizen of this place, who had abused his wife. They took him to a telegraph pole and tied him. A cat-o'-nine-tails was then produced and each member gave him two blews. His screams were heartrending. After this the trumpet was sounded and each man mounted and rode out of town on a run. Some of the citizens who were aroused removed him to his home. He was cut up in a horrible manner and blood was smeared all over his person. There is considerable excitement but nothing yet done to find the mob.

KANSAS CITY, Dec. 16.—James McDonald, the man who was so unmercifully beaten by White Caps at Agria, Kan., last Monday, died early yesterday morning. His body was badly lacerated and he suffered terribly, so badly, in fact, that opiates were given him and he died while under their effect.

The above press dispatch is from free Kansas, mind you, and not from the barbaric regions of the far South. The man beaten to death is not a negro, but a white man. Now if this had been a son of Ham, who had been whipped to death for stealing chickens in South Carolina, or Mississippi, we should have had both a Senate and House investigating committee, with an appropriation, to go South and spend $50,000 in Congressional champagne, stenographers, printing and telegraphing, to show the flendish spirit of the Southern rebellion up to the gaze of all mankind. But as it happened in Kansas, it will all subside with a seven line telegraph squib.

When the United States war ship Galena was to have started from the Brooklyn navy yard it was found to be stuck in the mud and had to wait for high tide.

Representative William H. Martin, of Texas, charged with assault on George H. Harris, a reporter on the evening Star, appeared in the police court at Washington, D. C., pleaded guilty and was fined $15.

Mr. and Mrs. Levi P. Morton arrived at Indianapolis to visit the Harrisons at their home.

The New York Mail and Express threatens to tell the whole truth about the scandals just now being so much denied, concerning the present administration, if the counter attacks upon its friends are not stopped. It says it has the whole matter pigeonholed.

THE ORGANIZATION SAID TO BE SPREADING TO ALL PARTS OF TWO NORTHWESTERN COUNTIES.
AGRA, KAN., Dec. 15.—James McDonald, the man who was so unmercifully beaten by the mob calling themselves the "Kansas Division of White Caps," died early this morning. His body was badly lacerated and he suffered terribly, so badly in fact that opiates were given him and he died while under their effect.

A farming living here stated that he saw the White Caps pass his house on two different nights. On the second night he was very near them without being seen and their caps bore numbers. They appeared to be under the command of a bugler, who would blow the bugle for different commands. He followed them until they halted, when they seemed to hold a council. The chief, instead of calling by name, would address tham as No. "1," "2," "3," etc. Enough was overheard to convince him they were organizing Phillips and Smith counties, instituting a division in each township, with the principal headquarters at Phillipsburg. Nos. 8, 11 and 19 were appointed to go to some place that night. This farmer appears to know too much about the council, and it is believed he is closely connected with them.

On the following morning a tenant on Joseph Millgrove's place found a notice pinned on his door reading thus:

Frank Sage:

Your thievin' is troublesome; quit it. We have you on the list. If you don't quit we'll cowhide you. Let this warnin' be sufficient. We're organized to clean this country out of objectionable characters. Don't try to bluff us, but mind. We mean business. WHITE CAPS.

THE VERY LATEST.
December 24, 25 and 26 are holidays in all of the Chicago markets this year.

Rev. John Curts, a prominent Methodist minister, died suddenly at Abilene.

George H. Russell, treasurer of the Bee Line road, is dead at Cleveland, O.

The steamer Chateau La Fitte from Bordeank arrived at New York with small pox in her steerage.

A man froze to death in Albany, N. Y., last Saturday, while Kansas farmers were plowing without coats.

A construction train in Arizona rolled down an embankment and killed seven of the sixty laborers on it.

Sheriff Smith of Birmingham, Ala., who is under bonds of $100,000, will have his trial at the January term of court.

A deputy sheriff from El Dorado, Kan., has brought August Sittingeen from Snaw-neetown, Ill. He is charged with rape.

The mercury at the signal station at Saranac Lake, N. Y., registered 23 degrees below zero Saturday morning, December 22.

Hermansville, a lumbering settlement of Michigan, has been destroyed by fire. The weather is very cold there, causing much suffering.

The giant oak at Woodbridge, Conn. which is twelve hundred years old, has been cut down. The trunk is twenty-five feet in circumference.

Specific directions have been issued at the general land office to the officers of the Wa-Keeney land office to place the Fort Wallace reservation on sale.

The supreme court of Ohio has decided that church property of which the title is held by a bishop is exempt from claims against the bishop as an individual.

The garrison at Fort Assinabonie, six companies of infantry and three of cavalry have been fighting a prairie fire with no certainty of saving the garrison buildings.
The garrison at Fort Assinabone, six companies of infantry and three of cavalry have been fighting a prairie fire with no certainty of saving the garrison buildings.

The commissioners of Phillips county, Kansas, are determined to fix the responsibility of the lie published by the Kansas City Times concerning alleged outrages by White Caps at Agra.

A fire in Cincinnati resulted in the death of Captain Bray, of the fire department, and the serious injury of several firemen by the falling of a wall upon them. Some of them will likely die.

A hot water pipe exploded in a day coach on the Illinois Central which caused a dangerous panic among the passengers. Mrs. Ida Pierce, of Tuscola, Ill., kept her head and pulled the bell cord.

The switchmen at Denver employed by the Union Pacific have demanded 5 cents more an hour and six more men, and that they be no longer under a local agent but be placed under a yardmaster.

Dr. Richmond, the slayer of Colonel J. W. Strong, editor of the St. Joseph Herald, and who escaped from the lunatic asylum, has returned and given himself up. He wants a discharge as cured for business interests.

A Belleville and Caroudelet train was detailed eight miles from Belleville, Ill., and Thomas Ash, a fireman, was crushed and scalded to death. His brother William Ash and George Sacks, a brakeman, were fatally injured.

Southern republicans in conference at Washington have decided not to present the name of any man to the president as their choice for cabinet positions, but will urge the desirability of some southern man being so placed.

Judge Conrad, at Des Moines, Ia., has decided that packages not labelled on the outside so as to denote the character of their contents are not subject to seizure under the state law until they are delivered to the consignee by the common carrier in charge.

The fast line train on the Panhandle road, ran into a freight train near Idlewood, Pa., wrecking the engine, postal car and freight car. Fireman W. T. Barker, of Pittsburg, Pa., was caught in the wreck and crushed to death. The engineer saved himself by jumping.

SAVANNAH, Ga., Nov. 7.—A mob of 200 negroes endeavored to take the life of James Thompson, a colored man who was found voting the Democratic ticket. Thompson lives six miles from the city and walked in to vote. When the mob surrounded Thompson a knot of white men protected him and hustled him away from the polls. C., says: An unknown negro fired from ambush into a Democratic parade here Monday night, the ball striking a man named Sams, but not seriously wounding him. Brutality of a Father. ALBANY, N. Y., Nov. 7.—At 7 o'clock a. m. Henry Lindeman, a laborer, aged 40, who lives at 24 First avenue, shot and killed his 14-year-old son Willie. INDIANAPOLIS, Nov. 7.—In the Fifth ward a young colored man who was peddling Democratic tickets was set upon by his irate father and mother and given a sound thrashing.

Desperate Attack on a Chinese Brothel by the Notorious Gang.

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 7.—A desperate fight occurred in a Chinese brothel between the proprietors and a gang of highbinders who attempted to rob the place. The highbinders had a confederate sleeping in the place, who admitted them. Chin, the highbinder leader, threw red pepper in the eyes of the woman at the door, beat the wife and the proprietor over the head with an iron bar and badly wounded the proprietor. Wong Too, one of the highbinders, received wounds from which he died. The police arrested all the parties. The raid grew out of the failure of the brothel keepers to pay blackmail to the highbinders.

The Returns Show That Gen. Harrson is Elected.
NEW YORK—Returns received at the United Press office by counties, by majorities which are estimated, indicate that Harrison has carried New York by about 10,000 plurality.

Total city vote, Cleveland 162,907; Harrison 105,921; Fisk 1,300; Cowdrey 1,567.

911 outside districts give Harrison 222,509; Cleveland 176,851; Fisk 104,-657.

The same in '84 gave Blaine 198,552, Cleveland 162,457, St John 9,620.

The city complete gives for Mayor, Grant 107,527, Hewitt 68,135, Erhardt 67,725, Coogan 9,455.

Brooklyn complete gives Cleveland 79,-736, Harrison 68,167.

Cleveland carries his own Ward in Buffalo by 318 majority, a gain of 43.

NEBRASKA—The Republicans claim this State by 28,000 to 30,000. The Democrats concede 18,000 to 20,000.

ALABAMA—The indications are that Alabama has given a Democratic majority of 40,000 to 55,000. All the Democratic nominees for Congress have been elected.

RHODE ISLAND complete, Harrison 21,-968, Cleveland 17,496. A Republican majority of 2,196.

MAINE—One hundred and twenty towns gave Harrison 35,891, Cleveland 23,500, Fisk 1,175, Scattering 712. Republican gain of 1,902, or 18 per cent, indicating a plurality of over 23,000.

VIRGINIA—Richmond city gives Cleveland 8,210, Harrison 6,372; a Democratic loss of 55. Wise, Democrat, for Congress 8,040; Waddell, Republican, 6,320, a Democratic loss of 121. Wise will probably carry the district by 500 majority.

Norfolk gives Harrison five hundred and eighty, Portsmouth, Virginia, gives Cleveland three hundred and sixty-eight majority. Isle Wight county reported Democratic by a small majority. James City county gives Harrison three hundred and eighty-six majority. Williamsburg gives Harrison sixty majority.

Elizabeth city and county give Harrison 1,358, Cleveland 547, Fisk 18. Republican majority 811, Democratic gain 145 over 1884.

Lynchburg gives Cleveland 2,053; Harrison 1,796. Democratic majority 259.

In the Sixth Congressional District, Edmonds, Democratic, is elected to succeed Hopkins, Labor.

CALIFORNIA—A dispatch received from San Francisco says that California will give Harrison 22,000 plurality and will elect a full quota of Republican Congressmen.

MICHIGAN has gone Republican, electing Luce, Republican, Governor.

NEW JERSEY—The indications point to a majority for the Democratic ticket in this State.

SOUTH CAROLINA—No contest at all and all Democratic nominces elected without opposition. At Yorkville there were only 5 Republican votes and only 7 at Rock Hill.

NORTH CAROLINA—The State has gone Democratic by an increased majority.

Salisbury town gives 275 Democratic majority, a gain of 162 over Scales' vote. Rowan county gives a Democratic majority of 1,600, an increase of 326 over Scales vote.

Mecklenburg county goes Democratic by 1,050 majority. This is a gain of four hundred votes over the vote of Cleveland in 1884.

Indications are that Forsyth has gone Republican.

Returns from Cleveland county indicate that Cleveland will get two thousand majority, Fowle about 50 less, State candidates, Judge and Congress tickets to court tickets, or amendment. Democrats gain is over five hundred.

The election in Davidson county passed of quietly, and was one of the hottest contested political fights ever known in the county, both parties polling their full strength. The county has gone Republican.

The Rutherford Democratic ticket was elected without opposition.

Columbus county, Democratic by 1,185 majority.

Jay Gould's Latest Acquisition. Chicago, Dec. 17.—It is reported here that instead of the Santa Fe system, Jay Gould has secured control of the Chicago, Santa Fe & California road. This road cost the Atchison Company over $15,000,000, and has always been a "white elephant" on their hands. If it should prove correct, that Mr. Gould has secured control of the Atchison's Chicago extension, the road will be operated as part of the Missouri Pacific system, which will then have through line from Chicago to Texas and Colorado. Freight rates, both east and west-bound, between Chicago and St. Louis and the seaboard, will to-morrow be restored to the tariff of last April. Traffic is very heavy now and promises to continue so all winter. Striking For Their Wages.
NEW YORK, Dec. 17.--A special to the World from the City of Mexico says strikes are reported from several points on the line of the Mexican National Railroad owing to the non-payment of wages. On Thursday a north-bound train was delayed for some time at the depot in the City of Mexico on account of the refusal of the men to take the train out until they received their pay. The station agent telegraphed to the city office, and funds were forwarded to the station.

Destroyed by Fire.

GREENCASTLE,IND., Dec. 17.—Fire destroyed the entire works of the Putnam Wire Nail Company here last evening. The loss is placed at $15,000, and is only partially covered by insurance. About $6,000 insurance was held on the building and contents.

CHARLES CITY, IOWA, Dec. 17.—J. S. Fussel's farm-house, together with a large barn, forty tons of hay, thirty head of cattle and some horses and hogs, was consumed by fire Saturday. There was no insurance on the property.

Killed by a Horse Thief.

TOPEKA, KAN., Dec. 17.—A Stevens County farmer, named Howell, on Friday, discovered Jim Newton, a notorious horse thief, stealing three horses from his barn. Howell attacked the thief unarmed, and was brutally beaten about the head and knocked senseless. Newton then fired three bullets into Howell's body, and rode off into Indian Territory with the horses. The body of the farmer was found Saturday, and a posse started after Newton, bent upon lynching him.

Suicide of Chicago's Fire Marshal.

Suicide of Chicago's Fire Marshal. CHICAGO, Dec. 17.—Fire Marshal Frank Swenie, chief of the Town of Lake Fire Department for five years past, committed suicide this morning at 5 o'clock by nearly severing his head from his body with a razor. He was in apparent good health last night, and it is believed he committed the act while temporarily insane. The deceased was 52 years old, and a brother of Fire Marshal Swenie of Chicago. Mr. Swenie leaves a wife and three children.

Whittier's Eighty-first Birthday.

DANVERS, MASS., Dec. 17.—John G. Whittier, the venerable poet, to-day reached his 81st birthday at his winter home at Oak Knoll, one of his most favorite residences. The day was observed in the poet's modest way, receiving friends, neighbors and others. Mr. Whittier is in fairly good health, but rarely goes out and then not far from his house.

A Clergyman Suspended.

NEW YORK, Dec. 17.—The Rev. John F. Hooper, pastor of St. Paul's Reformed Church at Morrisania, has been suspended from the ministry. This action is on account of the recent decision of the California courts granting Hooper's wife a divorce on account of his cruel and inhuman treatment of her.

jim-newton-1888-12-14.A15:
JIM NEWTON'S RECORD. The Kansas Murderer and Horse Thief Well Known in Missouri.
Nevada, Mo., Dec. 19.—Jim Newton, the notorious desperado, horse thief and murderer, who shot and killed a farmer named Howells in Newton county, Kansas. last Friday night, while trying to get away with three of the farmers' best horses was well known in southwest Missouri. Judge C. T. Davis, ex-prosecuting attorney of this county, said to-day: "Some ten or twelve years ago Newton stole seventy-five or 100 head of cattle up in Bates county, and was in jail here for the offense. I do not now remember how he got out of it, but numerous other offenses in these parts were charged up against him as well. After leaving here he committed a theft or burglary in Linn county, Kansas, and was captured and placed in jail. One day he took a leg from a stool and when the jailer entered his cell with a meal, he flew upon him with the ferocity of a lion. After knocking his keeper senseless he made his escape and several fruitless attempts were made to capture him. At one time a woman at whose house he was stopping learned who he was by taking a letter from his pocket, and then notified the officers but he was too quick for them and again got away. Later he was overtaken on the Marmaton bridge at Ft. Scott, but his dexterity with a revolver again enabled him to make his escape. It would be hard to say how many times he was connected with thefts and other depredations or how often he found himself in jail. He was afterward sent to the penitentiary and nothing more was ever heard of him till the last bloody encounter in which he figured."

Newton had been living at Bear City, in the neutral strip, and was engaged in the business of stealing horses from Kansas farmers and running them across the line into the neutral strip, where he was safe from the law.

The "hero", of this story is Nelson Moore, who lived on Williams river, about ten miles from Hillsboro. It seemed that Moore became enamored of a beautiful young girl of sixteen years, daughter of Mr. M. W. Gordon, living in that neighborhood. WANTED TO TAR AND FEATHER HIM.

The people of Grafton came within one of tarring and feathering Isreal A. Beverlin a few days ago. It is alleged by the press of that town that Beverlin's outrageous and inhuman treatment of his wife, caused her death. The Eagle-Sentinel says: "Mrs. Beverlin gave birth to a child on the 15th inst. and seemed to be improving rapidly. Beverlin had returned before and appearing on the streets denounced her as unchaste, using her name in the most wanton manner. This coming to her ears greatly excited her and she became delirious and wild and grew rapidly worse. This Beverlin well knew, yet he never went near her, not even when informed that she was dying, but he walked our streets, whistling and grinning, while his poor victim was writhing in the agonies of death. After her death he went to Mr. Good's, took charge of the body, and on Saturday morning shipped it to Seneca, Ohio, accompanying it on the same train. A crowd collected on the platform at the depot and threats of tar and feathers and lynching were freely made and it only awaited a leadership to have carried the threats into execution. The feeling among our best citizens is intense against this monster in human form, remembering his life as he has lived it here for the past 25 years."

HIS CONSCIENCE TROUBLED HIM.

On last Monday Aaron Tatterson, who lived on Seaman's Fork of Reedy, in Roane county, became tired of life and left the world by the strap line. It is reported that he and one Maclin Cain had concocted a blackmailing scheme by which they got into trouble with a young man named Schafer and another named Delaney. The plan as we learn was about as follows: Cain would get one of these young men to go somewhere with him, and on the road they would find a coat or vest and Cain would tell him to take it, and they would have some fun. About this time Tatterson would appear from behind some object and demand his money of the young man with a large bonus not to report the matter to the authorities. It was the forfeits of these young men in the way of property that disclosed their methods, and Mr. Tatterson's conscience troubled him so that he committed suicide by hanging himself until dead in a shed in the rear of his stable. Before he killed himself he tacked a note on the stable door telling where he might be found. He was a man about 35 years old, with a wife and five children.

LOOKOUT FOR SWINDLERS.

There were several strangers selling a patent wire fence in Monongalia last week. They, we understand, employed some agents, agreeing to pay them a certain per cent. for every thousand rods of the fence sold, on condition that they would execute their negotiable notes for a certain sum payable to the strangers. The persons who bit at this inscrious bait took it for granted that they would not be called upon to pay the notes until after they had sold enough of the fence for their per cent. on same to equal the amount of their notes. Well, they were slightly mistaken in this calculation. The notes, aggregating about eighteen hundred dollars, were discounted by one of our banks, and they will have to be paid when due, whether or not the agents ever sell an inch of the fence. The strangers have, of course, gone to pastures new.

FATAL ACCIDENT.

On Friday last, as Mr. George Eyler, of Mineral county, was coming into Keyser with two loads of bark, the driver of the foremost team looked around and saw Mr. Eyler pulling on his line. He turned his attention to his own team for a minute, and on looking around again saw that Eyler's team looked excited, and that their master could not be seen. Jumping from his horse and running back, he found Mr. Eyler lying senseless in the road, and borrowing the horse of Mr. L. S. Evy, who came up just at the moment, he started for a doctor. Returning, he found Mr. Eyler lying motionless upon his face in the road. He picked him up and turned his face upward, but found that life was extinct.

A WEST VIRGINIAN IN TROUBLE.

The Ritchie Review says: About a year ago Joe. Taylor, formerly of Cairo, this county, married in Parkersburg Miss Sallie Knight, daughter of Ed. Knight, a msot beautiful and estimable young lady, and in a day or two thereafter most cruelly deserted her, and eloped with a woman from Cairo, his home. Nothing was heard of him since his escapade until last week, when a dispatch came to his brother Cam that Joe had shot a man in Texarcanna, Tex., and was about to be lynched. If we have been correctly informed, we suppose ere this Joe's carcass has been hung up as food for the buzzards.

Lucie Green, colored, kills Lizzie Burns, also colored, at a festival at Corregan, by stabbing her to the heart.

Some person entered the residence of Mr. Frank Jagel, at Atascosa, and robbed it of what money he could lay hands on, which was a small amount fortunately.

There is great enthusiasm at the Hazel mining camp, at Carriza, a small town on the Texas Pacific railway, 100 miles east of El Paso, over a rich find of silver.

Today is the "county exhibit day" at Dallas, the chief feature of which will be the opening of the races, under the auspices of the Dallas Driving club.

A row occurs at Pittsville, ten miles north of Richmond. A party of armed men rode up to a negro church and opened fire on a crowd of negroes, killing one and wounding several others.

The working force of the Aransas Pass road have finished grading their line from the Brazos river, 56 miles, to a connection with the Santa Fe railroad, in the city limits of Houston.

The quarantine camp on the west side at Texarkana has had large accessions lately, and there are detained there 72 persons who hail from various sections east of the Mississippi, where yellow fever is said to exist.

Mr. Geo. A. Johnson, who lives about nine miles east of Waco, came to the city and sold a bale of cotton he had brought to the city. He has not reached his home, and it is feared he met with foul play, as he had $100 on his person.

Important testimony is said to be coming to the front in support of the remarkable suit of Mrs. Kate Knight Edwards, of Terrell, against the heirs of C. C. Alexander, of Bonham, for the Hunt-Alexander lands. It will have great weight, it is stated, as evidence in the Bean will contest.

The light keeper's residence at Point Isabel, Brownsville, occupied by Mrs. Schreiber, widow of the late keeper, was struck several nights in succession by numbers of shingle nails, shells and brick bats. The closest search by the sheriff and others have failed to discover the source whence the missiles come. Superstitious mariners say it is the ghosts of drowned seamen.

KEEPING THE SOUTH
From The Galveston News.
Jim Garvey, of Richmond.

Jim Garvey, of Richmond, the sheriff of Fort Bend County, was in the city yesterday. Fort Bend County was, on Saturday night, the scene of another of those unwarranted and unprovoked political assassinations which are, for the reputation of Texas, becoming too frequent of late in this section of the State. The recent assassination at Pittsville, in Fort Bend County, was from all accounts, one of those unprovoked, cold-blooded murders, traceable to no apparent cause whatever except the bitter political feeling which prevails there resulting in a recourse to bloodshed by a class of citizens almost morally incapable of appreciating the responsibility attaching to the crime of murder when the victim chances to be a negro. A crowd of young white men of Pittsville rode up to a colored church, and calling the negroes out, fired into them, killing Lamar Johnson and wounding Taylor Randon, who has since fled the county for safety. Both of these are well-known
lamar-johnson-1888-10.A3: colored men of Fort Bend County, and good, law-abiding citizens. While the political feeling there is the only cause assigned for this act, it fell short in accomplishing anything in a direct way except the killing of one more negro and the natural intimidation intended to be consequent upon such an act. What is known as the Jay Bird Club, a new Democratic organization in Fort Bend County, is directly responsible for the present condition of affairs existing there, and consequently responsible for this last unprovoked assassination.

Items and Comments Culled From State Exchanges.
A cannery and evaporator is now an assured fact for Mexia next spring. This means money for the farmers and the town all through the year.

The members of the Mexia Light Guards, who disbanded on account of not being able to procure arms two years ago, held a meeting last Saturday night to dispose of the surplus of $34 in their treasury. The amount was unanimously voted to the Mexia Silver Cornet band to aid them in purchasing instruments.

The new Methodist church at Mexia was occupied by the congregation for the first time Sunday. It is a handsome structure inside and out, and an ornament to the town. Bishop McIntyre will dedicate it the first Sunday in November. Rev. G. W. Wyatt, the deservedly popular minister of that congregation, has been untiring in his efforts to build his church. He and his congregation have cause to feel proud of their success.

Yesterday at the Grand Central depot a young couple attracted the attention of passengers waiting for the trains, by their ludicrous actions. The young man was considerably under the influence of liquor, and was very demonstrative in his feeling of love for his better half. He was so boisterous at times that Officer Tom O'Leary was kept busy in seeing that he did not disturb anyone in the waiting rooms. His wife was equally as loving, and it was supposed was more so, in order to keep him quiet. After they had boarded the Southern Pacific train he asked frequently for whisky, when at last she put a stop to him by saying: "Yes, my darling, you shall have a drink; not a bottle; yes, a whole gallon." They left, and it is supposed he got the gallon when they reached their destination.—Exchange.

Deputy Sheriff Anderson succeeded in hunting down the Mexican, Joe Mentana, who was engaged in the cutting affray last Saturday night and then skipped by the light of the moon. He retired in good order to the quiet precincts of the ancient town of Harrisburg, and had already commenced work upon a tamale factory, when the the arm of the law reached him. Thus have the good people of Harrisburg been saved from the seducive influence of the ever-doubtful tamale, and Deputy Anderson scored a point for his vigilance. Mentana will be tried this morning before Justice Railey, but as Mexicans are the only witnesses, and they do not seem inclined to tell what they know, he may yet be restored to the tamale industry.—Houston Post.

Capt. P. E. Pearson, a prominent and able lawyer of Fort Bend county, has been in the city for the past two days waiting for the calling of the Gallahger murder case, removed to this county from Wharton upon change of venue. Captain Pearson is not only prominent at the bar, but he is a leading democrat of his county. Captain Pearson says that the killing of the negro, Lamar Johnson, near Pittsville, was not the result of political feeling. In fact he says the statement of Randall Taylor, as already given to the press, is believed to be correct as to the cause.—Houston Post.

The school started by the Sisters of Charity in San Angelo on the first of last month has given so much satisfaction, and so many applications from ranchmen have been received, that it has been decided to put up a convent at once. It will be a handsome building, and is to be erected on the Catholic church block in that city.

Captain Fowlkes, of Bryan, has purchased the 900 acre Lackey irrigated farm, the price paid being $12,500. It is situated between the south and middle Concho rivers, eight miles from San Angelo. The new owner will bring several German families and settle them on the land at once.

Sixteen hundred of fine beef cattle for the Chicago market went out yesterday from Laredo, on the International in the latest and most improved cattle cars, fitted up with an automatic appliance for feeding and watering the cattle on board the cars.

When Henry H. Smith, of San Francisco, died he left a will in which he directed that his son should be taught Chinese, and the cost defrayed out of the estate. The young man is still pegging away at the language, and the widow has appealed to the courts to save the unconsumed remnants of the property.—Exchange.

The first creamery in Texas will be established at Lampasas. It is to be built within the next ninety days and have a capacity of 2,000 pounds of butter per day.

The success of the big Dallas fair is another argument in favor of a big winter exposition at Galveston. It is too late for this season, but it is not too early to set the ball in motion and get good and ready for the next. As hitherto observed about one hundred times, it would attract thousands of money spending visitors and prove of permanent benefit to the city.—Galveston Tribune.

The same element that waged war in McLennan county in 1878 against the democracy makes the contest this year. Then this element went by the name of the greenback party. Now, it is called union labor, non-partisan or independent. Some men have shifted sides since then, but in the main it is the same crowd that made the fight ten years ago. The democracy won then and has held power ever since. Will any candid man rise up, look the public square in the eye and affirm that the victorious, power-holding democracy has not given the people good government in those ten years—good government in state as well as county affairs? Is there any reason to hope that a new party, if in power, could or would do better? These are questions for voters to ask themselves. —Waco Day.

PREPARING TO LYNCH A CHINAMAN.
A UNION HILL, N. J., MOB EXASPERATED BY AN ATTEMPT AT ASSAULT.
A UNION HILL, N. J., MOB EXASPERATED BY AN ATTEMPT AT ASSAULT.

Lee Lung, a Chinaman who keeps a laundry in Bergen Line-ave., Union Hill, N. J., narrowly escaped having his earthly career brought to a sudden termination yesterday. Lydia Giboran, age seventeen, went to the laundry to get some clothes which had been left there to be washed. The Chinaman was alone and attempted to assault her. An able-bodied young man named Mullins, who had been attracted by her cries, broke in and dragged her away from her assailant. Mullins then proceeded to give the scoundrel a sound thrashing.

The girl went to Recorder Schleicher's court, where she told her story. The Recorder sent Policeman Stahl to arrest the Chinaman. Meanwhile the story of the assault had spread among the neighbors, and an angry crowd gathered in front of the laundry. Preparations were being made to take Lung out and lynch him when Policeman Stahl arrived and persuaded the crowd to desist. He took the Chinaman out by a rear door and brought him before the Recorder, who placed him under $500 bonds. Bail was furnished by Lung's landlord, and Lung hastened away not during to return to his shop.
lee-lung-union-hill-1888-01-13.A2:
LEE YUNG ESCAPED UNHUNG.
A Celestial named Lee Yung, who has renovated linen on Bergenline avenue, Union Hill, for several months, came precious near dangling at the end of a rope yesterday or being trampled to death by a mad crowd. Lydia Givoran, a sixteen-year-old miss, visited the laundry to get some washing. Lee attacked her and forced her to the floor. She fought and screamed lustily. John Mullins ran in and released her. While she was escaping he gave Lee a severe drubbing and then notified the police. When Policeman Stahl arrived an angry crowd was collecting and muttering threats. The policeman with difficulty forced his way through the throng. On reaching the locked door he warned them not to follow him or molest his prisoner. The door was forced and the Chinaman, shaking with fright, was found in a dark corner of the kitchen. He legged for protection. The policeman cleverly deceived the crowd by taking his prisoner out by the rear door. He was arraigned before Recorder Schleicher, who fixed the bail at $500. Mr. Palmer, owner of the building occupied by Lee, qualified as bondsman, and the accused was released. He immediately shook Union Hill dust from his clogs.

Chicago, Jan. 13.—Wood work in the Irving public school engine room took fire this afternoon. A thousand children were in the building when smoke filled it, and for a little while a panic was imminent. Though the pupils left their seats, the teachers held the doors shut until they could give danger signals, which the children obeyed. At the first stroke of the gong they caught up their wraps and books, at the second formed in line, at the third, marched in order to the street. Out of the thousand children, but one lost his presence of mind. He was a lad of 11, and became so excited that he threw slate and books through a window, and then dashed his fist through a pane of glass. His teacher forced him into line after he had badly cut himself. This was the only accident, and the building was not damaged much.

MINNEAPOLIS, Minn., Jan. 13.—Reports from all over the Northwest indicate the prevailing blizzard is the worst and most extended of the season. Its area of operations is from the Rockies to Lake Michigan, but Minnesota and Dakota are the worst sufferers. On roads running west from here all freights are abandoned and passenger trains are run at long intervals—though every effort is being made to keep them moving. At Huron, Dakota, the blizzard filled the air with blinding snow so that business men lost their way on the drive from home to the office. An inexperienced teacher dismissed her scholars in the storm at noon yesterday, and they were only rescued by extraordinary efforts. Men organized themselves in parties of ten each, armed with a hundred feet of rope and marching in a line gathered all the lost children in but one child who is doubtless frozen to death.

CHARLESTON, S. C., Jan. 12.—The earthquake shock this morning was generally felt throughout the coast country and as far west as August. No damage has been reported.

An Amarchist's Bullet.

IT GOT INTO OFFICER WEINKE' HEAD AT THE HAYMARKET RIOT AND HAS JUST BEEN TAKEN OUT.

CHICAGO, Sept. 24.—Officer John H. Weinke underwent an operation yesterday to obtain relief from an injury received in the Haymarket riot, May 4, 1883. Immediately after the bomb exploded a pistol ball struck Weinke in the back of the head and lodged under his skull. At the hospital the physicians deemed the removal of the bullet not necessary to his complete recovery, and it was allowed to remain. At intervals since it has troubled him greatly, sometimes causing him the most intense pain for a week at a time. Yesterday afternoon Doctors Heenreut and Hoeisler operated for the removal of the bullet, which was found completely covered with a long growth. The bullet had been flattened into a shape resembling a horse shoe.

LYNCHED BY MASKED MEN.
Missourian Who Murdered His Friend Taken From Jail and Hanged.
A sensational lynching took place at Steelville, Mo. On the 2d of January, 1888, Lewis Davis and David Miller, friends and neighbors, started to town to pay their taxes. Miller never reached town, and two weeks later his body was found with a bullet through his head and the pockets turned inside out. Davis was arrested and the bullet fitted the pistol of the prisoner, which was a peculiar bore. Davis was taken to St. Louis for safe keeping, and was returned to Steelville a few days ago for trial. A few days after, fifty masked men road into town, captured the Sheriff and jailor, and battered their way into the jail. When Davis' cell door was forced a terrible fight took place. The prisoner, armed with a piece of iron from his bedstead, knocked three of the lynchers senseless and wounded a half dozen others. He was shot through the arm before he was finally overpowered. A rope was placed around his neck and he was led a half mile from town, where he was swung up. He defied the mob to the last.

LEWIS DAVIS LYNCHED.
Brutal Work of a Mob in Crawford County, Mo. CURA Mo. Sept. 24 - Lewis Davis
CUBA, Mo., Sept. 24.—Lewis Davis, who for six months has been confined in the St. Louis jail on the charge of murdering his neighbor and friend, David Miller, and who was brought here last Tuesday for trial at the Circuit Court now in session, was taken from jail and hung by a mob. Masked men came into town about two o'clock this morning, battered down the iron doors of the jail, led him away and lynched him.

HIS CRIME.

Davis was charged with the murder of David Miller on the 2d of last January. On that day Miller left home to meet Davis and go to town twelve miles off, to pay his taxes. He never returned and, after a week's search, was found murdered, shot through the head and his pockets rifled. The bullet found in his brain fitted the pistol found on Davis, which had a peculiar rifle in the bore. There were other circumstances that pointed to Davis' guilt including proven falsehoods told by Davis as to his whereabouts. He would have been mobbed at the time he was arrested, but was taken to St. Louis for safe-keeping. A jury had been selected to try him and the case would have been called at 11 o'clock to-morrow.

THE LYNCHING.

This morning, between 2 and 3 o'clock, a runner came to the Sheriff and informed him that there was a mob coming, and he sent R. P. Dunlap, deputy sheriff, to inform Judge Bland, who was stopping at the hotel, and got some advice as to what to do; but the deputy only got a short distance when he met the mob, about forty masked men, who took him in charge and marched him back to the jail. They then went to a blacksmith shop and procured coal chisels and hammers and returned to the jail and cut the door down.

Only one guard was on duty at the jail and he was soon mastered. Davis fought desperately with a piece of the heavy bedstead in his cell, but was overpowered and led away with a rope around his neck. Every street was guarded; no one was allowed to witness the tragedy.

They put a rope around Davis' neck and forced him out and took him about a half mile north of Steelville, on the Cuba road, and hung him to the limb of a post oak tree, immediately over the grave of Pat Wallace, who was hung by a mob October 4, 1886, for the murder of the Logan family.

Circum Court was in session last week and will meet next week. Davis' case would have come up for trial Monday. The jury was already selected and was composed of the best men in Crawford County, and there is no doubt that Davis would have been convicted of murder in the first degree. No doubt the mob was enraged by the acquittal of Elbert Clonts, who was tried here last week under an indictment for the murder of his father some three years ago.

WILL BE INVESTIGATED.

The better class of society of this county discourage mobs and mob violence, and are very anxious that the guilty parties be brought to justice. There is strong suspicion that the leaders of this mob are some of the same parties that lynched Pat Wallace two years ago, and the matter will be investigated, as Judge Bland has ordered a special grand jury composed of the representative men of the county to inquire into the matter, and says all violators of the law must be punished to the full extent of the law.

The light brightening—that is, the fog growing more luminous, without appearing to thin—the boat's outline lay visible, together with her furniture, such as the sail and the oars. I tenderly laid Imogene's cold hand down, and turning the sail over found—as I had expected—the mast lying under it; and, partly peering and partly groping, I made out an iron clamp fitted to the foremost thwart or seat, with a hollow under it in the bottom of the boat for receiving the heel of the mast.

I lifted the spar and very easily stepped it, discovering that the halliards for hoisting the sail were ready rove through a small block seized to the head of the mast. I hauled upon this rope to clear the sail, and perceived it to be shaped like a lug, fitted to a pard, only the yard was arched, causing the head of the sail to appear like a bow when the arrow is drawn upon it. Before setting the sail I went aft, and by dint of feeling and staring discovered a rope grummet or hempen hook fastened to the larboard horn, but close in, so that it lay out of sight against the boat's stern. 'Twas very clear that this was meant to receive an oar for steering, but whether or not it would serve my turn for that purpose. So, without more ado I rove an earth through the grummet, then hoisted the sail, making the tack fast to the larboard horn on the bow, and came aft with the sheet.

The boat instantly felt the pressure, and the wind being abaft the beam she slipped along like a sledge, as you will suppose, when I say that her bottom was shaped like the side of a pea shell, and that her whole frame might have been imitated from one of those black pods of seaweed which are furnished by nature with wire-like projections, and which may be found in plenty upon our seacoast. The oar controlled her very capitally.

The double motive I had for getting away from this place—dest, to run out of the fog and so get light to enable me to minister to Imogene, and next to remove myself so far from the Death Ship as to render pursuit hopeless even should the thickness in the bay clear up and enable Vanderdecken to recover his boat which I had cut adrift; this double motive. I say, lifted my anxiety and eagerness to the height of madness. My dearest lay with her head toward me, and in the glistening white obscurity I could discern her pale face upon the pillow of my coat, but could not tell whether her eyes were open or shut. She did not moan: she lay as still as the dead. I asked her if she was in pain. She said no, but in a voice so feeble that I had to bend my ear to catch the syllable.

I could not think of her but as slowly dying to the streaming away of her precious blood. What to do I knew not. And in addition to this dreadful state of despair was the obligation upon me to watch the boat, and shrewdly and seriously attend to my course by the warning suri-thunder floating back against the wind from the echoing strand. From time to time I would address Imogene, always with a terror in me of winning no reply, of touching her and finding her dead. Once she answered that she believed the bleeding in her shoulder had stopped; the icy coldness was gone, and there was a small smarting there as if she had been burnt, but nothing that she could not easily endure. But I knew by the tone of her voice that she spoke only to give me comfort; either that she was suffering above the power of her love for me to conceal in her faltering whispers, or that her strength was unequal to the labor of utterance.

Yet, as I have said, what could I do? I was no chirurgeon; and I wonder that my heart did not break to the bending of my scorching eyes upon my love lying wounded and bleeding at my feet.

An hour passed; the fog still compassed us, but the white splendor of the moon was upon it. Methought that I heard Imogene whisper. I dropped on my knee, and she asked for water. I let go the steering oar that jammed in the grummet and that could not therefore go adrift, and with great trouble found the little cup that I had hidden in one of the bags, and poured some water out of the pitcher into it. She moaned in pain when I put my arm under her head to raise it; but she drank greedily, nevertheless, and thanked me in a whisper when I tenderly let sink her head on to the jacket.

I resumed my place at the oar, and through the blackness drove the boat, the sail pulling briskly, the water shining very brightly in our wake, and, as my ear seemed to fancy, the noise of the surf dwindling somewhat, whence I conjectured we were hauling off the coast and standing more directly seaward. I do not know that I should have been without hope for my teloved if it had not been for the haunting and blasting thought that nothing but misery could attend association with Vanderdecken and his doomed ship. It seemed to me now—though on board I had been too eager to escape with her, too wrapped up in my love for such consideration to occupy my mind—that nothing less than the death of one of us could expiate our involuntary and unhappy connection with the banned and fated craft. Ships that spoke her perished, often with all hands; misfortunes pursued those who merely sighted her. What sort of death could the Curse involve for one who had lived for years or for weeks in the monstrous fabric, who had conversed familiarly with her abhorred occupants, who had been admitted into close inspection of her secret life, beheld the enactment by Vanderdecken in his sleep of the impious and horrible drama of his Christ-defying wrath, eat of his bread, drank of his cup, yea, and hearkened with sympathy to his talk of home, to his yearning speech concerning those he loved there?
Suddenly the fog broke up. It was then about 2 o'clock. The vapor floated into league-long streaks, lunar tinted here and there into an aerial mockery of the rainbow, and over the edge of one great steam-like body the moon, with an ice-like diamond splendor of radiance looked down upon us out of a pool of black sky. The lustre had something of the sharpness of daylight, only that the flooded pearl of it wore the complexion of death, all things showing out wan. And in that illumination the delicate gold of Imogene's hair melted into the extreme pallor of the forehead on which it stirred to the wind, and her lips were of the color of her cheeks, and her half-closed lids like wax.

I let go the ear to kneel and look at her. She lay so still, with such unheeding eyes that I made sure she was dead, and my brain reeled as though my heart had stopped.

I said hoarsely and hollowly, "Imogene."

The fringe of her eyelids trembled, and I marked a faint smile on her lips.

"Dearest," cried I, "how is it with thee?"

She returned no answer.

I said: "I shall be able to see the wound now, and perhaps check the bleeding. I can cut the dress clear of the shoulder and you need not stir."

She exclaimed—but, my God how feebly!—"Dearest, let me lie as I am," speaking with a sort of sigh between each word. And then she added, "Kiss me."

I pressed my lips to hers; they were cold as the mist that was passing away in wroaths and clouds. I saw how it was and let her have her way. It would have been cruel to touch her with more than my lips. And even though I should have cut away her apparel to the wound and saw it, what could I do? Suppose the bleeding internal—the bullet lodged within, the lung touched, or some artery severed?

HE BEATS HIS WIFE TO DEATH, DROWNS HIS CHILD AND TRIES TO EVADE ARREST BY SUICIDE.

HOPKINSVILLE, Ky., Oct. 29.—Information from Guthrie, Todd County, gives the details of an inhuman tragedy that occurred near there Saturday. A colored man named Smith became infuriated at his wife and beat her to death. Being pursued by the sheriff, he then grabbed up his little child and fled, and upon reaching the barnyard he threw the child into a pond, where it was drowned. The officer attempting to arrest him, Smith also sprang into the water, resolved to perish rather than be taken alive, but help was called and he was drawn out and carried to Springfield, Tenn., where he is in jail. The feeling is so strong against him that he may be lynched. The tragedy had its origin in family matters, Smith being jealous of his wife.

In the United States Circuit Court in New York, yesterday, Judge Benedict sentenced six counterfeiters of United States currency to various terms of imprisonment. Five of the men were Sicilians, members of the band of which counterfeiter Russo—already sentenced—was the head, and one of them, Condetero Bettini, was the associate of the men now in prison for murdering Flaccomio.

An unknown man claiming to be from Chicago was among the strikers at the spike mill of Dilworth, Porter & Co., at Pittsburg, yesterday, endeavoring to influence them to use dynamite to gain their aims. The strikers, however, would give him no encouragement but told him they would win the strike by peaceable means or not at all.

Mrs. Carrie Turner, a teacher in the Little Rock (Ark.) University, is supposed to have committed suicide. The lady disappeared and her body was found in the Arkansas river. Mrs. Turner is a daughter of Judge Chamberlain, a prominent citizen, and ranks high as an artist. An unfortunate marriage and separation is given as the cause.

The second session of the Mexican Congress committee, before whom the accusation against ex-President Gonzales has been pending since 1884, reported yesterday that there was no foundation for the charge. The Chamber of Deputies approved the report, thus ending the case. Great excitement followed the action of the Deputies.

Charles Diete, a German carpenter, 53 years old, committed suicide by hanging himself during Sunday night in his room, at 408 Seventh avenue, New York. Diete was a non-union man, and had work only in spells when labor was scarce. Lately he had run behind in his rent, and his landlord had notified him Saturday to move.

Gen. Henry B. Clitz, of the army, retired, who has been missing from his home in Detroit since Thursday last, his mind being disordered by ill health, was seen at London, Ont., on Saturday, and took an East-bound train in the afternoon. Nothing further is known of his movements.

The steamer Saganaw, of the Clyde Line, was at her dock in New York yesterday loading for a trip to the West Indies, when she suddenly listed to the right side toward the dock; the water poured into her open portholes, and before the port-holes could be closed the steamer sank. No one was hurt. She will be raised.

A herd of sixty cows was struck by a Hartford and Putnam train on Saturday night at a grade crossing and curve near Bolton Notch, Conn., and fourteen were killed. The high rate of speed alone saved the train from being hurled down a forty-five-foot embankment. The train ran a mile before it could be stopped, the air-pipe having been broken by the shock.

A decision has been given at Winnepeg, Man., continuing the injunction against the crossing of the Canadian Pacific tracks by the local government until such time as the decision of the Supreme Court at Ottawa has been given upon the constitutional point of the right of Manitoba to charter the road in question.

Judge Blodgett, of the Federal Court, yesterday morning, on the petition of the Bell Telephone Company, granted an injunction restraining the Cushman Telephone Company from infringing upon the patents of the former company in Indiana.

Captain Merriman, of the American ship Syren, arrived in New York yesterday on the Ablianca. The Syren, which was bound from Baltimore for San Francisco, put into Rio Janeiro on June 28 and was condemned and sold. Her cargo of coal was sold for $12,000.

The corner-stone of the big Spreckels sugar refinery at the foot of Reed street, Philadelphia, was laid with appropriate ceremonies yesterday afternoon. Adolph Spreckles, the son of Claus Spreckels, placed the corner-stone in position amid the cheers of the invited guests.

Adrian C. Lave, who holds $3,800 in bonds of the Virginia Midland and Richmond Terminal Railroad Company, has obtained an injunction preventing the payment of interest on the bonds of the company until his own claim for interest from January, 1885, is forthcoming.

Twenty-one women in convention yesterday nominated Miss Alice D. Stockton of Wheaton as candidate of the Equal Rights party for Governor of Massachusetts. The candidate is twenty-six years of age.

The report that Eli Perkins, the lecturer, got into difficulty with a railroad restaurant keeper at Winehistor, Ky., last Saturday, proves to have been unfounded. The genial lecturer was in New York city at the time.

Captain Steent and seven sailors of the German bark Apotheker Diesing arrived in New York yesterday from Rio Janeiro on the steamer Ablianca. Their vessel was lost on October 7, fifty miles east of Point Adelaide, Brazil.

Tom Standifer, a noted deperado and horse thief of the Pan Handle, has been captured by Deputy United States Marshal Bowling and will be taken to Wichita, Kan., on a charge of stealing a herd of ponies from Commanche Indians.

P. S. Matthews, the wealthiest saw-mill owner and lumberman of Texarkana, was fatally stabbed by a negro employed at the mill yesterday morning.

Early yesterday morning fire destroyed the Fariday Carbon Works and Ackerman's axle factory on Thirty-third street, Pittsburg. Loss about $90,000; fully insured.

John Carle, jr., head of the old wholesale drug house of John Carle & Sons, New York, died Sunday in the eighty-fourth year of his age.

Fire in West Covington, Ky., yesterday destroyed the tannery of J. H. Deglow and damaged the brewery of Meyer & Reidlin. Loss, $30,000.

The statement is made that Mike Conly, who was last week defeated by Joe McAuliffe in a glove contest, will permanently retire from the prize ring.

Emperor William, in a speech on Saturday, sharply rebuked the Berlin press for quoting the Emperor Frederick in unfavorable comparison with himself.

The schooner Pensaukee, with 36,000 bushels of "Old Hutch's" wheat on board, sank in the St. Clair River yesterday.

A colored man named Smith murdered his wife and child in Todd County, Ky., on Saturday. Lynchers are after him.

John Hillfoyle, a letter-carrier, was killed by Patrick Pedar, a bar-tender, in a saloon in Halstead street, Chicago, yesterday afternoon.

The little town of Hale, Mo., on the Chicago, Burlington and Kansas City Railway, was nearly wiped out by fire Sunday night.

The Czar and Czarina reviewed the maneuvers of the Black Sea fleet at Sebastopol yesterday.

The Emperor visited Hamburg and laid a corner-stone.

The English papers continue to comment on the Sackville-West letter.

Lord Claude Hamilton is coming to America.

Suicide.

HOPKINSVILLE, Ky., Oct. 29.—Information from Guthrie, Todd county, gives the details of an inhuman tragedy that occurred near there Saturday. A colored man named Smith became infuriated at his wife and beat her to death. Being pursued by the sheriff, he then grabbed up their little child and fled, and upon reaching the barnyard he threw the child into a pond, where it was drowned. The officer attempting to arrest him, Smith also sprang into the water, resolved to perish rather than be taken alive. But help was called, and he was drawn out and carried to Springfield, Tenn., where he is in jail. The feeling is so strong against him that he may be lynched. The tragedy had its origin in family matters, Smith being jealous of his wife.

PITTSBURGH, Sept. 25.—About 9% o'clock last evening a north-bound engine on the southwest branch of the Pennsylvania Railroad, running at the rate of thirty miles an hour, struck a cow between Fairchance and Uniontown, throwing the engine off the track and completely overturning it, instantly killing Leander Miller, residing at Fairchance. SENATOR SHERMAN thinks that the annexation of Canada is near at hand, and Representative Butterworth proposes some steps toward the attainment of that end. Professor Goldwin Smith, however, argues that political union is far remote and that the practical need of both parties is an assimilation of customs duties. Both are probably right in maintaining that political union is the ultimate destiny of the Dominion, but wrong in their present theories. The assimilation of duties is impracticable. Sixty-five millions of people will not change their tariff laws to accommodate four millions.
