At Rocheille, Saturday night, a Mr. Walker, while walking with his friend, Mr. Harrold, shortly after dark, was shot in the head by a negro man with a shotgun. One shot entered the head in front, and hitting the bone glanced and made only a scalp wound. The proper medical attention was given him, and the shot was soon found. The negro was at once arrested and placed in the county jail. It is believed, both by Mr. Walker and Mr. Harrold, that the shot was intended for the latter gentleman. In a riot at Eastman years ago, Mr. Harrold and the negro were engaged on opposite sides, and it is thought that the negro tried this method of putting an end to his antagonist after this long time. At one time lynching was feared. When it became known that a man had been shot in so cowardly a manner there were numerous threats of making short work of the would-be assassin.

A case showing criminal neglect on the part of some of the city or county officials, was brought to light in the City Court at Atlanta, Monday. March 20 a negro girl was sent to the stockade for a short time for disorderly conduct and quarrelling with a woman named Robinson. At the expiration of this sentence, she was taken to the jail, where she has been ever since. Solicitor O'Bryan has been working on this case for some time, but can find no warrant nor any other paper to justify the woman's incarceration. Bailiff Crim has spent several days searching for the Robinson woman, but has failed to find her. Monday Mr. O'Bryan called the attention of Judge Van Epps to the girl, and informed him of his inability to find anything more about her than the date of her reception in jail. "The grand jury should make an investigation and find out what officer has been so derelict in the discharge of his duty," said Judge Van Epps. The girl stated that she had been charged with stealing a hat, but didn't know why she was in jail so long. Judge Van Epps ordered that she be set at liberty.

WOULD-BE LYNCHERS. A Georgian Makes a Dash for Liberty and Escapes the Rope.
ATLANTA, Ga., July 20.—A desperate attempt at lynching took place Tuesday night in Fayettesville, a little town twelve miles out. Last week an eighteen-year-old colored boy named Rube Jones was arrested for assault with intent to rape. He entered the room of a young lady, who held him until help came. The day after there were rumors of lynching. These were quelled, however, and the committal trial was had.

Testimony for the defense seems to have aroused the ire of some of the citizens, and Tuesday night a body of armed men presented themselves and demanded that the prisoner be turned over to them. J. W. Brown, the sheriff, refused to comply. Some one suggested breaking down the doors, and no sooner had some one taken the lead than a rush was made for the blacksmith shop. Supplied with tools, a rush was made for the doors.

The jail is a good one, having three doors fastened by good locks. It took but a few minutes to batter down the first, a wooden door. The second was unlocked and received no damage. The third, an iron door, was locked and then again the blows fell fast and hard. The powerful blows rained upon the lock soon forced it back so that it could be pried off.

Then four of the party sprang into the jail to secure the man. He was not caged, and as they went around one side of the cells he made a dash for liberty right through the crowd at the entrance. So unexpected was his attempt that he got beyond the crowd before they realized what had happened. Some one exclaimed "Shoot him!" and the report of a pistol aroused a number of the citizens. On went the criminal, with the crowd in pursuit. Three more shots were fired, and then nothing more was heard of the lynching party. Every one thought that the man had been killed.

Wednesday morning, however, A. E. Stokes, clerk of the court, said that he went out on the porch Tuesday night and inquired the cause of the shooting. Some one told him to get back in the house and he would not be hurt. After all was quiet he ventured out again, and saw some one on the porch. It was the rapist. He had eluded his pursuers by crawling under Mr. Stokes' house. He told Mr. Stokes that he had been shot in the head. The last seen of him he was going by the Red Wine hotel. Wednesday morning he was tracked two or three hundred yards from Mr. Stokes' house, but nothing further has been heard from him. He is still at large.
rube-jones-fayetteville-1888-07-17.A3:
GEORGIA.

Gainesville's electric lights have just begun to glimmer.

A branch of the Farmers' Alliance has been organized at Tennille.

A number of commissions await the governor's signature at the executive department.

Wednesday, a commission was issued to Adam Davenport as school commissioner of Fannin county.

Hanna & Marsh of Florida will establish the daily and weekly Herald in Rome. The daily will be an afternoon paper.

Sallie Peek (colored) of Athens, who had a child badly turned Monday, lost a $10 bill and a check for $40 by the fire.

Gen. James Longstreet has written that he would be at the reunion of the Phillips Georgia legion, which occurs at Dalton on Aug 17.

Edwin Williams cut Robert Gill three times with a penknife in self-defense at St. Simon's Wednesday. The wounds are not dangerous.

The legislative race in Oglethorpe county has narrowed down to three candidates, O. H. Arnold, J. T. Olive and W. C. Birchmore, and they are putting in lively work.

The Georgia Pacific telegraph company and the Buena Vista telegraph company sent their quarterly returns to the comptroller Wednesday, the former $9 40 and the latter $1 75.

At Jasper, Ben Davis went to John Mann's Wednesday morning, called him out, and shot him twice in the back as Mann turned to leave him. Mann is in a dangerous condition. Davis left.

Murray county has ordered primaries to be held on Aug. 4 for the purpose of ascertaining the choice of the county for governor and congressman. The vote will be taken by ballot direct for the candidates.

At Fayetteville a desperate effort was made Tuesday night to lynch a colored prisoner who was held for attempted rape. It took about an hour to batter down the doors, when the victim jumped through the crowd and escaped in the darkness.

At a meeting of the directors of the Northeast Georgia fail a few days ago, John E. Talmadge was elected to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of President W. D. O'Farrel. Wednesday Mr. Talmadge declined the office, as its duties would interfere with his business.

Hon. Thomas Hardeman of Macon is wearing a smile at having been pleasantly remembered by Mrs. Hayes, daughter of ex-President Jefferson Davis. The lady sent from Colorado Springs to the duly appreciative colonel, five excellent photographs of herself and husband and children.

At Atlanta Wednesday, Capt. Kell commissioned George B. Boddis as junior second lieutenant of the LaGrange Light Guards. An application was filed by Col. Jesse Bull of the Sixth Georgia battalion for tents to use in an encampment. The tents will be sent on receipt of bond for their safe return.

A half nude negro man was perambulating about Georgetown last week frightening women and children. He was caught by the colored people and furnished an escort of three, who conducted him between two loaded muskets across the bridge, and after exacting a promise from him never to return, set him free.

At Athens workmen commenced work, Wednesday, on the new store houses of Messrs. Talmadge and Caruthers, which will be rapidly pushed to completion. The contractors will also commence immediately on Capt. Bucker's cotton warehouse, which will be finished in time for the storage of the next cotton crop.

Mrs. Mary E. Hill, an old lady of Ben Smith district in Gwinnett county, received notice Tuesday that her application for pension was allowed, and that she was entitled to $2,731 13. She is the widow of Joshua Hill, who enlisted with the federal army and as such she thus receives the bounty. She has been in hard circumstances for long years.

At Rome Wednesday, at a meeting of the stockholders of the Merchants' national bank, it was resolved to increase the capital stock to $150,000. The bank is in a very good condition. The stock of the First national bank will also be increased at an early date. A magnificent new building is being erected by this bank, which will be finished by Sept. 1. The stock of both banks is far above par.

A call is to be issued for the reunion of the Second Georgia battalion, composed of the following companies: Company A, of Columbus; companies B and C, of Macon, and company D, of Griffin. This battalion was commanded by Maj. Thomas Hardeman, and did good service. It is suggested that the surviving members of this battalion meet with other veterans at Newnan on July 21 and hold a grand reunion.

Charles Rose, the escaped convict from Senator Brown's coal mince, is said to be in Florida. A few days ago an Atlanta man saw him in Jacksonville and spoke to him. The following day, after being recognized and spoken to by the Atlantian, Rose turned up missing. He probably thought that it would not do for him to remain there any longer under the circumstances.

At a mass-meeting of the democracy of Lowndes county, held at Valdosta Tuesday, Dr. N. A. Williams, C. Converse, Jr., T. M. Ray, Col. W. S. West, Hon. J. W. Hogan and Hon. J. W. Harrell were elected delegates to attend the gubernatorial convention. A resolution was adopted indorsing the administration of Governor Gordon, and instructing the delegates to vote for his renomination and the renomination of the present statehouse officers.

The melon raisers along the line of the Georgia Southern and Florida railroad are getting in their returns, and it is now found that they have averaged from $80 to $85 a car. These are net receipts and are entirely satisfactory. So far there have been eighty cars brought up from the melon region, and Col. Henry Feagin and others have more in the field. It is estimated that no less than 5,000 cars of melons will be shipped over this road next season.

Col. A. E. Buck, chairman of the republican central committee, has put his foot down on another state convention, and in lieu has called a meeting of the committee to put out an electoral ticket. The colored contingent prefer a convention, and when the committee is called together, they will try and get a convention ordered over Col. Buck's protest. The committee is to meet on July 26. A state ticket is hardly probable, as no one can be secured who will run for governor.

The amount of money paid out on July 14 by Treasurer Jewett for labor performed during the month ending on that day, was $32,000. This did not include materials of any kind. Capt. Tecel Smith.

CONDENSED NEWS.
Benjamin McKenzie, another member of the Johnson gang of counterfeiters, has been arrested at Sarnia, Ont.

Three boys, all about 12 years of age, have been arrested at Chicago for picking and tapping tills. They had about matured a plan to rob a bank.

Six lumbermen were swept away by the mad current and drowned in the Bow river, Manitoba.

Senator Gorman says the reason he did not want the national chairmanship is that it would seriously interfere with his business.

It is thought the threatened strike on the Chicago street railways has been averted.

Col. Dan Lamont's house at McGranville, N. Y., has been burglarized, and important papers relating to the Cleveland campaign of 1884 and the Hill campaign of 1885 have been stolen. He has an army of detectives looking for the thieves.

Some drunken men took a keg of beer in a small boat at Louisville, and went for a ride. The boat capsized and three were drowned.

An old lady, named Carr, alighted from one train and was run over by another and fatally injured, at Wyoming, Ont.

The report that Sister Mary Frances Clare Cusack, known as the Nun of Kildare, had renounced Catholicism is pronounced untrue.

Three little girls went to bathe in the Coon river at Des Moines and were drowned.

When a mob broke open the jail at Fayethville, Ga., to lynch Rube Jones, he made a dash for liberty and escaped.

Congressman Randall's condition is unchanged.

The body of J. D. Scott, manager of the M. R. Townsend farm, near Little Rock, has been found in the woods near by. He had been missing since Saturday. It is supposed he was murdered.
rube-jones-fayetteville-1888-07-17.A5:
Escaped from the Lynchers.
ATLANTA, Ga., July 20.—At Fayetteville, Ga., a mob broke open the doors of the jail expecting to lynch Rube Jones, aged 18, imprisoned on a charge of rape. Jones was not manacled, and made a successful dash for liberty, escaping through the mob. He is at large, but wounded.

Coast Cullings.
A band of eight buffaloes was seen a few days ago near Fort Miles, Mont., northwest of the Popular River. The Indians are greatly excited at the news.

The Assessor completed the assessment rolls of Fresno county weich shows that the total taxable property amounts to $38,225,267, an increase of $21,302,671 over last year.

At a special committee meeting of the American party at San Francisco an address was adopted embodying the fundamental principles of the party, which, will soon be printed and distributed throughout the State.

Company C, of the Second Cavalry regiment, stationed at the Presidio, has been ordered from Fort Bidwell to proceed to the Klamath reservation in Oregon, where the command will be engaged to eject squatters from Indian lands.

President Wetmore, of the Viticultural Commission, who just returned from a tour of inspection, says the grape crop is very promising. There has been no mildew or grasshoppers to interfere with the crop. Should the vineyards escape dry north winds the yield will probably reach from twenty to twenty-five millions.

At Fresno, about 2 o'clock Friday morning, while the barkeeper of the Fountain saloon was making up his cash preparatory to closing up for the night, two masked men sprang in from the rear of the saloon and at the point of pistols compelled him to give up the contents of the safe, some $300. The robbers escaped.

In the roundhouse at Winslow, Arizona, Thursday evening, a fireman named Snyder had a few words with a night watchman about some oil, and the latter shot Snyder twice. The latter died in ten minutes. The murderer narrowly escaped lynching by a mob, and was taken to St. Johns for safe-keeping.

Three San Francisco Chinese highbinders fired at Yee Lock, a member of a rival highbinder society, on Clay street, in the Chinese quarters, Friday afternoon, one shot taking effect in Lock's hand. Three detectives who had witnessed the attack started in pursuit of the assailants and captured them all after a hard chase.
Over 500,000 cocoons have arrived at the headquarters of the State Board of Silk Culture, from various counties in California. These cocoons have been spun by worms reared from eggs sent out by the Board in the months of May and June, of the present year. Several hundred thousand more cocoons are arriving in daily installments of six or seven thousand. Operators will be engaged in reeling silk until the beginning of next season.
snyder-killed-winslow-1888-07-05.A3: L. W. Davis shot and killed a man named Reinhold Schneider at Winslow on the afternoon of the 4th. The coroner's jury found that Davis did the killing criminally, unlawfully and with malice aforethought.

WASHINGTON, July 6.—Pension was granted to Chas. E. Miller, of Kingman, Ariz.

A postoffice was established at Edith, Maricopa county, Ariz., and Judson G. Todd appointed postmaster.

WASHINGTON, July 6.—The President vetoed the bills granting pensions to Nathaniel D. Chase, Harriet Hooper and William M. Campbell, Jr., and the bill for the relief of Van Buren.

HELENA, Montana, July 6.—A band of about eight buffalos was seen a few days ago forty miles northwest of Poplar River. The Indians are greatly excited at the news.

SAN FRANCISCO, July 6.—Company C. of 2nd Cavalry regiment stationed here has been ordered from Fort Bidwell to proceed to Klamath reservation in Oregon, where the command will be engaged to eject squatters from Indian lands.

SAN FRANCISCO, July 6.—Judge Wilson has refused to grant the application of Y. Nanlander and Fred Sharon for change of venue in the suit brought against them as executors of Sharon's estate by Mrs. L. H. Burling to recover $500,000 paid to Sharon in trust for her husband.

HELENA, Mont., July 6.—Daniel P., a two-year-old, belonging to the stable of Morehouse, Blevins & Co., Helena, ran three-eighths of a mile yesterday at the Montana Association meeting in 34% seconds, beating the record for distance by one fourth of a second as made by Cyclone, a California horse last year.

ALBUQUERQUE July 6.—In the round House at Winslow Arizona, yesterday evening a fireman named Snyder had a few words with the night watchman about some oil and the latter shot Snyder twice and he died in ten minutes. The mnrderer narrowly escaped lynching by a mob and was taken to St. Johns for safe keeping.

WASHINGTON, July 6.—The house went into committee of the whole on the tariff bill, the pending paragraph being that relating to iron or steel railway fish plates or splice bars. Buchanan's motion to strike out the paragraph was rejected. The reading of the bill then progressed the motions made on the republican side to strike out many of the paragraphs being rejected generally without division and with little debate.

Pittsburgh July 6—The Battery of boilers at the tannery of A. & J. Grasez & Ingler at Alghany City, exploded this afternoon wrecking several buildings and seriously injuring six persons. Three will die. Engineer Witzle was thrown through the roof of the tannery and landed in the yard against his residence 60 feet away. A section of the boiler struck the school house 1200 feet away. Fully 60 men were at work in the tannery.

Chicago July 6—Banerism gave bail for $5,000 this afternoon and was released. Bail was furnished by J. A, Feidler of Chicago, merchant. Three more arrested yesterday are still in jail unable to give bail. Attorneys Donahue and Davis have been retained to defend them in connection with any attorneys selected by the Brotherhood of Engineers. In conversation with Chairman Hogel to-day the men denied all knowledge of dynamite in the car.

Wilksbarne, Pa., July 6—Two passenger trains on the Pennsylvania Northern traveling at thirty miles per hour collided at Butzback station this morning by mistake of an operator. The engineers both saw the danger and after reversing their engines jumped down a hugs embankment. Both engines went down the embarkment into the Susquehanna river. The baggage cars on both trains crashed into the first passenger car and the passengers in this car were all injured. The total number injured reaches twenty-two. Three are believed to be fatally injured.

Chicago, July 6.—J. A. Bauerism, chief engineer of the Aurora, Illinois, Division of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers, was brought here this morning under arrest charged with complicity in the alleged dynamite plot against the Burlington Railway on account of which several arrests were made yesterday. Bauerism's arrest is regarded as very important by railroad officers. Bauerism was seen this morning and stated he knew nothing whatever of the charges against him and that his arrest was a complete surprise. He said he had been quietly at home in Aurora since the strike began. Concerning a letter which Broderick, one of the men who was arrested yesterday, threw out of a car window so hurriedly, neither the U. S. Marshal nor District Attorney would say anything and they positively refused to allow it to be seen.

WASHINGTON July 6.—Farquahart's amendment to the tariff bill increasing and scaling duties in proportion to the size of files prevailed by a vote of 64 to 61. Milla however demanded tellers and the amendment was rejected.

On motion of Vance of Connecticut, the paragraph imposing duty of 35 per cent ad valorem on wood screws was struck out thus restoring the present rate of duty.

Dubois of Idaho protested against the reduction of duty on lead ore which he declared would have injurious effect on silver mining. He offered an amendment restoring existing duty and providing that combination of lead ore with gold and silver ore not to be exempt from duty as lead ore, rejected by a tie vote of 63 to 62. Stone of Missouri offered an amendment providing that combination of lead with silver ore shall not exempt the lead therein from duty.

Reed, Mills and Burrows then had a political debate lasting some time. Mills in reply to Reeds demand for him to define his position attacking the Republican party and its platform.

On vote being ordered Stone's amendment was rejected as was one by Warner restoring the present rate of duty on lead ore. On motion of Mills the clause imposing 35 per cent ad valorem on pen knives and razors was struck out thus restoring the present rate of duty.

Cannon spoke strongly in support of his amendment. The committee rose without action and House took recess till 8 p. m.

ALBANY, N. Y., July 7.—Gov. Hill has called a extra session of the legislature for July 17th, to appropriate funds to provide for convicts in the state prison.

snyder-killed-winslow-1888-07-05.A5:
Murder at Winslow.
Another shooing affray took place at Winslow, Arizona, on the evening of July 4th, which resulted in the death of a fireman named Snyder. It appears that the fireman went to the night watchman, Davidson, for supplies, and a warm discussion ensued which resulted in a fist fight. Davidson was worsted in the melee and went away with the avowed intention of procuring a gun, which he did. Meeting Snyder he immediately opened fire, two of the bullets taking effect in the unfortunate man's body and he expired a few hours after the occurrence. The firemen and engineers organized a vigilance committee for the purpose of hanging the murderer, going so far as to place a rope around his neck, and great excitement prevailed. Two engineers who were cooler than the balance of their comrades, addressed the mob, and urged upon them the necessity of allowing the law to take its course and give the man a chance for life. After a great deal of discussion pro and con, wiser counsel prevailed and the mob dispersed. The murderer, who is an old man, was taken to St. Johns for safe keeping.

Later several shots were exchanged between the Lee boys and Deputy Sheriff McKinny, but no blood was spilled. These young men are the sons of John D. Lee, who was leader of the famous Mountain Meadow massacre.
snyder-killed-winslow-1888-07-05.A7: L. W. Davis was brought up from Winslow by Constable McKinney and lodged in jail, charged with the murder of Reinhold Schneider. From accounts published, this promises to be a hard case, and Davis, if he escapes hanging will, in all probability, get a long term in the penitentiary.

TELEGRAPHIC.
An Epitome of the Principal Events Now Attracting Public Interest
The academy of music was burned at Haverhill, Mass. Loss, $100,000; insurance, $50,000.

A construction train and engine on the Joliet & Eastern road was wrecked by obstructions on the track. Three Italian laborers were instantly killed.

Gus Boyles, aged 19, was hanged for the murder of Wm. Morgan, in the Creek nation, a year ago. He died very hard.

At Buena Vista, Ill., Charles Deckler, a farmer, aged 55, sent his children out of the house and then shot his wife, killing her instantly, and shot himself and cut his throat.

R. B. Parrish, a wholesale shoe dealer at Louisville, Ky., reputed to be worth $100,000, committed suicide because he could not pay a five dollar board bill.

The street railway stables at Wichita, Kan., were burned. Three employees were very seriously burned and otherwise injured. The loss was not ascertained.

David Clark and his wife were found hanging in a corn crib near Saudwich, Ill. They left a paper signed by both, saying they died for each other. Clark was thirty years old.

Fire destroyed half the business portion of Elmoro, Colo., some half a dozen business houses, with contents, being consumed. The loss is estimated at $75,000; insurance $6,000.

The body of Alice Kelly was found in the ou skirts of Ottumwa, Iowa, with the throat cut and the head badly beaten. The nature of the wounds indicate murder.

Hattie de Baum, aged 18 years, was shot and killed by her aunt, Mrs. Jennings, at Terre Haute, Ind. The two had been quarreling for some days.

Josiah Wilder, 62 years of age, a prominent business man of Cincinnatt, committed suicide. The only known cause is an effection of the head which gave him great pain and rendered him despondent.

Three men entered the office of an insurance company at Milwaukee, and engaged the cashier and clerk in conversation. Before they left one of them stole $2,000 from the cash drawer.

In the roundhouse of Winslow, Ariz., a fireman named Snyder had a few words with a night watchman about some oil, and the latter shot Snyder twice. The latter died in ten minutes.

A freight train on the Louisville, New Albany & Chicago railway ran into a small land slide. The locomotive and ten cars were wrecked. David Julian, a brakeman, Engineer Harnet and Fireman Blachman were killed.

Henry Soper, a farm hand, confesses to killing 6 year-old Frankie Williams, kicking him to death because the child followed him to the field to see the cows milked, at Huntington, Long Island.

Mrs. Elizabeth Simon shot and instantly killed Wm. Dowling at Bury's ranch, Wyo. Dowling was assaulting her 8-year old daughter. Mrs. Simon was given a hearing and discharged amid cheers.

A large fire in the business blocks opposite the Erie railway depot broke out at Patterson, N. J. Escape by the ordinary way for the inmates was cut off in a few minutes. Numbers jumped from windows and escaped with slight bruises, but it is reported that several lost their lives.

Fire originating in a sawmill at Alpena, Mich., spread rapidly, and was soon beyond control. All buildings for a space of three blocks wide and half a mile long were consumed causing a loss of about $300 000. Fifteen hundred persons are homeless and several seriously injured.

Matthias Schreiner, a whitewasher, was discovered at Chicago, Ill., burned horribly and diving. He had come home drunk, and his clothes had been saturated with kerosene and fired. His wife, mother-in-law and a boarder are under arrest, and indications are that they were the perpetrators of the horrible deed.

While 300 or 400 people were seated in the grand stand on the grounds of the Yalobusha county, Mississippi, fair association, the supports gave way without warning, and the structure fell to the ground. No one was killed outright, but nearly fifty people were taken from the ruins with broken arms and legs.

Laural Fork meeting house in Weakley county, Tenn., was a scene of a terrible tragedy. Just as the minister was announcing his text a volley of firearms was discharged outside the door. When the smoke cleared away it was found that Ewell Lawson and his son, John, were killed and that three Fuston boys, Tom, Jim and EnoS, and John Porter, were fatally wounded.

— Arrangements for the reunion of the survivors of the Army of the Potomac with the survivors of the Army of Northern Virginia, at Gettysburg, on July 1, 2 and 3, are progressing satisfactorily. George William Curtis will deliver the oration, George Parsons Lathrop a poem, and Bishop Horatio Potter, of New York, the address of welcome.

— Another "prophet" has arisen. His name is Horace Johnson, and he lives at Middle Haddam, Conn. Two months ago he predicted a beard-plucking blizzard between March 12 and 15. Elated at the outcome of his first essay in reading the meteorological riddles of the future, he has predicted that a severe storm will strike the Eastern States between April 7 and 15.

— The Presbyterians of the United States will hold in May a centennial celebration in honor of the completion of the first century of the Church's existence in this country. When the Church was organized in America it had 16 Presbyteries, 177 ministers, 419 churches, and 10,000 members, while to-day it has 389 Presbyteries, 8,328 ministers, 11,212 churches and 750,000 members.

— George N. Hawes died at Millersburg, Ky., last Thursday. During the cholera scourge of 1849 young Hawes had a violent attack of cholera and to all appearances died. He was placed in his coffin, but during the funeral services he recovered consciousness and arose. Since that time he has lived a recluse. He remained in an upstairs room for over five years, and was never known to speak to any one during that time.

A colored man named Hamilton was arrested in Savannah four years ago charged with the murder of the Haertel family. The evidence against him was strong but not sufficient for conviction and he was released. He was employed in the work of tearing down the old jail, and on Saturday, while he was digging at the foundation directly under the cell he occupied while under arrest, the bank caved in on him and a timber fell on him and broke his neck.

A Nogales, Arizona, dispatch says: The recent seismic disturbances and subterranean noises along the Pacific slope in Mexico, have terrified those who remember the earthquake of last May. The people are moving out of the dangerous localities by hundreds. Ever since the first severe shock, on May 3, 1887, the noises and tremblings have continued with increasing violence. The indications of the coming of a serious earthquake or of the bursting forth of a volcano are shown by the peculiar moisture of the earth and the appearance of hot springs which usually precede such disturbances.

A Memphis dispatch of Thursday says: News received here to-day from the Sledge and Mason plantations, a few miles below Australia landing, tells of a killing and lynching which occurred there on Saturday last. Robert Taylor, a white man, shot and killed a negro who attempted to strike him. Another negro, who became involved in a game of cards and cut with a razor a very popular negro, was lynched by men of his own race. They put a rope around his neck and dragged him a hundred yards or so through a creek and up on a levee, where they swung him to a tree.

Prof. John M. Langston, of Virginia, has joined ex-Senator Bruce and Fred Douglass (all negroes) in opposing the scheme to bring about a negro exodus to South America. He thinks the proposed exodus is a fraud from first to last, and that there is no need for it. The negro, he says, is advancing slowly and surely in this country, and cannot better himself by any other country. Langston was for seven years Minister to Hayti, where he saw enough to convince him that negroes are not yet prepared to live in communities by themselves where they have to manage their own political affairs.

On Tuesday of last week, Charles E. Cross, the president, and Samuel C. White, the cashier, of the State National Bank of Raleigh, N. C., absconded, taking a large amount of the funds of the bank with them. They were speedily traced to Toronto, Canada, where they were shadowed until the affairs of the bank were examined; and it being soon ascertained that they had committed extensive forgeries, indictments were obtained against them and they will be extradited and tried in the Wake superior court for that crime. When arrested in Toronto they had with them about $24,000 in cash. It is said their forgeries will reach over $50,000.

Last Friday closed the sixth week of the trial at Brandon, Miss., of Col. Hamilton for the murder of the young Prohibition editor Gambrell. The sensation that day was caused by the Court ordering the sheriff to search every person applying to be admitted into the court room Saturday morning, saying that if any pistols or other deadly weapons were found that he would visit the severest punishment in his power. Since the trial began it has been a notorious fact that the partisans of both sides had pistols in their pockets, and since the trouble between the opposing lawyers, a few days ago, in which the Sheriff prevented blows, a row has been imminent.

The prohibition people of North Carolina have decided to assert themselves during the campaign of this year, and have issued a call for a State convention to be held in Greensborough on May 16 next. The call states the business of the convention to be the election of twenty-six delegates and as many alternates to attend the National Prohibition Convention to be held at Indianapolis June 6, the selection of eleven candidates for Presidential electors, the nomination of a full set of candidates for State offices, the election of a State executive committee, and the full and complete organization of the State.

In an address recently delivered by Major E. A Burke, of the New Orleans Times-Democrat, facts are produced which indicate that the losses in recent years of Southern farmers in the value of their farms have been attended by a large transfer of capital to manufacturing enterprises of various kinds. The number of factories in the South in 1887, according to Major Burke, was 54,176, as against 34,563 in 1880. Capital in factories increased in the period indicated from $179,366,000 to $371,285,000, and the product from $315,024,794 to $529,- 835,000. Despite the fall in prices of farm products there has been an increase of the amount produced, the figures for 1887 being $745,050,696, as against $612,278,318 in 1880.

The railroads in the State of Alabama have been very much damaged by the late heavy rains. The loss of life and property by the recent floods in northern Europe is reported to be very great. At one place on the Elbe fourteen soldiers were killed while endeavoring to break an ice blockade by blasting. A manufacturing chemist in New York says that the world takes a ton of pills a week. There are 292,160 persons in New York city who do not speak English. Four times has the White House been draped in mourning since President Cleveland became its occupant—for Grant, for Hendricks, for Arthur and for Waite. A Kansas widow rode six miles during the recent cold snap to put a mortgage on her place, and the first thing she bought was a celluloid toilet set in a plush case. SAN FRANCISCO, Aug. 1.—At last night's session of the republican state convention, additional nominations for representatives for congress were made, as follows: First district, Judge J. J. DeHaven, Humboldt; Second, John A. Enagar, of Amador; Sixth, General Wm. Van Dever, Reno county; for presidential electors-at-large, John F. Swift and W. H. L. Barnes; First district, T. C. CARTHAGE, Tenn., Aug. 1.—At 10 o'clock last night fifty armed men visited the jail here and took out W. H. Handly, who on September 17th last killed J. B. Worman, deputy sheriff. Handly was to have been tried today. The sheriff refusing to give up the keys, the mob, with axes, crowbars, etc., broke into Handly's cell, took him across the river and hanged him to a tree within sight of the jail.

Revere House, Chicago, Closed.

CHICAGO, August 1,—The Revere house, the leading house on the north side, has been closed, under judgments amounting to $15,000 against the landlord, J. D. Fanning. The guests were requested to vacate, after which the house will be closed. The fixtures cost $50,000 and it is supposed that the liabilities will thus be net.

Hot Weather and Storms.

CHICAGO, Aug. 1.—Dispatches from various points in northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin report yesterday to have been the hottest day in the season, the temperature ranging from 92 to 105. Violent thunder storms are reported from several points and much damage done by lightning, especially about Clinton, Iowa.

MOB LAW.

W. H. Handley Lynched at Carthage

A Band of Fifty Determined Men Take Him from the Jail.
The Courageous Sheriff Does All He Can to Prevent It.
The Self-Assumed Court and Jury Overpower the Officer.
The Murderer of Deputy Sheriff Warman is Then Strung Up to the Nearest Tree Until He is Dead.
CARTHAGE, Tenn., Aug. 1.—At 11 o'clock last night fifty armed men visited the jail at this place and hung W. H. Hanley who killed J. B. Warman, a deputy sheriff, near Rome, in this (Smith) county, while the latter was arresting another party. His trial was set for today, and when his mother and family arrived in town this morning to attend the trial they were met with the news of his death. His mother is now prostrated on account of the affair and it is thought the shock will kill her.

FRUITLESS APPEALS MADE.

When the mob arrived at the jail they found it well guarded by the sheriff and a posse of men, who evidently had some inkling that Judge Lynch's court would hold a stormy session by starlight. The sheriff pleaded with the mob to let the law take its course, and announced his determination to do his duty and protect his prisoner. Neither his appeals or the gun-shots fired from his fortification were of avail. The mob broke down the barred door leading into the family room of the jailer and demanded the keys to Handley's cell. The sheriff reiterated his determination to protect Handley and said he would die before he would surrender the keys, whereupon the mob secured axes, crowbars and other rude implements and battered their way into the apartment of the trembling victim.

THE PRISONER HANGED.

With a rope around Handley's neck the mob hurried across the river with him and swung him up to a large tree within sight of the jail. The body was allowed to hang until this morning when Coroner A. M. Fisher impaneled a jury of inquest the verdict of which was that the deceased came to his death by hanging at the hands of unknown parties. When Handley's remains were brought to Carthage this morning the body showed several severe bruises. There were two large cuts on his head supposed to have been given with the butt of a gun, his arms and wrists were also considerably bruised and showed signs of a great struggle for life.

EXCHANGE OF SHOTS.

During the hanging about thirty shots were exchanged by the mob and posse, but no one was hurt so far as heard from. Great excitement prevails here and in the vicinity, public opinion being about qualily divided for and against Handley. Handley had been confined at the jail at Nashville for quite awhile for protection, and was taken to Carthage but a few days ago. He was well liked during his confinement in Nashville, and made a favorable impression upon the officers. He was about twenty-three years of age.

HANDLEY'S CRIME.

Deputy Sheriff Warman was killed on the 17th of September, 1887, about a mile and a half from Rome, near the fair grounss. Warman had, while attending the fair, arrested a man named Adams, and was returning with him to Rome, when he was overtaken by Handley, who demanded Adams' release. Warman refused to release his prisoner, and Handley shot him. Handley escaped, but was arrested a short while afterward at a house of ill-fame near Riddleton. He was immediately taken to Rome for preliminary trial but a mob had formed and it was with difficulty that the prisoner was taken to Carthage. The mob having learned that he was in jail at Carthage and started for that place. The officers took Handley to the woods. After spending some time in the bushes and eluding a third mob the officer succeeded in getting Handley to New Middleton. There the prisoner was taken by a circuitous route to Lebanon and thence to Nashville by train. Upon being committed to jail at Nashville Handley denied having any connection with the killing and said he knew nothing of the crime until after he was arrested.

LOUISVILLE, Aug. 2.—Dr. Robert Morris, one of the oldest and best known Masons in the United States, died Tuesday morning at his home in Lagrange. About six weeks ago he was stricken with paralysis, since which time he has been slowly sinking. Dr. Morris was born in Mississippi August 31, 1816, and became a Mason in 1846 in Oxford, Miss. He advanced to the Cypic rite in New York city in 1864, and the Rite of Memphis to the nineteenth degree in 1865. Dr. Morris was the acknowledged authority on all Masonic matters, and with Albert Pike, was considered the best posted Mason in the country.

A Juvenile Murderer.

LAFAYETTE, Ind., Aug. 2.—This morning while a number of young boys were congregated on Brown street bridge Burt White and Willie Ellsworth got into a wrangle, and during the controversy White drew a revolver and shot Ellsworth dead, then ran away. He was captured an hour or two after the shooting. White is only seventeen, and for some time has been recognized as the chief cf the "Dirty Dozen," a set of hardened young vagabonds of this city.

Attempted to Murder a Sheriff.

NEW ORLEANS, Aug. 2.—The Picayune's Natchez, Miss., special says a cowardly attempt was made Tuesday night to murder Dr. W. E. Robb, the newly elected sheriff of Catahoula parish, at Harrisonburg, by William and Henry Haltman, who fired on the doctor without warning. Robb is in a critical condition.

Murderer Recaptured.

HELENA, Mont., Aug. 2.—Alexander Wood, colored, who recently escaped from jail at Blackfoot, Idaho, where he was to have been hanged for wife murder on July 20, has been recaptured, and is now on his way to Idaho. He will be hanged on August 17.

Thatcher's steam ginhouse, at Texarkana, worth $5,000, together with twenty bales of cotton, were burned
Thatcher’s steam ginhouse, at Texarkana, worth $5,000, together with twenty bales of cotton, were burned on last Thursday night in Lafayette county, opposite Garland City. One-half the loss on machinery is covered by insurance.

A report reached Warren Friday morning of the killing of two negroes the night before. It seems the trouble grew out of a settlement between a negro and a white man by the name of Gorman. At the settlement the negro was indebted to Gorman and there were some hard words. The negro, accompanied by several others, visited Gorman’s house twice, when rumor says a squad went to the negro’s house and in the difficulty that followed one negro was killed and another mortally wounded, and one report says a white man dangerously cut with a knife.

Jim Sparks, who stabbed Tom Nicholson to death on the 14th of December, 1872, and who has been at large ever since, was arrested Monday in Helena and is now in jail. Sparks, after the murder, eluded the officers and has been living in Missouri and Texas under the assumed name of Wm H. Simms. He came to this county about four years ago and has been engaged in farming. He would probably never have been apprehended except for the treachery of his brother-in-law, one Doc Wise, who became offended at Sparks and reported him to Sheriff Pilloes.

Col. Benjamin F. Hawkins, of Rocky Comfort, and the oldest citizen of southwest Arkansas, died of pneumonia at his home on Red River, four miles from Richmond, on the night of December 30. He was born on December 25, 1812, and was married in 1831. His aged wife still survives him. He came to that county in 1837, and has been an honorable and noted citizen for over fifty years. He was the largest planter in the county, and a great loss to the county and community in which he lived. The remains were buried at Rocky Comfort on Sunday at 3 p. m. at the old amily burial ground, and was witnessed by many of the old settlers, friends and relatives of the departed pioneer.

Last Thursday a stranger rode up to T. P. Varnell's stock yard at Hope and offered for sale two mules for $75. Mr. Varnell did not want to buy and declined the offer. The stranger finally offered to take $60 for the mules, which proposition was accepted by Mr. Varnell, and the money was paid over and the stranger departed. About two hours later another stranger appeared on the scene and claimed the mules, stating that they had been stolen from him. Parties left at once in pursuit of Stranger No. 1, who was overtaken several miles out and brought back Later, a third party, giving his name as Gib Watson, and was known to be connected with the first two strangers, after considerable coaxing, etc., gave the whole game away, and, saying that the scheme was to let the first man get away with the $60, and No. 2 was to come up and claim the property and prove his ownership by No. 3. The booty, it is supposed, was to be divided equally among the three. The first two gave their names as Bill Mitchell and J. J. Goodall, and hailed from Lewisville, Fayette county. All three are under arrest, and will have a preliminary trial on a charge of robbery.

Looks Like Another One.
BALTIMORE, June 29. — A. D. Layton is a farmer living at Florence, Howard county. Yesterday afternoon, while he was working in the fields, and his wife absent from home, a 10 year-old colored boy, who had been left in charge of their two babies, ran to him and said the throats of the children had been cut by a strange man. One of the children is dead, the other may recover. The colored boy is suspected of having committed the deed himself.

Mr. and Mrs. Layton were driven almost frantic with grief, and rushed about like mad and wrung their bands.

The news of the boy's terrible crime spread rapidly throughout the county, and an hour afterward the excitement in the neighborhood was intense. The young fiend bad not gone far from the scene of the terrible crime, and was arrested as soon as the facts became known by Sheriff George Day, who found the boy roaming about the street at Florence. The boy seemed not in the least to realize the fiendishness of his act, and at first denied any knowledge of it. When pressed by the sheriff to give an account of the crime Washington said that he had been playing with the children when a bad man entered and knocked the children down, and that he ran off. Subsequently, however, he admitted that he had cut the children's throats because he was tired nursing them, and that he was left to take care of them too often.

The feeling in Florence and throughout this section of the country toward Washington was intense, and threats of lynching could be heard on all sides. Owing to the boy's age, however, it is not probable that he will suffer mob violence. The boy was brought to Ellicott City and placed in jail.

The boy is very dark and repulsive-looking, having a bead shaped like a cocoanut. He cut the two little girls' throats with a keen-edged butcher-knife which he got from the kitchen, adjoining the room in which he slaughtered his victims.

At a late hour to-night the younger child is sinking rapidly, but it is thought the elder one will recover, though the gash made by the knife will leave a scar.
washington-florence-1888-06.A8:
An Almost Incredible Crime.—A
special dispatch from Mt. Airy to the Baltimore Sun, under date of June 28th gives the following:

Charles Washington, a colored boy, only 10 years old, on Tuesday displayed a criminal propensity seldom seen in one of his age. He deliberately cut the throats of two white children, both of whom are still alive, but in a very precarious condition. The father of the children is Mr. R. D. Layton. He is a tenant on the farm of Mr. Beal A. Warfield, a prosperous farmer, who lives about a mile south of Florence, in Howard county.

On Tuesday afternoon the colored boy was left by the children's mother to attend them while she went to the home of Mrs. Rufus Ridgely, a neighbor, where for some time she has been nursing an invalid. It was nothing unusual for the boy to be intrusted with such a charge. The children's father was at work in full sight of the house, and as he hoed his tobacco he caught frequent glimpses of them as they played in the open doorway. Late in the afternoon he called to the colored boy and told him to bring him some water. The boy was long in obeying the summons. In the meantime Mr. Layton had worked his way over the hill which rises from the house and could no longer see his children. When again near the house and in full sight of it, the boy came with the water. He told Mr. Layton in the most matter-of-fact manner that some one had cut the throats of his children. So incredible did the assertion seem to be that Mr. Layton at first declined to believe it, but he went to the house, and there on the bed lay his two children with the blood streaming from terrible gashes across their throats. The older one is a girl three years of age and the younger is only fourteen months old. The blood had clotted, and the tiny hands of the little ones had besmeared their faces with it. Both were unrecognizable, and both seemed to be in death's grasp. The father for a minute was at a loss how to proceed. He relieved the sufferings of the little ones as best he could. He then closely questioned the colored boy as to who had committed the deed. The boy, in a straightforward manner, told him that a white man had cut the throats and had jumped over the fence and made his escape to the woods. So thorough was he in his account of the affair that he pointed out the exact place where the man had leaped over the fence. On the side of the fence from the house was a plowed field.—Mr. Layton examined this very carefully, but he could discover no footprints, and he was at a loss in what direction to pursue the perpetrator of the crime.

In the meantime Mr. George Ellicott, a neighbor, who had been summoned, reached the house and made the children as comfortable as possible. Later their mother arrived, and she was overcome when she found her children so terribly mutilated. The neighbors rendered such assistance as they could, and Dr. Crawford, of Laytonsville, Montgomery county, was summoned. The windpipe of the boy was found upon examination to be severed just at the prominence known as Adam's apple. His condition is critical and his death is hourly expected. The neck of the girl was gashed severely on the right side, but no arteries were severed. While her condition is serious, it is not regarded necessarily fatal. When her wounds had been dressed and restoratives applied, the little girl rallied, and, in response to a question as to who had cut her, she pointed to the colored boy, and said that he had done it with a big butcher knife, which was subsequently found. The boy then confessed that he had cut the children's throats, and explained as his motive that he was tired minding them.

When Mr. Layton heard the confession he drove to Lisbon, about four miles distance, and swore out a warrant before Squire E. M. Owings for his arrest. The warrant was sent to Constable Stephen Hobbs, but when it reached him, it found him sick, and he at once forwarded it to Sheriff Geo. D. Day, who went to Mr. Layton's house this afternoon and placed the boy under arrest. He was with his mother at the time, and she was only too glad to place him in the officer's charge, as she feared that the anger of the neighbors would manifest itself in violence toward the boy. He was taken before Squire Owings, at Lisbon, this afternoon. Before the crowd of men who gathered to hear the trial he confessed that he had cut the children's throats. He was not at all abashed, and while being examined he most strenuously denied that he had cut the windpipe of the boy, declaring that it was done while the neck was being washed. He was bright and alert, and could not be tripped in his cross examination. He said that he did not wish to kill the children, but he was tired of attending them. He wanted to get them out of the way, and he thought he could do it without killing them. He expressed himself as willing to go with the sheriff if he would treat him kindly. He was committed for the action of the grand jury of Howard county. Sheriff Day this afternoon took his youthful prisoner to Ellicott City, where he was locked up in the county jail. He is a bright-eyed boy, but has a bad face. He is not black, his complexion being a gingerbread color. With his mother he left Washington two or three years ago and removed to Mr. Layton's place. He says his name is not Washington, but Hawkins.

Beulah, the eldest of farmer Layton's two children, whose throats were cut by a ten-year old colored boy a week ago, died on Wednesday morning last.
washington-florence-1888-06.A15: The trial of the boy murderer, Charles Washington at Ellicott City, Md., yesterday, resulted in a verdict of acquittal. This leaves the case shrouded in mystery, and the question arises if the boy did not commit the deed of which he was charged, who did ?
washington-florence-1888-06.A16:
TRIAL OF A LITTLE BOY.
A STRANGE SCENE IN THE HOW-ARD COUNY COURT.
Charles Washington Accused of the Murder of Beulah Layton — Her Little Sister Running Around in the Court—Was the Lad Gullty of the Crime?—The Evidence.

From the Baltimore American.

ELLICOTT CITY, Sept. 11.—A very peculiar case was brought up in court to-day at this place. A small boy, who is supposed to be 10 years old, yet who hardly looks 7, was put on trial for his life. He is charged with the murder of a child not 2 years old. The crime was a cold-blooded one, and it seems incredible that he could have committed it. So incredible does it appear that many will not believe that the youngster did not. This boy is Charles Washington, a copper-colored young thing. He lived in the house of R. D. Layton, a farmer in the Fourth district, near Florence. Their father left this kid with his two little girls, Sadie and Beulah—Sadie nearly 3 years old, and Beulah just 16 months—and an hour after the father found the two children on the bed with their throats cut. The younger was hurt so badly that it died.

The case was set for Monday, but there was so much on the docket that it was not reached until late to-day.

WHEN THE YOUTHFUL CRIMINAL
was brought in every one stared. Here was the smallest shrimp of a boy, looking more like a veritable brownie than anything else. As he sat in the dock he looked lost. Every one stared at him in wonder. When the clerk arose and read the indictment, in which the name of Charles Washington was heard so frequently, the brownie didn't know whether to cry or not. He rubbed his hands and shirt sleeves over his eyes, not quite decided what to do. He held in the salty tears, and wriggled and squirmed till one thought there must be several worms tied in one and sitting there. He rather airily clad. The costume of Eve after the fall was rather less scanty. He wore a ripped shirt, through which his copper skin showed. His trowers, whose lower extremities reached half way between his knees and his waist, were no better. That was all. Judge Miller had the boy placed in a chair before the jury,

SO THEY COULD SEE HIM.

There he wriggled, while his black eyes flashed, though there was a troubled look in them. Late in the afternoon he looked so appealingly at Mr. Wooten that that gentleman said: "What's the matter?"

"I've so hungry," replied the kid. He had had nothing since breakfast.

While the trial went on another child divided the attention of the court. This was another actor in the strange crime. Little yellow-haired Sadie Layton was running around the room, laughing cheerily and making friends with the men. Once she ran past Charlie and even grabbed his arm. The boy wouldn't even look at her as she played around him. The child frolicked on as the trial went on.

There was but little trouble getting a jury, and then State's Attorney J. D. McGuire stated the case. Henry E. Wooten said that if the state could prove that the boy committed the crime they must also show that he was capable of appreciating the enormity and consequences of the crime. William A. Hammond and Mr. Wooten were counsel for the boy.

EVIDENCE OF THE DOCTORS.

The first witness was Dr. Basil Crawford, who attended both the children. He said: I reached the house on the evening of June 20. A lady, a stranger, held one of the children, which afterward proved to be the oldest, in her arms. She told me the child was badly mutilated. There was a deep incision in the neck over the windpipe. The cut extended almost to the vertebrae in the back. After dressing the wound, I asked if the other child was as badly hurt, and said: "I hope the other one's wound is not so serious." "Oh," she said, "she's worse hurt than the other; her windpipe is nearly severed." I found in the younger one's neck an incision from the left margin almost straight across, deep, and nearly severing the windpipe.

Two knives were shown the doctor, one a kitchen knife, and the other a butcher knife. He was asked if either could have made the wounds. His reply was that the butcher knife might have made them. The butcher knife is supposed to be the one with which the wounds were given.

Dr. Ridgely Warfield of Baltimore, who assisted Dr. Crawford, said he helped to dress the wounds next day, and that he considered the wound necessarily fatal, owing to the extreme youth of the patient and the loss of blood. He considered the boy to be between 6 or 8 years old.

STORY OF THE CHILD'S FATHER.
R. D. Layton, the father of the child, was called. He lives in Howard county, near Florence. He said: "I was working about eighty-five yards from the house, in a potato patch, with Baker Bowie. The only persons in the house were the two children and Charlie. When I went into the potato patch Charlie was in one part of the yard and Sis (Sadie) was in another. She started to follow me, when I drove her back. After I had been in the potato field some time I called for Charlie to bring me some water. He answered me, though I didn't see him, and he came to me a few minutes later. He said: 'Mr. Dolph, somebody is in the house cutting the children's throats.' I said; 'Oh, pshaw; there ain't nothing like that,' and then told him to go to the spring. When he came back with the water he told me this again. Then the colored man called to me and asked what the boy had said. I told him, and I went to the house. The steps were bloody, and there was blood upon the floor. Charlie had walked up to the house with me. Both children were on the bed, which was bloody. Sadie had her head toward the head of the bed and was lying on her face. Beulah was at the head of the bed, lying on her face. When coming in from the field Charlie told me that some one had done it and gone up the road. I sent Charlie for my wife and went out to see if I could find any man. Next morning I took Charlie out behind the woodshed, and I told him I would hang him if he didn't tell me the truth. I made a pretense as if to hang him."

By Mr. Wootten—How did you pretend you'd hang him?

"I had a rope. He said a man had done it. Then I made him go and show me where the man had gone after he had done it." Mr. Layton also told how he had discovered a man's tracks and how he had followed them. They turned out to have been made by a neighbor as he returned from his work. Layton considered the boy an intelligent one for his age, and thought he was about 6 or 7.

Meets His Deserts.
ST. LOUIS, Mo., June 26.—William Moore, the colored man who assaulted Mary A. Bingardiner, at Mattoon, Ills. Saturday night, was taken from the county jail at Charleston, at 3 o'clock this morning, and lynched by masked men. Moore's victim is only 16 years old.
william-moore-charleston-1888-06-25.A9:
MOB LAW IN ILLINOIS.
"THE LAW'S DELIY" EXCUSES ONE MORE LAWLESS DEED.
A Negro Charged with Rape Hung at Charleston by a Mob from Other Towns, Which Bulldozed a Railway Conductor—A Worthless Citizen's Deadly Work—Criminal Occurrences in Variety.

CHARLESTON, Ills., June 27.—William Moore, a negro, aged about 43, was taken from jail here by a mob about 1 o'clock yesterday morning and hanged to the framework of a water-tank. On Saturday evening a young girl named Mary A. Bumgardner came here from her home at Effingham by train. Moore was at the depot when the train arrived and she asked him the way to the house of a friend. He said he would direct her, but instead of doing so took the girl to a lonely spot on the roadside and criminally assaulted her. She returned to Charleston and told an officer of the crime. The girl is not well balanced mentally, but she told her story in such a straightforward manner as to convince the authorities of her truthfulness, and Moore was arrested at his home in Mattoon. Monday morning he was brought before Squire McFadden, who, on hearing the girl's statement, held the prisoner in $1,000 bail for the action of the grand jury. He had up to that time been confined in the calaboose at Mattoon, but as there had been some talk of summary vengeance it was deemed advisable to remove the prisoner to the jail here. This was accordingly done Monday night, and, although the threats of lynching were still being occasionally made, the sheriff paid little or no attention to them, not thinking it likely any mob would attack the jail.

Late Monday night, however, a party of men boarded an east-bound freight train at Mattoon, telling the conductor they had important business over east. He said that he could not allow them to ride on his train, but they paid no heed to his orders to get off. The conductor, not understanding the matter, and fearing violence to himself, gave up all effort to rid the trains of its unwelcome passengers, who rode to this city and quietly dropped off the various cars. A reconnoitering party sent on ahead learned that Moore had been securely lodged in jail a couple of hours before. The strangers remained quiet in various portions of town up to about 1 o'clock, when they came to the prison and aroused the jailer. He refused to hand out the keys, and the mob at once proceeded to break in the door. While the parleying was going on the state's attorney, sheriff and other prominent citizens appeared and vainly urged the crowd to refrain from carrying out its design. In a few minutes the avengers had gained an entrance to the jail, and, breaking open Moore's cell, dragged their victim out to the water tank near the depot. All of the lynchers who took actual part in the lynching wore silk handkerchiefs over their faces, and it is said none of them were recognized, although the voices of several sounded familiar to the sheriff and others who protested against lynching the terrified negro.

A turn of the rope was put around Moore's neck and he was asked if he was guilty. He replied that he was not, and in answer to a query as to whether he had anything to say asked to be allowed to sing a hymn. The request was granted and Moore began to sing a hymn, the crowd joining the chorus. The wretched criminal then prayed briefly and several onlookers begged the lynchers to take him back to jail. For answer there were repeated cries of "Hang him!" the victim meantime asking in piteous tones for mercy. He was again asked if he was guilty and reiterated his protestations of innocence, while acknowledging in terror stricken tones that he had taken the girl from the depot for immoral purposes. This satisfied the lynchers, who at once strung him up to the framework of the tank, the masked executioners only refraining from riddling his body with bullets on account of the fear that bystanders might be hit. Moore struggled terribly for a few minutes, but gradually the spasms subsided until at length only slight convulsive twitchings gave evidence that the miserable wretch still had life, these at length ceased also, and the lynchers quietly dispersed, leaving the body swinging in the air. It was cut down in twenty-five minutes by the sheriff, who cared for it until the dead man's wife and daughter came over from Mattoon and took it away.

Before leaving here some members of the lynching party announced that several colored profligates in this city and Mattoon would better leave the vicinity or they would receive early attention. A few years ago a negro who murdered his wife and threw her body into a well was sentenced to the penitentiary for a short term. The lightness of the punishment inflicted on that offender caused general indignation, and it was determined on this occasion to take no chances on the law's delay and uncertainty.

ILLINOIS.
Inundation at Hoopeston—An Incautious Bather Drowned in the Flood. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

HOOPESTON, June 27.—The heaviest rain-fall ever known in this section of the country occurred this morning. Rain commenced falling about 1 o'clock and continued with greater or less force till noon. The Daily Chronicle office, in the basement of the First National Bank building, was flooded to the depth of four feet, and publication was suspended until the water subsided. The office was dry until 7:30, when the rain fell in torrents, and in ten minutes the floor was covered to the depth of four feet. Fred Manly, together with several others, went bathing in the rising water this afternoon at the tile factory, south of the city, and Manly was taken with cramps and drowned before he could be rescued. He was twenty-eight years old and lived with his widowed mother.

Hanged for a Crime He Did Not Commit. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

ALTAMONT, June 27.—To-day's St. Louis Globe, and also the Chicago papers, contained reports of the lynching of Wm. Moore, a colored man, of Mattoon, for the rape of an innocent girl of seventeen years, a resident of this place. This girl, Mary Bumgardner, is known throughout this vicinity as a woman of very bad repute. She is absent from here at present to escape prosecution for the burning of a barn belonging to one of the citizens. The people of this vicinity are very indignant over the affair, from the fact that they are confident this man has been hanged for a crime he never committed.

Struck Hard in His Father's Behalf. Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

CHAMPAIGN, June 27.—A stranger from Texas, with another man, assaulted Hans Hutchinson, at his house here, last night, inflicting knife wounds on the face and head,

while the other man held Hutchinson. A son, aged fifteen, came to his father's rescue, dealing the Texan a blow on the back of his head which crushed his skull. He lies unconscious, and is expected to die. Young Hutchinson is in jail.

Bitten by a Rattlesnake.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MATTOON, June 27.—Thomas Wells, residing near Arthur, was bitten on the finger by a rattlesnake, this morning, while pulling weeds in his garden. He procured medical aid immediately, but the finger is swollen to four times its original size, and his recovery is doubtful, as the poison has permeated his system.

Brief Mention.

The Illinois Division, Sons of Veterans, is in annual encampment at Moline.

James A. Wilson was killed near Sparta on Tuesday by the premature discharge of a blast.

The six-year-old son of William Rostetter was drowned in Walnut creek, near Eureka, on Tuesday.

The Chicago, Wilmington & Vermillion coalworks, at Braidwood, was damaged $10,000 by fire on Tuesday.

Rev. J. H. Stevenson, of Anna, has accepted a call to the pastorate of the Presbyterian Church at Mount Carmel.

Rev. Gilmore Cunningham, Methodist minister at Warensburg, and a well-known member of the Illinois Conference, and Miss Harriet Thompson, daughter of George W. Thompson, a wealthy farmer, were married on Tuesday evening, at the home of the bride's parents, near Decatur.
william-moore-charleston-1888-06-25.A13:
GIVEN BUT TEN MINUTES. A NEGRO RAPIST HANGED BY A MOB AT CHARLESTON, IL.LINOIS.
The Law Takes its Course With a Wife-Murder at Albion, New York — A Mob Defeated at Lebanon, Kentucky — A Negro Brute Shot to Death in Georgia. CHARLESTON, Ill., June 28. —Last Sunday morning at 1 o'clock Mary Baumgardner, a seventeen-year-old servant girl of good reputation, arrived in Mattoon to change cars for Shelbyville, there to visit her uncle. While awaiting the train she allowed William Mtore, a colored man who professed to be employed by the railroad company to wait upon the passengers, to pilot her, as she supposed, to a restaurant to obtain a cup of coffee, but in reality to an isolated place along the railroad, where he assaulted her.

Her screams brought assistance. The man was apprehended and identified, and, after concealing him at Mattoon from a mob which threatened to lynch him, he was brought here Monday night and put in jail.

A fire alarm at 1 o'clock Tuesday morning aroused the people of this city. It was found that two hundred determined and heavily armed men from Mattoon had taken possession of the jail and all approaches thereto, as well as of the person of the sheriff. Resounding sledge hammer blows from the direction of the jail told what was going on.

Soon steel and iron yielded, and the stretch was at the mercy of the mob, which took him to the depot, and, after allowing him to deny the commission of the crime and to pray and sing about ten minutes, hanged him to the water tank until he was dead. The crowd then dispersed.

The sheriff and state's attorney tried in vain to stay the violence. All here condemn the act, but, although scarcely any concealment of identity was attempted, it is not likely that any prosecution will follow. Moore was married and the father of four children.
william-moore-charleston-1888-06-25.A21:
The Beauty of Mob Law.
MATTOON, Ills., July 2.—It has transpired since the lynching of W. A. Moore for alleged outrage on Mary A. Bumgardner, of Altamont, Ills., that the girl has an exceedingly bad reputation for purity, and also that she is suspected of arson. On account of the indignation of the citizens of Altamont at her and her mother's "goings on," and the suspicion of arson, she left Altamont and came to this city. Her story about Moore was contradictory and the people of this city are now, when it is too late indignant at the lynchers, and there is talk of prosecuting the "best citizens" of Charleston who are implicated in the affair.
william-moore-charleston-1888-06-25.A23:
Innocent Man Lynched.
ALTAMONT, ILL., June 28.—The people here are very indignant over the lynching of William Moore, at Charleston, Ill. The facts are that the girl, Mary A. Bumgardner, upon whom it is alleged the assault was made, lives some two miles from this place, and is not so very young, being about nineteen or twenty years old, and the people here who know her doubt the truth of her story. It is the general opinion that the people of Mattoon and vicinity were deceived, and, in acting hastily, have put to death an innocent man.

They Settled the Coon. William Moore, the colored man who assaulted Mary A. Bingardiner at Mattoon, Ill., was taken from jail at Charleston and lynched by masked men. Moore's victim is from Shelbyville, Ill., and is only sixteen years old. Forest Fires in Sweden. The town of Umea on the Delta of the Pothnia has been partially burned. The damage at Sundsvall and Umea will reach $5,000,000. Immense tracts of forest lands have been burned over. A drought has prevailed for a long time rendering the wood very dry. Business Trouble. H. Hodger, Son & Co., of New York, straw goods dealers, have failed. Liabilities, $60,000 to $100,000. White Caps Again at Work.
Word has just reached Vincennes, Ind., that a masked mob went to the house of William Shell, who lives at Hazelton, twelve miles south of that city, and demanded John Henry Kirk. They were apprised of his presence and at once ordered him to leave within the next forty-eight hours. Kirk arose from his bed, and, jumping through a window, took to flight. He was discovered and pursued, but he escaped their clutches. Mr. Shell had no firearms, but seizing an ax he marched out among the Whitecaps and cleared the yard of their hateful presence. These men recently located there from Crawford county, Indiana, the home of the night raiders, and it is believed they were followed. They are industrious men, and the action of the mob cannot be explained.

Hanged by a Mob.

Wallace Mitchell, the murderer who was brought back to Syracuse, Kansas, from Trinidad, Col., charged with the murder of a boy named Johnson, and the wounding of his father June 9, was taken from the sheriff by a body of armed men who led him to the spot where he committed the butchery and hanged him.

Hold to Answer.

Mrs. George Diggle, who was having her preliminary examination on the charge of poisoning her husband, was bound over to await the action of the grand jury. Diggle was a barber, who lived in Clarlon, Ia., and the case excited much comment.

Cleveland at a College,
President Cleveland, Secretaries Bayard and Vilas and several others attended the exercises of closing day at the University of Virginia,

Indian Wedding.

Charles Pecot and Miss Margaret LaFlesche were married recently at the home of the bride at Bancroft, Neb., by Roy. Mr. Copley, a Presbyterian missionary to the Omaha Indians. Miss LaFlesche is a sister of Mrs. Bright Eyes Tibbles and belongs to the Omaha tribe. She was well educated in one of the eastern colleges and has been teaching at the Omaha agency the past year. The bridegroom is a prominent Sioux Indian and he has been a leading teacher in the Sioux nation in Dakota territory for some time. The bride was beautifully dressed in trimmed cream colored albatross, trimmings of ribbons and surah silk to match. The wedding was a grand affair and the happy couple were the recipients of many beautiful and useful presents.

They Have no Value.

A case involving the value of pool tickets came up in the general session at New York a few days ago. Ward Vaughan and John Bindy stole pool tickets on the Jerome Park race on May 29 for which Charles A. Whittier paid $299. They were indicted for grand larceny, but before the trial opened their lawyers stated that the tickets had no value except what the pasteboard might be worth. He offered to accept a plea of petit larceny. The district attorney took the same view and the men were sentenced to thirty days in the penitentiary for petit larceny.

Wants the Earth.

It now transpires that Charles A. Pitcher, the absconding Providence bar' Miller, purchased a draft on a Parisian bank for 100,000 francs at the Mochelaga bank at Montreal. Another draft for £1,000 from Boston on an English bank was found on him. It is understood that he offers for $50,000 to give up $400,000 worth of securities. If the bank won't compromise, Pitcher says he will take a few years in prison and then come out and live luxuriously the rest of his life. He will fight the bank to the very last, and has engaged the best firm of lawyers in Montreal. Unfortunately for Pitcher, the Montreal Guarantee company was on his bond for $2,500, and he can be imprisoned for that, but he expresses no concern about this phase of the matter, saying the company would rather have its $2,500 than have him in prison, and says he can compromise it. He is wonderfully cool, and seems to have been making arrangements for a long while for flight.

Fatal Stunway.

Mrs. Griffith and Mrs. Dr. Walker, of Jamestown, Pa., started in a buggy to visit relatives in the country. Each lady

was accompanied by ner little daughter. While descending a hill the horse ran away. The Griffith child was instantly killed by being thrown from the buggy, and both ladies were fatally injured. The other child escaped uninjured.

Coal on Government Lands.

The house resumed the consideration of the Pacific land bill, and ayes and nays being taken on on Holman's amendment relating to the title of the government to coal mines found on public lands, but allowing entry men to mine such coal deposits until congress acts further in the matter.

Planing Mill Burned.

The extensive planing mill and box factory of Henry Ganes & Sons, at St. Louis, Mo., was destroyed by fire. Loss, $100,-000; insurance, $60,000.

Struck by a Steamer.

A small steam pleasure yacht was struck by a steamer one mile north of Newberry, N. J. There were eight persons in the small boat and two of them, Miss Anna Miller and the wife of Benjamin B. Ode'l, jr., were drowned. The rest were rescued.

Double Murder and Suicide.

Silas Robinson, of Minneapolis, Minn., shot his wife and her companion, Nick Weiss, and afterwards put three bullets in his own body. Robinson has been a shrunken, profligate fellow, and his wife left him about eight months ago. At the time of the shooting she was walking with Weiss.

Fire in a Fort.

Fire at Fort Apache, near Holbrook, A. T., destroyed the entire quartermaster's and commissary supplies. The estimated loss to the government, including buildings, is $100,000.

The Cardiff-Kiln Fight.

The long anticipated g'ove contest between the two bitter rivals for the championship of the northwest, Pat Killen and Patsey Cardiff, came off in the Washington rink at Minneapolis. Minn., a few days ago. The arrangements were for fifteen rounds, revised Marquis of Queensbury rules, for 75 and 25 per cent. of the gate money. Every seat in the house was occupied, the audience numbering 4,000 people. The battlemen had been trying hard and were in good condition. Killen tipped the scales at 185 pounds and Cardiff weighed 180. At the end of the fourth round Mr. Cardiff received a punch in the neck which caused him to retain a reclining position until after the expiration of the sixteen seconds allowed, and the fight was declared ended in favor of Killen.

Officials Beheaded.

Nine government officials at Seoul have been beheaded in the streets by the populace. Foreigners have taken refuge at consulates. The outbreak is attributed a Chinese instigation.

PROMINENT CITIZENS OF CHARLESTON, ILL., INCLUDING A FORMER MAYOR, AKE INDICTED.
CHICAGO, Oct. 10. — A dispatch from Charleston.
PROMINENT CITIZENS OF CHARLESTON, ILL., INCLUDING A FORMER MAYOR, ARE INDicted.
CHICAGO, Oct. 10.—A dispatch from Charleston, Ill., says: The indictment by the grand jury of nine citizens of Mattoon for the lynching of Wm. Moore on June 25, is the sensation here. Those under indictment are J. B. Beauchel, ex-mayor; H. M. O'Thoose, L. D. Weaver, John Byers, Wm. Kincaid, R. Brewer, N. H. Kickpatrick, Adopa Waaker, and En Aiers. The social standing of the d tenants and the unusual procedure have led to conjectures as to the result. Moore was arrested for alleged assault upon Mary Baumgartner, who, it is claimed, was of immoral character. At 10 o'clock at night one of the saenft's deputies received a telegram from Mattoon stating that a mob was being organized there for the purpose of lynching Moore. When the mob, to the number of 150 armed and masked men arrived at the jail, they found the iron doors fastened, but after much difficulty succeeded in breaking the barriers. They soon had the prisoner out and hanged him to a water tank half a mile from the jail.
william-moore-charleston-1888-06-25.A47:
Illinois Lyachers Indicted.
MATTOON, Ill., Oct. 8.—Nine indictments were returned by the special grand jury at Charleston Saturday, which was called August 4 to investigate the William Moore lynching. Three men who reside in this city have been placed under heavy bonds, two at least are known to have skipped while others have not yet been apprehended.
