In the senate Mr. Blair offered a resolution calling on the president for information as to the trial, conniction and execution for treason in Canada on Nov. 16, 1885, of Louis David Reil, who claimed to be a naturalized citizen of the United States.

John Fitzgerald, a boatman of Staten Island, and a Swedish woman named Anna, the cook at Hoffman Island, in attempting to go to the island from South Beach in a small boat, were blown out to sea by the strong northwest wind. The last seen of them was at 12:30 p. m., off the dumb beacon.

Pauline Lucca in an interview in Vienna, declared that the American tour in which she starts in November, will close her career on the stage, and that she had bought a villa at Omunden, where she intended to devote the rest of her life to the establishment of a school for opera singers.

Last July a negro named Moore was lynched at Charleston, Ill., for an alleged criminal assault upon a woman. Afterwards it was found that the man was innocent and that the mob had been guilty of murder. The grand jury indicted ten well-known citizens who are alleged to have taken part in the lynching. The men are among the best known in the county.

The fund opened by the Dublin Freeman to enable the Parnellitie members to defend themselves before the royal commission on the Times charges now amounts to £6,600 pounds. A special from Dublin says: The very Rev. Dr. Comerford has been appointed coadjutor to the Bishop of Kildare, and Leighlin by the Pope. Dr. Comerford is fifty-seven years old and a well-known Archaeologist.

Fatally Hurt by Running Against a Clothes-Line. Special to the Indianapolis Journal SHELBYVILLE, May 17.—Mrs. Lydia A. Hobbs, wife of Robert Hobbs, the well-known detective of Fairland, was out playing in a yard yesterday when she started to run, when her chin was caught by a clothes-line and she was thrown backward to the ground, inflicting injuries which will cause her death. It was reported this evening that she was dying. Murder at Spencer. Special to the Indiana Journal.
Special to the Indiana. Otis Journal.

SPENCER, May 17.—William Patrick, a frequenter of caloons, shot William Carter, bartender for T. Keen, at 10 o'clock last night. The ball passed through the right nipple. Carter lived but an hour. The men had a quarrel, which brought on the shooting. Patrick was conveyed to Ellettsville or Bloomington by friends during the night, and is still at large.

Minor Notes.

A hen at Waveland has adopted three kittens, which are being reared with her flock of chicks.

Mrs. Willis Canary, of Crawfordsville, is lying at the point of death, from the effects of taking a dose of oil of tanacetum with suicidal intent.

Small-pox is prevalent in the village of Pierceville, a few miles east of Seymour. Two deaths have occurred and many people have been exposed to the contagion. The County Health Board has quarantined the village.

Mrs. Joseph Jackson, of New Albany, whose husband was adjudged insane a few days ago, went crazy on Wednesday. Saturday night she was quite drunk and set fire to her house. The children requested that she be confined, and she was in the station-house when her mind gave way.

The Winchester Rock and Oil Company are sinking their seventh gas well. Rock was struck at a depth of 100 feet. They already have abundance of gas to supply the town from well No. 6, which is pronounced the equal of any of the Muncie wells, with a capacity for 1,000,000 feet per day.

While Mrs. Alex. Penn, her grown daughter, and young son were driving on the Killbuck pike, near Moonsville, Madison county, the horse took fright at a cow that suddenly crossed the road. The buggy was overturned and the boy fatally hurt. Mrs. Penn's arm was broken and the young lady's hip dislocated.

A large barn belonging to Fred Gardiner, who lives near Russellville, was set on fire Wednesday night, and was destroyed, with contents. Nine horses perished, among the number being four brood mares valued at $1,000. The barn also contained farming implements, hay, grain, etc. The loss will reach $3,000; no insurance.

The case of the State vs. Joseph Welling, charged with the murder of Henry Seibel, at Hamburg. Franklin county, in January last, was decided by the jury finding the defendant guilty of manslaughter and fixing his punishment at three years in the penitentiary at Jeffersonville. Welling is twenty-one years old. The verdict is considered very light.

An interesting discovery of mastodon bones has been made in Liberty towship, Howard county, by Isaac Murphy, who measured the tusks, unearthed at a depth of three feet, and found them to be nine feet long and eight inches in diameter at the base. The two tusks lay in the ground four feet apart. Mr. Murphy will organize a searching party to hunt for the skeleton of the huge animal. The discovery made is thought to be a valuable one.

"I AM GOING TO KILL YOU!"
A MIDNIGHT MURDER AT SPENCER.
Other Important State News—The Hon. Jason Brown Nominated for Congress
—Drowned in the Ohio—Scarlet Fever at Huntington.
SPENCER, May 17.—[Special.]—Our town is much excited to-day over the murder of William Carter by William Patrick. At last midnight Patrick entered Keene's saloon, where young Carter was the bartender, and demanded a glass of beer, which was given him. Patrick asked for a spoon, and young Carter dropped the spoon in the glass of beer, and in so doing some of the beer was thrown in Patrick's eye, when Patrick threw the glass at Carter, barely missing him. Young Carter said, "You might have killed me with the glass. Patrick replied: "I wouldn't care if I had." Patrick called for more beer, and Carter at first refused it, but afterward gave it to him. Patrick then remarked, "You are a 'demn' saloon-keeper any how, and I am going to kill you." As he said this he fired, the ball entering above the right nipple and lodging in Carter's spinal column. He lived only half an hour, but long enough to leave a dying statement of the affair. Patrick had been drinking during the night and was in the habit of getting drunk. He was considered a dangerous man when intoxicated. Carter was a quiet, inoffensive young man of good habits and was well thought of in the community. Carter's parents reside seven miles from town and are respected people. This makes three murders here in the last two years. The people are becoming tired of such crimes and will give the law aid in checking them. Prtrick is still at large but he will be arrested, as he is now hidden near by.

Senator Valentina Zimmerman Named for Congress by Tenth District Democrats.

HAMMOND, May 16.—[Special.]—The democratic congressional convention of the Tenth district met here to-day and nominated Senator Zimmerman, of Rochester, for congress. The attendance was very large, every county in the district being represented. Resolutions indorsing the national and state administrations and reaffirming the resolutions of the state platform were adopted; also one indorsing Senator Voorhees' recent speech in the U. S. senate and his rebuke of the Kansas home-guard. Great enthusiasm prevailed. The nomination is regarded as a strong one. Mr. Zimmerman is a native-born German, a practical, hard-working man. At the age of thirteen he learned the shoemaker's trade, and then traveled over large portions of Europe. In 1865, when he was twenty-one years old, he emigrated to America and settled at Rochester, Fulton county, where he has ever since resided. Following his trade of shoemaking in connection with a large boot and shoe store until 1878, he embarked in the sale of machinery and agricultural implements. He has served as councilman of Rochester and also secretary of the Fulton county agricultural and mechanical society. He has been the chairman of the Fulton county democratic central committee and has served one term of four years in the state senate. He enjoys a reputation at home for industry, integrity, sobriety and enterprise—a practical business man and popular with all classes.
